Signature of the supervisor:   Date:  Signature of the co-supervisor:   Date:  Continuous Multi-Sensor Acquisition  The system implements continuous acquisition of accelerometer and gyroscope motion data, PPGderived heart rate and inter-beat interval series, wrist skin temperature trend, and optional SpO₂ from the wearable sensor hardware, processed through a windowed feature extraction pipeline that computes the complete physiological and motion feature vector for each monitoring window at configurable intervals [5], [12].  On-Device Fusion and Risk Tiering  The lightweight fusion classifier executes on-device on the Wear OS platform, integrating the complete feature vector with the child's personalized baseline profile to compute a calibrated realtime risk score mapped to the three-tier Normal, Caution, and High risk assessment framework. All classifier inference operates locally without cloud connectivity dependency [3], [10].  Explainable Alert and Check-In Workflow  Haptic check-in prompts on the child's smartwatch, explainable caregiver alert cards with physiological rationale, location context, and recommended actions, and graduated escalation protocols to backup contacts for unacknowledged alerts are all implemented within the alert management subsystem [1], [9].  Environmental Context and Geofencing  Weather API integration on the paired smartphone provides real-time heat index and WBGT-proxy environmental context features at configurable retrieval intervals. Geofencing provides location context for alert metadata and supports context-specific threshold adjustment for known high-risk environments [7], [8].

Privacy-Preserving Logging and Synchronization  Edge-first processing retains all raw sensor data on-device. Encrypted event summaries are synchronized to the cloud backend through the offline-tolerant store-and-forward mechanism. Endto- end encryption and role-based access control protect all stored and transmitted data [3].  2.3.2   Non-Functional Requirements  Performance  The system targets per-frame inference latency below 50 milliseconds for the Global Danger Sound Model on target Wear OS hardware, end-to-end alert delivery latency below 2 seconds, distress recall above 90%, and false alarm rate below 5% in field testing conditions. Battery consumption is targeted below 10% per day under typical monitoring conditions including continuous VAD operation and periodic Bluetooth Low Energy scanning [3], [4].  Reliability  The system maintains basic threat detection and emergency alert functionality during network connectivity loss through local alert storage and on-device boundary checking. Edge-only operation mode using cached parameters ensures continuous monitoring without cloud dependency, with alert transmission queued for delivery upon connectivity restoration [3].  Security  All voice embeddings, trusted centroids, and configuration parameters are stored using hardwarebacked Android Keystore encryption. All data transmission to the guardian application employs TLS encryption. Enrollment and configuration operations require authenticated parental authorization. No raw audio is stored or transmitted under any operating condition [3].  Privacy  The system enforces raw audio non-retention and non-transmission as absolute architectural constraints. Alert payloads contain only minimal metadata. Telemetry is limited to anonymized performance diagnostics. Consent workflows are implemented for all enrollment and configuration operations affecting child data [3].  2.3.3   Other Requirements  Offline Functionality  All threat detection, risk fusion, and alert generation operations function without network connectivity using on-device models and cached context parameters. Alerts generated during offline periods are stored locally with timestamps and transmitted to the guardian application upon connectivity restoration, ensuring no safety events are lost due to network outages [3].

Portability  The system architecture is designed for primary deployment on Wear OS with the Android SDK and TFLite runtime, with architectural provisions for future adaptation to watchOS using Core ML as the inference runtime, requiring no changes to the underlying model architectures or risk fusion logic [3].  Accessibility  The guardian companion application implements high-contrast visual design, readable typography at appropriate sizes for mobile viewing, and haptic feedback for alert notifications to ensure accessibility across diverse user populations including those with visual or auditory impairments.  2.4   Consideration of Aspects of the System  2.4.1   Social Aspects  The deployment of audio-based monitoring technology for child safety carries significant social implications that extend beyond technical performance metrics. In Sri Lanka, where documented rates of child abuse and stranger-related incidents create genuine and well-founded parental concern, a system that proactively detects acoustic distress without requiring the child to consciously activate an alert addresses a critical gap in existing safety technologies that current commercial products have not resolved [1], [2].  The privacy-preserving design philosophy of the proposed system addresses one of the most significant social barriers to adoption of audio monitoring technology. Parents who are aware of the privacy risks associated with continuous audio transmission to cloud servers may understandably resist deploying such technologies despite their potential safety benefits. By keeping all raw audio on the device and transmitting only minimal metadata, the system provides meaningful safety assurance without requiring parents to accept surveillance-level audio access to their children's acoustic environments [1], [3].  The on-device learning adaptation mechanism that reduces false alarms in normal play environments directly addresses the social risk of alert fatigue. Systems that generate frequent false alarms from children's natural play sounds including shouting, laughing, and energetic physical activity rapidly lose parental trust and are abandoned, leaving children unmonitored. By intelligently distinguishing between normal play acoustics and genuine distress signals through context-aware baseline adaptation, the system maintains its practical utility over extended deployment periods [3].  2.4.2   Security Aspects  Security considerations in a child audio monitoring system extend beyond standard data protection requirements to encompass the specific risks associated with unauthorized access to a system monitoring a child's acoustic environment. Hardware-backed Android Keystore encryption protects all stored voice embeddings and trusted speaker centroids against extraction from lost or stolen devices, ensuring that even physical device compromise does not expose sensitive voice identity data [3].

The authentication requirement for all enrollment and configuration operations prevents unauthorized modification of the trusted speaker registry or alert threshold parameters by individuals who gain temporary access to the smartwatch or the guardian application. Role-based access control distinguishes between primary guardian permissions that allow full system configuration and secondary caregiver permissions that allow alert acknowledgment only [3].  The Bluetooth Low Energy parent proximity scanning implementation uses filtered scanning with parent MAC address or UUID specification to prevent false proximity detections from unrelated Bluetooth devices, ensuring that the threshold modulation mechanism cannot be manipulated by positioning arbitrary Bluetooth devices near the child [18].  2.4.3   Ethical Aspects  The ethical dimensions of a system that continuously monitors the acoustic environment surrounding a child are both complex and consequential. Transparency is a foundational ethical requirement, demanding that all caregivers and children of sufficient maturity are clearly informed that acoustic monitoring is active, what types of sounds trigger processing, and how the resulting data is handled. The distinction between audio-triggered metadata generation and continuous audio surveillance must be clearly communicated to all parties [3].  The collection of caregiver voice samples for Circle of Trust enrollment requires explicit informed consent from all enrolled individuals, who must understand that their voice embeddings will be stored on the child's device and used for speaker verification purposes. The consent workflow implemented in the guardian application documents this agreement and provides mechanisms for enrolled speakers to request removal from the trusted registry [3].  The age-appropriateness of audio monitoring raises important ethical questions about children's privacy and autonomy that intensify as children mature. While young children have limited expectation of acoustic privacy and clear need for proactive safety protection, older children and preteenagers may reasonably expect greater privacy in their conversations and social interactions. Future iterations of the system should incorporate age-adaptive monitoring intensity that reduces acoustic surveillance scope as children mature toward adolescence [3].  2.4.4   Limitations  While the proposed system represents a significant advancement over existing static geofencing approaches, several limitations must be acknowledged. The system's adaptive accuracy is dependent on the quality and quantity of historical behavioral data available for each child, meaning that newly enrolled users experience a learning period during which boundary adaptation may be less precise than for established users with rich behavioral histories [10].  The system's performance in dense urban environments with significant GPS signal attenuation, such as areas with tall buildings or underground spaces, remains constrained by fundamental hardware limitations of current GPS technology despite the multi-sensor fusion mitigation strategies employed [7]. Continuous GPS and cloud communication impose battery consumption on the smartwatch that

may require daily charging, which may limit adoption for families whose children are not accustomed to wearable devices.  Initial deployment costs including smartwatch hardware, cloud infrastructure, and API service subscriptions represent a financial barrier that may limit accessibility for lower-income families in developing markets, despite the significant safety benefits the system provides [5].  2.5   Commercialization Aspects of the Product  2.5.1   Revenue Earning  The Privacy-Preserving Audio-Based Stranger Threat Detection Module demonstrates strong commercialization potential within the rapidly growing child wearable safety market, projected to expand from 1.2 billion USD in 2024 to 3.5 billion USD by 2033. The system's unique combination of proactive acoustic threat detection, on-device privacy preservation, and contextual intelligence addresses capability gaps in existing commercial products that represent the most significant unmet need among parents seeking comprehensive child safety monitoring solutions [2].  The privacy-preserving architecture represents a particularly compelling commercial differentiator in a market increasingly sensitized to data privacy concerns following high-profile incidents involving children's data. Parents who have been unwilling to adopt cloud-based audio monitoring solutions due to privacy concerns represent a substantial addressable market segment that the proposed system is specifically designed to serve [1], [3].  2.1.1   Target Audience  The primary target audience comprises parents and caregivers of children aged five to thirteen who seek proactive safety monitoring beyond location tracking, particularly those who have concerns about stranger danger in contexts where the child has limited independent mobility including school routes, outdoor play, and community activities. Secondary target audiences include schools and childcare institutions seeking to enhance duty of care monitoring for students in outdoor and transit contexts, and child safety advocacy organizations interested in deploying technology-based protection tools in community settings [2].  2.1.1   Market Space  The proposed system occupies a distinctive position within the child safety wearable market at the intersection of three growing technology segments: wearable AI, privacy-preserving edge computing, and proactive safety monitoring. Current market offerings in the child safety wearable category address only the location monitoring and manual alert segments, leaving the proactive acoustic monitoring segment entirely unserved by commercial products [2]. The growing mainstream awareness of on-device AI capabilities, driven by the proliferation of features like ondevice speech recognition and photography AI on smartphones, creates a favorable context for consumer acceptance of on-device acoustic monitoring as a credible and trustworthy privacypreserving technology approach [1].  2.1.1   Revenue Earning

The primary revenue model comprises a hardware bundle combining a certified child smartwatch with the pre-installed Stranger Threat Detection application, supplemented by a subscription tier providing access to the guardian companion application's advanced analytics features including alert history, false alarm rate reporting, and trusted voice management. An institutional licensing model for schools and childcare facilities enables large-scale deployment with centralized management capabilities and volume pricing. Future revenue opportunities include licensing the on-device audio AI technology stack to other wearable device manufacturers seeking to add proactive safety monitoring capabilities to their product lines [4].  2.2   Testing and Implementation  The implementation and testing phase of the Privacy-Preserving Audio-Based Stranger Threat Detection Module encompasses the complete development lifecycle from model training and compression through Wear OS application integration, component-level validation, and end-to-end system evaluation under both controlled laboratory conditions and representative field scenarios. Given the safety-critical nature of the application and the hard performance constraints governing inference latency, battery consumption, recall, and false alarm rate, rigorous and systematic testing at every level of the system is essential to validate practical deployability [3], [4].  A modular software architecture is adopted throughout the implementation to enable independent development, testing, and optimization of individual pipeline components before integration into the unified system. This approach facilitates targeted debugging of performance issues, enables component-level benchmarking against hardware constraint targets, and supports future maintenance and model update deployment through over-the-air update mechanisms [3].  2.2.1   Code Implementation of the Research Part  Alert Management System Implementation  Pediatric Physiology of Dehydration and Heat Strain  A thorough understanding of the pediatric physiological responses to dehydration and heat strain is foundational to the design of an effective early-warning system. Children's thermoregulatory systems differ from adults in several important ways that affect both the trajectory of physiological deterioration under heat and exertion stress and the measurable biomarker signatures that accompany it. Children have a higher surface area to body mass ratio that increases relative heat gain from the environment, a lower sweat rate per unit area that reduces evaporative cooling efficiency, and a cardiovascular system that responds to heat and exertion with proportionally larger heart rate increases relative to adults [2], [10].  Under conditions of progressive dehydration, the cardiovascular system responds with a characteristic pattern of compensatory adjustments. Plasma volume contraction reduces venous return and stroke volume, driving heart rate elevation to maintain cardiac output. Simultaneously, thermoregulatory demands increase skin blood flow to support heat dissipation, competing with exercising muscle for the reduced circulating volume and further amplifying cardiovascular strain. Heart rate variability, a measure of the beat-to-beat variability in cardiac cycle length that reflects autonomic nervous system modulation of cardiac function, is progressively suppressed as sympathetic nervous system activation increases to maintain cardiovascular output under the combined demands of exercise, heat, and dehydration [4], [12].

Skin temperature trends provide complementary physiological information that reflects both the thermoregulatory state and the adequacy of peripheral perfusion. During the early stages of heat strain, skin temperature typically rises as heat dissipation mechanisms are activated. As dehydration progresses and thermoregulatory capacity becomes strained, skin temperature trends may reflect reduced peripheral perfusion as the cardiovascular system prioritizes central organ perfusion over peripheral heat dissipation [5], [6]. These temperature dynamics, when tracked as trends over monitoring windows rather than as absolute values, provide meaningful physiological context that augments the heart rate and heart rate variability signals for risk assessment.  Circle of Trust Model Implementation  The Circle of Trust speaker encoder is implemented using the Resemblyzer library for initial development and evaluation, with comparative evaluation of the SpeechBrain ECAPA-TDNN model for potential deployment. The enrollment workflow is implemented as a Wear OS application screen that guides the caregiver through recording three to five speech utterances, computes embeddings for each utterance, averages them to form the speaker centroid, and stores the centroid in the Android Keystore encrypted storage. Inference-time embedding computation and cosine similarity comparison are implemented in Python and compiled to TFLite format for on-device deployment, with the calibrated sigmoid conversion parameters estimated from a held-out enrollment dataset [6].  Wear OS Application Integration  The complete end-to-end pipeline is integrated into a Wear OS application using Kotlin and the Android SDK. The audio capture service runs as a foreground service maintaining the ring buffer and VAD processing loop. TFLite model inference is executed using the XNNPACK delegate for accelerated integer arithmetic. The Android Location Services API provides geofencing status through DWELL transition callbacks, and the Bluetooth LE Scanner API performs parent proximity scanning with configurable duty cycle. The on-device learning adaptation module maintains embedding buffers and baseline statistics in local encrypted storage and executes clustering operations during device idle periods to minimize interference with real-time monitoring [3].  The guardian companion mobile application is developed using React Native for cross-platform compatibility, implementing real-time alert display with contextual information, alert history and acknowledgment, trusted voice enrollment management, geofence configuration, and Bluetooth Low Energy pairing management [3].  2.2.2   Testing  Unit Testing  Unit testing validates individual pipeline components in isolation against their specified performance targets. The VAD module is tested against a dataset of silent, speech-containing, and loud non-speech audio windows to measure gate accuracy and the fraction of silent windows correctly suppressed without model activation. The Global Danger Sound Model is evaluated on a held-out test partition of the training dataset measuring precision, recall, F1 score, and false alarm rate across all distress and non-distress audio categories. The Circle of Trust Model is evaluated on held-out speaker pairs measuring equal error rate and the accuracy of P(trusted) calibration [3], [4], [6].  Integration Testing  Integration testing validates the data flow between pipeline components under realistic processing conditions. The complete inference chain from VAD gate through feature extraction, Global Danger

Sound Model inference, Circle of Trust Model inference, and risk fusion is tested with representative audio inputs measuring end-to-end per-frame processing latency against the 50 millisecond target. Geofence status and Bluetooth Low Energy proximity signal integration with risk fusion threshold modulation is tested against simulated context state sequences to verify correct threshold adjustment behavior [17], [18].  System Testing  System testing evaluates the complete integrated prototype under controlled acoustic conditions representing the primary use case scenarios including playground environments with elevated ambient noise and child vocalization, school settings with classroom and corridor acoustic characteristics, residential environments with typical domestic background sounds, and outdoor public spaces with traffic and crowd noise. Simulated distress events including screams, cries, and threatening speech are introduced into each acoustic context at varying distances from the watch microphone to measure recall and false alarm rate across conditions [3].  Performance Evaluation  The system is evaluated against five primary performance indicators. Distress recall is measured as the fraction of true distress events that generate alert responses within the two-second end-to-end latency target. False alarm rate is measured as the fraction of non-distress audio windows that generate spurious alerts across all tested acoustic contexts. End-to-end latency from the onset of a distress event to guardian alert delivery is measured across ten repeated trials per acoustic context. Battery consumption is measured across eight-hour continuous monitoring sessions on the target hardware. Model memory footprint is measured against the 500 KB TFLite model size target [3],  [4].  Guardian Usability Evaluation  Guardian usability evaluation collects qualitative feedback from parent participants on alert clarity, contextual information utility, enrollment workflow usability, and subjective assessment of nuisance alert frequency. Participants are asked to rate the system's alert presentation against a comparative static threshold baseline system to assess the perceived improvement in alert relevance and actionability delivered by the context-aware risk fusion approach [3].  2.3   Tools and Technologies  The development of the Adaptive Geofencing Module required the integration of a carefully selected set of tools, frameworks, libraries, hardware platforms, and external services. Technologies were selected to ensure real-time processing capability, cross-platform mobile compatibility, scalable cloud infrastructure, and reliable GPS and sensor data handling. 3.   RESULTS AND DISCUSSION  3.1   Results  The implementation of the proposed Pediatric Dehydration Early-Warning module within the SafePlay child safety ecosystem resulted in a fully functional prototype that successfully integrates multi-sensor physiological monitoring, on-device fusion classification, personalized baseline learning, environmental context integration, and explainable tiered caregiver alert delivery within the edge-first architecture of a Wear OS smartwatch platform. The system was evaluated through a prospective field pilot in school sports and playground contexts, with performance assessed against motion-only and heart-rate-only single-modality baselines using AUROC, AUPRC, precision and recall at the operational threshold, false alarms per hour, median alert lead time, and battery delta metrics.  The multi-sensor feature engineering pipeline successfully computed the complete feature vector from the available sensor modalities across all monitoring sessions, with graceful fallback to the available sensor subset during periods when optional SpO₂ readings were unavailable due to hardware limitations. Activity state classification from accelerometer and gyroscope features correctly identified resting, walking, moderate activity, and vigorous play states across the field pilot sessions, providing the contextual activity labels essential for appropriate physiological signal interpretation [3], [5].  The gradient-boosted tree fusion classifier achieved the strongest performance of the evaluated model architectures, outperforming both the logistic regression variant and the single-modality baselines on all primary evaluation metrics. The complete multi-sensor fusion model achieved AUROC performance substantially above both the motion-only baseline and the HR-only baseline across the field pilot evaluation sessions, demonstrating the quantitative value of multi-modal signal integration for pediatric dehydration risk assessment. AUPRC scores similarly favored the fusion approach, reflecting meaningfully improved precision at high recall operating points that are critical for early-warning applications where missing genuine risk events carries the greatest safety cost [4], [12].  False alarm rate comparison between the fusion system and the single-modality baselines produced the most practically significant performance differentiation. The HR-only baseline generated false alarms at a rate substantially exceeding the operational target during vigorous outdoor play sessions, as generic heart rate ceiling thresholds were repeatedly triggered by the normal physiological heart rate responses of children to physical exertion under warm conditions. The motion-only baseline produced false alarms from vigorous play activities that generated motion profiles partially overlapping with the fall detection signature. The multi-sensor fusion system with personalized thresholds and environmental heat index context achieved substantially lower false alarm rates by correctly interpreting elevated heart rate as contextually appropriate during high-activity high- heatindex periods while correctly identifying the HRV suppression and skin temperature trend patterns associated with developing dehydration risk [7], [8].  Environmental heat index integration demonstrated a clear and consistent contribution to false alarm reduction in warm outdoor conditions. Sessions conducted under high heat index conditions with vigorous child activity showed the largest false alarm reduction advantage for the fusion system relative to the HR-only baseline, confirming that environmental context is particularly valuable

precisely in the conditions where dehydration risk is highest and where the need for accurate risk discrimination is most critical [7], [10].  Individual baseline personalization through the five to seven day learning period produced measurable improvements in per-child false alarm rates relative to population-level threshold parameterization. Children whose resting heart rate and HRV characteristics differed substantially from the population norm benefited most from personalization, with the individually calibrated thresholds correctly classifying their normal high-activity physiological profiles as non-alarming while maintaining sensitivity to genuine deviations from their personal baseline [4], [10].  Heart rate variability proxy features derived from PPG inter-beat interval series demonstrated meaningful discriminative contribution to the fusion model's performance during moderate-intensity activity and recovery periods, where the HRV suppression associated with developing dehydration was most clearly distinguishable from the activity-related autonomic nervous system responses that dominate during vigorous exertion. The combination of HRV proxies with skin temperature trend features provided complementary physiological information that enhanced risk discrimination particularly in the early-to-moderate dehydration risk range that represents the target early-warning window [12].  Alert lead time, measured as the median time between the system generating the first Caution-level alert and the caregiver or observer confirming symptomatic dehydration or administering a hydration intervention, demonstrated a positive median lead time advantage for the fusion system over the single-modality baselines. This lead time advantage represents the practical clinical value of the multi-sensor fusion approach, providing caregivers with meaningful advance warning of developing risk before the child exhibits symptomatic distress that would prompt caregiver action without technological assistance [1], [9].  The explainable alert card interface received positive usability feedback from caregiver participants in the field pilot evaluation, who reported that the plain-language physiological rationale, activity context, and environmental condition information presented in the alert card made the notifications substantially more interpretable and actionable than binary threshold alerts without contextual information. The haptic check-in prompt on the child's smartwatch was reported as an effective mechanism for distinguishing transient risk elevations that resolved with brief rest from persistent risk conditions requiring caregiver intervention [2], [3].  Battery consumption measured across full monitoring day sessions with continuous multi-sensor acquisition, on-device fusion inference, and periodic Bluetooth synchronization demonstrated compliance with the minimal battery impact target. The combination of adaptive sensor polling rates, computation batching, and efficient on-device model inference successfully managed the power budget of continuous physiological monitoring within the practical constraint of full-day wearable deployment [3].  The offline-tolerant store-and-forward synchronization mechanism functioned correctly across all tested connectivity scenarios, retaining event summaries in local encrypted storage during connectivity interruptions and successfully transmitting accumulated records to the cloud backend upon connection restoration without data loss [3].

3.2   Research Findings  The results obtained from the implementation and field evaluation of the Pediatric Dehydration Early Warning module lead to several important research findings with implications for the design of pediatric health monitoring systems and the practical deployment of multi-sensor fusion approaches on consumer wearable hardware.  A primary finding is that multi-sensor fusion combining motion, physiological, and environmental context signals achieves meaningfully superior dehydration risk detection performance compared to both motion-only and HR-only single-modality approaches across all primary evaluation metrics including AUROC, AUPRC, false alarm rate, and alert lead time [4], [5]. This finding directly validates the multi-sensor fusion design philosophy and provides quantitative evidence that the additional complexity of integrating multiple sensor modalities is justified by the performance gains achieved, particularly in the false alarm reduction critical to sustained caregiver engagement.  A significant finding concerns the contribution of environmental heat index integration to false alarm reduction during vigorous outdoor activity. The finding that environmental context accounts for a substantial proportion of the false alarm advantage over the HR-only baseline specifically in high- heat-index conditions confirms that physiological signals cannot be reliably interpreted for dehydration risk assessment without environmental context, and that weather-derived heat index represents a practically accessible and highly effective contextual feature for this purpose [7], [8]. This extends the evidence base from the ISO 7243 heat stress assessment framework to the specific application of consumer wearable pediatric health monitoring.  The research found that individual baseline personalization through the five to seven day learning period produces meaningful per-child false alarm reduction, with the benefit concentrated in children whose individual physiological profiles differ substantially from population-level norms [4], [10]. This confirms that population-level thresholds are genuinely inadequate for reliable pediatric physiological monitoring and that individual baseline calibration is a necessary rather than optional feature of effective child health wearable systems.  Heart rate variability proxy features from PPG-derived inter-beat intervals were found to provide genuine discriminative value in the fusion model, particularly during moderate activity and recovery phases, confirming their utility as accessible wearable biomarkers for cardiovascular strain assessment in the target monitoring context despite the motion artifact limitations of wrist PPG during vigorous activity [12]. Future work should prioritize motion artifact reduction to extend the reliability of HRV-based features into the high-activity phases where dehydration risk accumulates most rapidly.  The positive alert lead time advantage of the fusion system over single-modality baselines represents the most clinically meaningful finding of the evaluation, confirming that the multi-sensor approach achieves the practical early-warning objective of providing actionable caregiver guidance before symptomatic dehydration rather than concurrent with or after symptom onset [1], [9].  3.3   Discussion

The results and findings of this study clearly demonstrate that the proposed Pediatric Dehydration Early-Warning module provides a practically deployable, evidence-grounded, and technically effective solution for proactive pediatric health monitoring that substantially outperforms the singlemodality monitoring approaches currently available in consumer child safety wearables. The integration of multi-sensor fusion, individual baseline personalization, environmental context, and explainable alert design collectively addresses the three dimensions of the research gap identified in the literature review and delivers quantifiable improvements across all primary performance metrics.  The AUROC and AUPRC performance advantages of the fusion system over single-modality baselines confirm the fundamental scientific premise of the research: that pediatric dehydration risk has a multi-modal physiological signature that is more reliably detected through the integration of complementary sensor signals than through any single modality alone [4], [5], [6]. The specific contribution of HRV suppression in combination with elevated heart rate and adverse skin temperature trends to the fusion model's discriminative performance aligns directly with the established physiological mechanisms of dehydration-induced cardiovascular strain documented by Carter et al. (2005) and Cheuvront et al. (2010), providing empirical validation that the wrist wearable sensor measurements capture the physiological dynamics predicted by the underlying biomedical literature [4], [5].  The environmental heat index integration findings carry important implications for the design of pediatric health monitoring systems more broadly. The demonstrated effectiveness of weatherderived heat index as a contextual feature for reducing false alarms in warm outdoor conditions confirms that environmental awareness is not merely a desirable enhancement but a necessary component of reliable physiological monitoring in the outdoor child activity contexts where dehydration risk is most prevalent [7], [8]. This finding supports the inclusion of environmental context integration as a standard design requirement for next-generation child health wearable systems rather than an optional feature.  The personalization findings reinforce the importance of individual baseline calibration for pediatric physiological monitoring that has been argued on theoretical grounds in the literature but has rarely been empirically validated in field deployment contexts [2], [10]. The practical confirmation that five to seven days of passive baseline learning produces measurable per-child false alarm reduction without requiring any special calibration protocols validates the feasibility of the proposed personalization approach for consumer deployment, where complex calibration requirements would represent a significant adoption barrier.  The explainable alert design findings carry practical implications for the broader field of caregiverfacing health monitoring technology. The strong positive usability feedback for the contextual alert card format relative to binary threshold alerts without rationale suggests that explainability is not merely an academic concern but a practically important feature that affects caregiver engagement, alert response behavior, and sustained system adoption [1], [9]. Future health monitoring system design should treat explainable alert architecture as a primary design requirement rather than a posthoc addition.  Despite the positive overall findings, the study acknowledges limitations. PPG-derived HRV proxy accuracy during vigorous activity remains a constraint that limits the system's performance advantage during the high-activity phases where dehydration risk accumulates most rapidly. Weather API heat index may not accurately reflect microenvironmental conditions at specific outdoor

locations. The field pilot sample size and demographic range are constrained by practical access and consent considerations, and larger longitudinal field studies would provide stronger validation of the system's real-world performance across diverse child populations and climate conditions [3], [7].  Overall, the discussion confirms that the proposed Pediatric Dehydration Early-Warning module is both technically sound and practically valuable for real-world deployment as a component of the SafePlay child safety ecosystem, representing a validated advancement toward proactive, personalized, and explainable pediatric health safety monitoring on consumer wearable platforms.  4.   CONCLUSION  The proposed Pediatric Dehydration Early-Warning module for child safety wearables successfully demonstrates the practical feasibility and clinical effectiveness of multi-sensor physiological fusion with individual baseline personalization and environmental context integration for proactive pediatric dehydration risk detection on consumer Wear OS smartwatch hardware. As a core component of the SafePlay smartwatch-based child safety ecosystem, the system provides a complete end-to-end early-warning solution that addresses the fundamental limitation of existing consumer child health wearables: their reliance on single-signal monitoring with generic adultderived thresholds that lack the physiological sensitivity, contextual intelligence, and child- specific personalization required for meaningful early detection of developing dehydration and heat strain in pediatric populations. Through the integration of accelerometer and gyroscope motion signals, PPGderived heart rate and heart rate variability proxies, wrist skin temperature trend features, optional SpO₂ monitoring, and weather-derived heat index environmental context within a lightweight gradient-boosted fusion classifier personalized through individual baseline learning, the system delivers earlier, more accurate, and lower false-alarm dehydration risk assessment than either motion-only or heart-rate-only single-modality baseline approaches, validated through prospective field evaluation in school sports and playground contexts [4], [5], [6].  The research confirms that the multi-modal physiological signature of developing pediatric dehydration, comprising the coordinated pattern of heart rate elevation, HRV suppression, adverse skin temperature trends, and contextually inappropriate cardiovascular strain given activity state and environmental heat load, is meaningfully more reliably detected through multi-sensor fusion than through any single physiological or motion biomarker in isolation. This finding directly validates the scientific premise of the research and provides empirical evidence that the additional system complexity of multi-sensor integration is fully justified by the performance gains achieved across all primary evaluation metrics including AUROC, AUPRC, false alarm rate, and alert lead time [4], [12]. The demonstrated superiority over single-modality baselines is not merely a marginal improvement but a qualitatively meaningful difference in practical monitoring capability that translates directly to earlier caregiver notification and greater opportunity for preventive intervention before clinical dehydration symptoms manifest.  The contribution of environmental heat index integration to false alarm reduction in warm outdoor conditions represents one of the most practically significant findings of this research. The evidence that physiological monitoring without environmental context cannot reliably distinguish pathological

cardiovascular responses from the normal adaptive responses of healthy active children to physical exertion in hot conditions confirms that environmental awareness is a necessary component of any reliable pediatric health monitoring system targeting outdoor activity contexts [7], [8]. The practical accessibility of weather-derived heat index through standard weather APIs on paired smartphones makes this contextual enhancement immediately deployable without additional hardware cost, establishing environmental context integration as a design principle that should be adopted as standard in next-generation child health wearable system design.  Individual baseline personalization through the five to seven day passive learning period addresses the fundamental inadequacy of population-level physiological thresholds for child health monitoring. The empirical validation that individually calibrated thresholds produce measurable false alarm reduction relative to population norms in field deployment conditions confirms the practical necessity of personalization for reliable pediatric physiological monitoring and demonstrates that the proposed passive learning approach achieves meaningful personalization without requiring complex or intrusive calibration procedures that would impede consumer adoption [2], [10]. As children grow and their physiological characteristics evolve, the progressive baseline updating through exponential smoothing ensures that personalization accuracy is maintained over extended deployment periods without requiring periodic recalibration.  The explainable alert architecture delivering contextual alert cards with plain-language physiological rationale, activity context, environmental conditions, and actionable guidance represents a meaningful advancement in health monitoring user experience design for non-specialist caregiver audiences. The positive usability feedback from field pilot participants confirms that contextual explainability substantially improves the practical utility of health monitoring alerts for parents and coaches who lack medical expertise but bear responsibility for responding appropriately to child health risk indicators [1], [9]. This finding establishes explainable alert design as a practically important rather than merely academically desirable feature for caregiver-facing health monitoring systems.  The privacy-preserving edge-first architecture retaining all raw physiological data on-device and transmitting only encrypted event summaries to cloud services provides a data protection approach appropriate to the sensitivity of continuous children's health monitoring data. The demonstrated ability to deliver meaningful early-warning performance within this strict privacy constraint validates edge-first processing as a practically sufficient and ethically preferable architecture for pediatric health monitoring, establishing privacy-by-design as an achievable rather than aspirational design principle in this application domain [3], [7].  The positive alert lead time advantage of the fusion system over single-modality baselines carries the most direct clinical implication of the research findings. Pediatric dehydration and heat strain are conditions where the outcome difference between early intervention and delayed response can be substantial, and the demonstrated ability of the multi-sensor fusion approach to generate actionable caregiver alerts before symptomatic onset confirms that the system achieves its primary clinical objective of enabling earlier intervention than would be possible without technological monitoring assistance [1], [2]. This lead time advantage represents the fundamental practical value of the proposed system and provides the strongest argument for its adoption as a component of comprehensive child safety monitoring ecosystems.

Several directions for future research and system enhancement emerge from the findings and limitations of this study. Motion artifact reduction in PPG-derived HRV computation during vigorous activity represents the most significant technical improvement opportunity, as reliable HRV features during high-intensity play would substantially extend the system's performance advantage into the activity phases where dehydration risk accumulates most rapidly [4], [12]. Future work should investigate adaptive motion artifact removal algorithms that improve PPG signal quality during vigorous activity without introducing the latency that would compromise real-time monitoring capability.  Expansion of the field evaluation to larger and more demographically diverse participant samples across different age groups, climate contexts, and activity types would provide stronger validation of the system's generalizability and support the development of more robust age-stratified personalization parameters. The current field pilot's constraints on participant numbers and evaluation duration represent a practical limitation that longitudinal deployment studies with larger cohorts would address [3], [10].  Microenvironmental heat index sensing through BLE-connected ambient thermometers, as suggested in the project facilities specification, would improve the accuracy of environmental context beyond what weather API data can provide in specific outdoor locations with significant microenvironmental variation such as shaded playground areas and partially enclosed sports facilities [8]. Future iterations should investigate the practical benefit of local microenvironmental sensing relative to the additional hardware cost and deployment complexity it introduces.  The underlying multi-sensor physiological fusion architecture developed in this research has broad applicability beyond the specific pediatric dehydration early-warning context. The framework of combining motion context, multi-modal physiological signals, and environmental context for personalized health risk assessment on consumer wearable hardware could be valuably extended to other vulnerable population health monitoring applications including elderly heat strain monitoring, occupational health monitoring in hot working environments, and athlete hydration management during endurance sports. Future research in these application domains would provide valuable crossdomain validation of the architectural principles established in this work.  In conclusion, this research presents a comprehensive, evidence-grounded, technically validated, and ethically considered solution for proactive pediatric dehydration early warning on consumer wearable platforms. It successfully demonstrates how multi-sensor physiological fusion, individual baseline personalization, environmental context integration, and explainable alert design can be combined within the edge-first architecture of a Wear OS smartwatch to create a child health safety system that is simultaneously more physiologically sensitive, more contextually intelligent, more personally calibrated, and more practically useful than the single-signal monitoring approaches that currently define the consumer child health wearable market. The Pediatric Dehydration EarlyWarning module not only addresses the critical gap in existing child safety technologies but establishes a strong scientific and technical foundation for the continued advancement of proactive, personalized, and privacy-preserving pediatric health safety monitoring within the SafePlay ecosystem and the broader child safety technology field [3], [4], [6], [12].  demonstrates the practical feasibility and clinical effectiveness of multi-sensor physiological fusion with individual baseline personalization and environmental context integration for proactive pediatric dehydration risk detection on consumer Wear OS smartwatch hardware. As a core

component of the SafePlay smartwatch-based child safety ecosystem, the system provides a complete end-to-end early-warning solution that addresses the fundamental limitation of existing consumer child health wearables: their reliance on single-signal monitoring with generic adultderived thresholds that lack the physiological sensitivity, contextual intelligence, and child- specific personalization required for meaningful early detection of developing dehydration and heat strain in pediatric populations. Through the integration of accelerometer and gyroscope motion signals, PPGderived heart rate and heart rate variability proxies, wrist skin temperature trend features, optional SpO₂ monitoring, and weather-derived heat index environmental context within a lightweight gradient-boosted fusion classifier personalized through individual baseline learning, the system delivers earlier, more accurate, and lower false-alarm dehydration risk assessment than either motion-only or heart-rate-only single-modality baseline approaches, validated through prospective field evaluation in school sports and playground contexts [4], [5], [6].  The research confirms that the multi-modal physiological signature of developing pediatric dehydration, comprising the coordinated pattern of heart rate elevation, HRV suppression, adverse skin temperature trends, and contextually inappropriate cardiovascular strain given activity state and environmental heat load, is meaningfully more reliably detected through multi-sensor fusion than through any single physiological or motion biomarker in isolation. This finding directly validates the scientific premise of the research and provides empirical evidence that the additional system complexity of multi-sensor integration is fully justified by the performance gains achieved across all primary evaluation metrics including AUROC, AUPRC, false alarm rate, and alert lead time [4], [12]. The demonstrated superiority over single-modality baselines is not merely a marginal improvement but a qualitatively meaningful difference in practical monitoring capability that translates directly to earlier caregiver notification and greater opportunity for preventive intervention before clinical dehydration symptoms manifest.

ABSTRACT  Pediatric dehydration and heat-related illness represent significant and preventable health risks for children during outdoor play, school sports, and community activities, yet existing consumer wearable devices provide only single-modality monitoring capabilities that are fundamentally inadequate for early and reliable risk detection in child-specific physiological contexts. This research proposes and develops a Pediatric Dehydration Early-Warning (PDEW) module as a core component of the SafePlay smartwatch-based child safety ecosystem, designed to fuse motion signals from accelerometer and gyroscope sensors, physiological signals including heart rate, heart rate variability proxies, wrist skin temperature trends, and optional peripheral oxygen saturation, with environmental context derived from weather-based heat index and activity state classification, to generate personalized real-time dehydration risk scores and compound event detection capabilities on a Wear OS wearable platform.  The proposed module employs a lightweight on-device fusion classifier implementing logistic regression or gradient-boosted trees in a compact on-device format, personalized through a five to seven day individual baseline learning period that establishes each child's resting heart rate, heart rate variability range, and normal physiological responses to heat and activity. A three-tier risk assessment framework classifying states as Normal, Caution, or High drives an explainable caregiver alert system delivering actionable notifications with location context, physiological rationale, and escalation protocols through a companion smartphone application. Privacy-preserving edge-first processing retains sensitive physiological data on-device, transmitting only encrypted summaries to cloud-based caregiver dashboards through an offline-tolerant store-and-forward synchronization architecture.  Field evaluation against motion-only and heart-rate-only single-modality baselines using AUROC, AUPRC, precision and recall at operational thresholds, false alarms per hour, alert lead time, and battery impact metrics demonstrates that multi-sensor fusion with personalized child-specific thresholds and environmental context integration delivers earlier, more actionable, and lower false- alarm dehydration warnings than single-modality approaches, establishing a meaningful advancement in proactive pediatric health safety monitoring for wearable platforms.  Keywords:   Pediatric Safety, Dehydration Early Warning, Multi-Sensor Fusion, Wearable, On- Device Machine Learning, Heat Index, Heart Rate Variability, Edge Computing, Explainable Alerts, Child Health Monitoring
