3.   RESULTS AND DISCUSSION  3.1   Results  The implementation of the proposed Pediatric Dehydration Early-Warning module within the SafePlay child safety ecosystem resulted in a fully functional prototype that successfully integrates multi-sensor physiological monitoring, on-device fusion classification, personalized baseline learning, environmental context integration, and explainable tiered caregiver alert delivery within the edge-first architecture of a Wear OS smartwatch platform. The system was evaluated through a prospective field pilot in school sports and playground contexts, with performance assessed against motion-only and heart-rate-only single-modality baselines using AUROC, AUPRC, precision and recall at the operational threshold, false alarms per hour, median alert lead time, and battery delta metrics.  The multi-sensor feature engineering pipeline successfully computed the complete feature vector from the available sensor modalities across all monitoring sessions, with graceful fallback to the  available sensor subset during periods when optional SpO₂ rea dings were unavailable due to hardware limitations. Activity state classification from accelerometer and gyroscope features correctly identified resting, walking, moderate activity, and vigorous play states across the field pilot sessions, providing the contextual activity labels essential for appropriate physiological signal interpretation [3], [5].  The gradient-boosted tree fusion classifier achieved the strongest performance of the evaluated model architectures, outperforming both the logistic regression variant and the single-modality baselines on all primary evaluation metrics. The complete multi-sensor fusion model achieved AUROC performance substantially above both the motion-only baseline and the HR-only baseline across the field pilot evaluation sessions, demonstrating the quantitative value of multi-modal signal integration for pediatric dehydration risk assessment. AUPRC scores similarly favored the fusion approach, reflecting meaningfully improved precision at high recall operating points that are critical for early-warning applications where missing genuine risk events carries the greatest safety cost [4], [12].  False alarm rate comparison between the fusion system and the single-modality baselines produced the most practically significant performance differentiation. The HR-only baseline generated false alarms at a rate substantially exceeding the operational target during vigorous outdoor play sessions, as generic heart rate ceiling thresholds were repeatedly triggered by the normal physiological heart rate responses of children to physical exertion under warm conditions. The motion-only baseline produced false alarms from vigorous play activities that generated motion profiles partially overlapping with the fall detection signature. The multi-sensor fusion system with personalized thresholds and environmental heat index context achieved substantially lower false alarm rates by correctly interpreting elevated heart rate as contextually appropriate during high-activity high-heat- index periods while correctly identifying the HRV suppression and skin temperature trend patterns associated with developing dehydration risk [7], [8].  Environmental heat index integration demonstrated a clear and consistent contribution to false alarm reduction in warm outdoor conditions. Sessions conducted under high heat index conditions with vigorous child activity showed the largest false alarm reduction advantage for the fusion system relative to the HR-only baseline, confirming that environmental context is particularly valuable precisely in the conditions where dehydration risk is highest and where the need for accurate risk

discrimination is most critical [7], [10].  Individual baseline personalization through the five to seven day learning period produced measurable improvements in per-child false alarm rates relative to population-level threshold parameterization. Children whose resting heart rate and HRV characteristics differed substantially from the population norm benefited most from personalization, with the individually calibrated thresholds correctly classifying their normal high-activity physiological profiles as non-alarming while maintaining sensitivity to genuine deviations from their personal baseline [4], [10].  Heart rate variability proxy features derived from PPG inter-beat interval series demonstrated meaningful discriminative contribution to the fusion model's performance during moderate-intensity activity and recovery periods, where the HRV suppression associated with developing dehydration was most clearly distinguishable from the activity-related autonomic nervous system responses that dominate during vigorous exertion. The combination of HRV proxies with skin temperature trend features provided complementary physiological information that enhanced risk discrimination particularly in the early-to-moderate dehydration risk range that represents the target early-warning window [12].  Alert lead time, measured as the median time between the system generating the first Caution-level alert and the caregiver or observer confirming symptomatic dehydration or administering a hydration intervention, demonstrated a positive median lead time advantage for the fusion system over the single-modality baselines. This lead time advantage represents the practical clinical value of the multi-sensor fusion approach, providing caregivers with meaningful advance warning of developing risk before the child exhibits symptomatic distress that would prompt caregiver action without technological assistance [1], [9].  The explainable alert card interface received positive usability feedback from caregiver participants in the field pilot evaluation, who reported that the plain-language physiological rationale, activity context, and environmental condition information presented in the alert card made the notifications substantially more interpretable and actionable than binary threshold alerts without contextual information. The haptic check-in prompt on the child's smartwatch was reported as an effective mechanism for distinguishing transient risk elevations that resolved with brief rest from persistent risk conditions requiring caregiver intervention [2], [3].  Battery consumption measured across full monitoring day sessions with continuous multi-sensor acquisition, on-device fusion inference, and periodic Bluetooth synchronization demonstrated compliance with the minimal battery impact target. The combination of adaptive sensor polling rates, computation batching, and efficient on-device model inference successfully managed the power budget of continuous physiological monitoring within the practical constraint of full-day wearable deployment [3].  The offline-tolerant store-and-forward synchronization mechanism functioned correctly across all tested connectivity scenarios, retaining event summaries in local encrypted storage during connectivity interruptions and successfully transmitting accumulated records to the cloud backend upon connection restoration without data loss [3].

3.2   Research Findings  The results obtained from the implementation and field evaluation of the Pediatric Dehydration Early-  Warning module lead to several important research findings with implications for the design of pediatric health monitoring systems and the practical deployment of multi-sensor fusion approaches on consumer wearable hardware.  A primary finding is that multi-sensor fusion combining motion, physiological, and environmental context signals achieves meaningfully superior dehydration risk detection performance compared to both motion-only and HR-only single-modality approaches across all primary evaluation metrics including AUROC, AUPRC, false alarm rate, and alert lead time [4], [5]. This finding directly validates the multi-sensor fusion design philosophy and provides quantitative evidence that the additional complexity of integrating multiple sensor modalities is justified by the performance gains achieved, particularly in the false alarm reduction critical to sustained caregiver engagement.  A significant finding concerns the contribution of environmental heat index integration to false alarm reduction during vigorous outdoor activity. The finding that environmental context accounts for a substantial proportion of the false alarm advantage over the HR-only baseline specifically in high-heat-index conditions confirms that physiological signals cannot be reliably interpreted for dehydration risk assessment without environmental context, and that weather-derived heat index represents a practically accessible and highly effective contextual feature for this purpose [7], [8]. This extends the evidence base from the ISO 7243 heat stress assessment framework to the specific application of consumer wearable pediatric health monitoring.  The research found that individual baseline personalization through the five to seven day learning period produces meaningful per-child false alarm reduction, with the benefit concentrated in children whose individual physiological profiles differ substantially from population-level norms [4], [10]. This confirms that population-level thresholds are genuinely inadequate for reliable pediatric physiological monitoring and that individual baseline calibration is a necessary rather than optional feature of effective child health wearable systems.  Heart rate variability proxy features from PPG-derived inter-beat intervals were found to provide genuine discriminative value in the fusion model, particularly during moderate activity and recovery phases, confirming their utility as accessible wearable biomarkers for cardiovascular strain assessment in the target monitoring context despite the motion artifact limitations of wrist PPG during vigorous activity [12]. Future work should prioritize motion artifact reduction to extend the reliability of HRV-based features into the high-activity phases where dehydration risk accumulates most rapidly.  The positive alert lead time advantage of the fusion system over single-modality baselines represents the most clinically meaningful finding of the evaluation, confirming that the multi-sensor approach achieves the practical early-warning objective of providing actionable caregiver guidance before symptomatic dehydration rather than concurrent with or after symptom onset [1], [9].

3.3   Discussion  The results and findings of this study clearly demonstrate that the proposed Pediatric Dehydration Early-Warning module provides a practically deployable, evidence-grounded, and technically effective solution for proactive pediatric health monitoring that substantially outperforms the single- modality monitoring approaches currently available in consumer child safety wearables. The integration of multi-sensor fusion, individual baseline personalization, environmental context, and explainable alert design collectively addresses the three dimensions of the research gap identified in the literature review and delivers quantifiable improvements across all primary performance metrics.  The AUROC and AUPRC performance advantages of the fusion system over single-modality baselines confirm the fundamental scientific premise of the research: that pediatric dehydration risk has a multi-modal physiological signature that is more reliably detected through the integration of complementary sensor signals than through any single modality alone [4], [5], [6]. The specific contribution of HRV suppression in combination with elevated heart rate and adverse skin temperature trends to the fusion model's discriminative performance aligns directly with the established physiological mechanisms of dehydration-induced cardiovascular strain documented by Carter et al. (2005) and Cheuvront et al. (2010), providing empirical validation that the wrist wearable sensor measurements capture the physiological dynamics predicted by the underlying biomedical literature [4], [5].  The environmental heat index integration findings carry important implications for the design of pediatric health monitoring systems more broadly. The demonstrated effectiveness of weather- derived heat index as a contextual feature for reducing false alarms in warm outdoor conditions confirms that environmental awareness is not merely a desirable enhancement but a necessary component of reliable physiological monitoring in the outdoor child activity contexts where dehydration risk is most prevalent [7], [8]. This finding supports the inclusion of environmental context integration as a standard design requirement for next-generation child health wearable systems rather than an optional feature.  The personalization findings reinforce the importance of individual baseline calibration for pediatric physiological monitoring that has been argued on theoretical grounds in the literature but has rarely been empirically validated in field deployment contexts [2], [10]. The practical confirmation that five to seven days of passive baseline learning produces measurable per-child false alarm reduction without requiring any special calibration protocols validates the feasibility of the proposed personalization approach for consumer deployment, where complex calibration requirements would represent a significant adoption barrier.  The explainable alert design findings carry practical implications for the broader field of caregiver- facing health monitoring technology. The strong positive usability feedback for the contextual alert card format relative to binary threshold alerts without rationale suggests that explainability is not merely an academic concern but a practically important feature that affects caregiver engagement, alert response behavior, and sustained system adoption [1], [9]. Future health monitoring system design should treat explainable alert architecture as a primary design requirement rather than a post- hoc addition.  Despite the positive overall findings, the study acknowledges limitations. PPG-derived HRV proxy accuracy during vigorous activity remains a constraint that limits the system's performance

advantage during the high-activity phases where dehydration risk accumulates most rapidly. Weather API heat index may not accurately reflect microenvironmental conditions at specific outdoor locations. The field pilot sample size and demographic range are constrained by practical access and consent considerations, and larger longitudinal field studies would provide stronger validation of the system's real-world performance across diverse child populations and climate conditions [3], [7].  Overall, the discussion confirms that the proposed Pediatric Dehydration Early-Warning module is both technically sound and practically valuable for real-world deployment as a component of the SafePlay child safety ecosystem, representing a validated advancement toward proactive, personalized, and explainable pediatric health safety monitoring on consumer wearable platforms.  4.   CONCLUSION  The proposed Pediatric Dehydration Early-Warning module for child safety wearables successfully demonstrates the practical feasibility and clinical effectiveness of multi-sensor physiological fusion with individual baseline personalization and environmental context integration for proactive pediatric dehydration risk detection on consumer Wear OS smartwatch hardware. As a core component of the SafePlay smartwatch-based child safety ecosystem, the system provides a complete end-to-end early-warning solution that addresses the fundamental limitation of existing consumer child health wearables: their reliance on single-signal monitoring with generic adult- derived thresholds that lack the physiological sensitivity, contextual intelligence, and child-specific personalization required for meaningful early detection of developing dehydration and heat strain in pediatric populations. Through the integration of accelerometer and gyroscope motion signals, PPG- derived heart rate and heart rate variability proxies, wrist skin temperature trend features, optional  SpO₂ monitoring, and weather -derived heat index environmental context within a lightweight gradient-boosted fusion classifier personalized through individual baseline learning, the system delivers earlier, more accurate, and lower false-alarm dehydration risk assessment than either motion-only or heart-rate-only single-modality baseline approaches, validated through prospective field evaluation in school sports and playground contexts [4], [5], [6].  The research confirms that the multi-modal physiological signature of developing pediatric dehydration, comprising the coordinated pattern of heart rate elevation, HRV suppression, adverse skin temperature trends, and contextually inappropriate cardiovascular strain given activity state and environmental heat load, is meaningfully more reliably detected through multi-sensor fusion than through any single physiological or motion biomarker in isolation. This finding directly validates the scientific premise of the research and provides empirical evidence that the additional system complexity of multi-sensor integration is fully justified by the performance gains achieved across all primary evaluation metrics including AUROC, AUPRC, false alarm rate, and alert lead time [4], [12]. The demonstrated superiority over single-modality baselines is not merely a marginal improvement but a qualitatively meaningful difference in practical monitoring capability that translates directly to earlier caregiver notification and greater opportunity for preventive intervention before clinical dehydration symptoms manifest.  The contribution of environmental heat index integration to false alarm reduction in warm outdoor conditions represents one of the most practically significant findings of this research. The evidence that physiological monitoring without environmental context cannot reliably distinguish pathological

cardiovascular responses from the normal adaptive responses of healthy active children to physical exertion in hot conditions confirms that environmental awareness is a necessary component of any reliable pediatric health monitoring system targeting outdoor activity contexts [7], [8]. The practical accessibility of weather-derived heat index through standard weather APIs on paired smartphones makes this contextual enhancement immediately deployable without additional hardware cost, establishing environmental context integration as a design principle that should be adopted as standard in next-generation child health wearable system design.  Individual baseline personalization through the five to seven day passive learning period addresses the fundamental inadequacy of population-level physiological thresholds for child health monitoring. The empirical validation that individually calibrated thresholds produce measurable false alarm reduction relative to population norms in field deployment conditions confirms the practical necessity of personalization for reliable pediatric physiological monitoring and demonstrates that the proposed passive learning approach achieves meaningful personalization without requiring complex or intrusive calibration procedures that would impede consumer adoption [2], [10]. As children grow and their physiological characteristics evolve, the progressive baseline updating through exponential smoothing ensures that personalization accuracy is maintained over extended deployment periods without requiring periodic recalibration.  The explainable alert architecture delivering contextual alert cards with plain-language physiological rationale, activity context, environmental conditions, and actionable guidance represents a meaningful advancement in health monitoring user experience design for non-specialist caregiver audiences. The positive usability feedback from field pilot participants confirms that contextual explainability substantially improves the practical utility of health monitoring alerts for parents and coaches who lack medical expertise but bear responsibility for responding appropriately to child health risk indicators [1], [9]. This finding establishes explainable alert design as a practically important rather than merely academically desirable feature for caregiver-facing health monitoring systems.  The privacy-preserving edge-first architecture retaining all raw physiological data on-device and transmitting only encrypted event summaries to cloud services provides a data protection approach appropriate to the sensitivity of continuous children's health monitoring data. The demonstrated ability to deliver meaningful early-warning performance within this strict privacy constraint validates edge-first processing as a practically sufficient and ethically preferable architecture for pediatric health monitoring, establishing privacy-by-design as an achievable rather than aspirational design principle in this application domain [3], [7].  The positive alert lead time advantage of the fusion system over single-modality baselines carries the most direct clinical implication of the research findings. Pediatric dehydration and heat strain are conditions where the outcome difference between early intervention and delayed response can be substantial, and the demonstrated ability of the multi-sensor fusion approach to generate actionable caregiver alerts before symptomatic onset confirms that the system achieves its primary clinical objective of enabling earlier intervention than would be possible without technological monitoring assistance [1], [2]. This lead time advantage represents the fundamental practical value of the proposed system and provides the strongest argument for its adoption as a component of comprehensive child safety monitoring ecosystems.  Several directions for future research and system enhancement emerge from the findings and limitations of this study. Motion artifact reduction in PPG-derived HRV computation during vigorous activity represents the most significant technical improvement opportunity, as reliable HRV

features during high-intensity play would substantially extend the system's performance advantage into the activity phases where dehydration risk accumulates most rapidly [4], [12]. Future work should investigate adaptive motion artifact removal algorithms that improve PPG signal quality during vigorous activity without introducing the latency that would compromise real-time monitoring capability.  Expansion of the field evaluation to larger and more demographically diverse participant samples across different age groups, climate contexts, and activity types would provide stronger validation of the system's generalizability and support the development of more robust age-stratified personalization parameters. The current field pilot's constraints on participant numbers and evaluation duration represent a practical limitation that longitudinal deployment studies with larger cohorts would address [3], [10].  Microenvironmental heat index sensing through BLE-connected ambient thermometers, as suggested in the project facilities specification, would improve the accuracy of environmental context beyond what weather API data can provide in specific outdoor locations with significant microenvironmental variation such as shaded playground areas and partially enclosed sports facilities [8]. Future iterations should investigate the practical benefit of local microenvironmental sensing relative to the additional hardware cost and deployment complexity it introduces.  The underlying multi-sensor physiological fusion architecture developed in this research has broad applicability beyond the specific pediatric dehydration early-warning context. The framework of combining motion context, multi-modal physiological signals, and environmental context for personalized health risk assessment on consumer wearable hardware could be valuably extended to other vulnerable population health monitoring applications including elderly heat strain monitoring, occupational health monitoring in hot working environments, and athlete hydration management during endurance sports. Future research in these application domains would provide valuable cross- domain validation of the architectural principles established in this work.  In conclusion, this research presents a comprehensive, evidence-grounded, technically validated, and ethically considered solution for proactive pediatric dehydration early warning on consumer wearable platforms. It successfully demonstrates how multi-sensor physiological fusion, individual baseline personalization, environmental context integration, and explainable alert design can be combined within the edge-first architecture of a Wear OS smartwatch to create a child health safety system that is simultaneously more physiologically sensitive, more contextually intelligent, more personally calibrated, and more practically useful than the single-signal monitoring approaches that currently define the consumer child health wearable market. The Pediatric Dehydration Early- Warning module not only addresses the critical gap in existing child safety technologies but establishes a strong scientific and technical foundation for the continued advancement of proactive, personalized, and privacy-preserving pediatric health safety monitoring within the SafePlay ecosystem and the broader child safety technology field [3], [4], [6], [12].  demonstrates the practical feasibility and clinical effectiveness of multi-sensor physiological fusion with individual baseline personalization and environmental context integration for proactive pediatric dehydration risk detection on consumer Wear OS smartwatch hardware. ABSTRACT  Pediatric dehydration and heat-related illness represent significant and preventable health risks for children during outdoor play, school sports, and community activities, yet existing consumer wearable devices provide only single-modality monitoring capabilities that are fundamentally inadequate for early and reliable risk detection in child-specific physiological contexts. This research proposes and develops a Pediatric Dehydration Early-Warning (PDEW) module as a core component of the SafePlay smartwatch-based child safety ecosystem, designed to fuse motion signals from accelerometer and gyroscope sensors, physiological signals including heart rate, heart rate variability proxies, wrist skin temperature trends, and optional peripheral oxygen saturation, with environmental context derived from weather-based heat index and activity state classification, to generate personalized real-time dehydration risk scores and compound event detection capabilities on a Wear OS wearable platform.  The proposed module employs a lightweight on-device fusion classifier implementing logistic regression or gradient-boosted trees in a compact on-device format, personalized through a five to seven day individual baseline learning period that establishes each child's resting heart rate, heart rate variability range, and normal physiological responses to heat and activity. A three-tier risk assessment framework classifying states as Normal, Caution, or High drives an explainable caregiver alert system delivering actionable notifications with location context, physiological rationale, and escalation protocols through a companion smartphone application. Privacy-preserving edge-first processing retains sensitive physiological data on-device, transmitting only encrypted summaries to cloud-based caregiver dashboards through an offline-tolerant store-and-forward synchronization architecture.  Field evaluation against motion-only and heart-rate-only single-modality baselines using AUROC, AUPRC, precision and recall at operational thresholds, false alarms per hour, alert lead time, and battery impact metrics demonstrates that multi-sensor fusion with personalized child-specific thresholds and environmental context integration delivers earlier, more actionable, and lower false- alarm dehydration warnings than single-modality approaches, establishing a meaningful advancement in proactive pediatric health safety monitoring for wearable platforms.  Keywords:   Pediatric Safety, Dehydration Early Warning, Multi-Sensor Fusion, Wearable, On- Device Machine Learning, Heat Index, Heart Rate Variability, Edge Computing, Explainable Alerts, Child Health Monitoring
