1   INTRODUCTION  Pediatric health and safety during unsupervised outdoor activity represents one of the most challenging and consequential domains in child safety technology design. Children engaged in outdoor play, school sports, and community activities are routinely exposed to conditions of physical exertion and environmental heat that place significant physiological demands on their developing cardiovascular and thermoregulatory systems. Unlike adults, children exhibit fundamentally different physiological responses to heat and exertion, including higher resting heart rates, different heart rate variability profiles, and less efficient thermoregulatory mechanisms that make them disproportionately vulnerable to dehydration, heat strain, and the compound events such as dizziness and falls that these conditions can precipitate [1], [6]. Despite this documented vulnerability, the consumer wearable technology available to monitor children's health during outdoor activity remains limited to single-signal features including motion-based fall detection, generic heart rate alerts, and passive hydration reminders that lack the physiological sensitivity, contextual intelligence, and child-specific personalization required for meaningful early-warning capability.  In Sri Lanka, children's outdoor activities including school sports, playground recreation, and community events frequently occur in high-temperature and high-humidity conditions that significantly elevate heat strain risk. The country's tropical climate creates prolonged periods of elevated ambient temperature and humidity that, combined with the physiological vulnerability of children and the common absence of structured adult health supervision during informal outdoor play, establish a compelling local context for technology-driven pediatric health monitoring. The consequences of undetected dehydration and heat strain in children range from performance impairment and discomfort through dizziness and falls to serious medical emergencies requiring immediate intervention, all of which are substantially more preventable when early physiological warning signs are detected and communicated to caregivers before clinical thresholds are reached [2], [9].  The convergence of multi-sensor wearable hardware incorporating accelerometers, gyroscopes, photoplethysmography-based heart rate and heart rate variability measurement, skin temperature sensing, and optional pulse oximetry with increasingly capable on-device machine learning inference frameworks has created a genuine opportunity to develop meaningful early-warning capabilities for pediatric dehydration and heat strain that go substantially beyond what single-signal monitoring approaches can achieve. The critical challenge lies not in sensor availability but in the intelligent fusion of multiple physiological and environmental signals into a unified, personalized risk assessment that is calibrated to individual children's baseline physiology rather than generic adult population parameters, and that incorporates environmental context to distinguish pathological physiological elevation from the normal responses to exercise and heat that characterize healthy active children [3], [8].  This research proposes the Pediatric Dehydration Early-Warning module as a response to this challenge, developing a lightweight on-device fusion model that integrates motion, physiology, and environmental heat index signals into a personalized real-time risk score that drives an explainable, tiered caregiver alert system designed for practical deployment within the SafePlay smartwatch- based child safety ecosystem.

1.1   Background and Literature Survey  The scientific and clinical foundation for the proposed Pediatric Dehydration Early-Warning module draws on a substantial body of literature spanning sports medicine, pediatric physiology, environmental health science, and wearable sensing technology, each of which contributes essential knowledge to the system's design and evaluation approach.  Exertional heat illness in youth is recognized as a significant and preventable health risk across multiple clinical consensus statements and evidence-based guidelines. Roberts et al. (2021) established comprehensive expert consensus on the recognition, management, and return-to-activity protocols for exertional heat illness, emphasizing the importance of early recognition and environmental awareness in prevention [1]. Schimelpfenig and Dobbs (2024) specifically addressed environmental heat illness in children, documenting the distinct physiological mechanisms that make pediatric populations more vulnerable than adults to heat-related health events during outdoor activity [2]. Bergeron (2011) synthesized evidence on climatic heat stress and exercising children and adolescents in a landmark Pediatrics publication, establishing the scientific basis for environment-aware practice modification including heat index monitoring and hydration protocols as essential preventive measures [10].  Evidence regarding heat strain in children during unstructured outdoor activity is particularly relevant to the proposed system's target deployment context. McGarr et al. (2021) demonstrated that children experience meaningful heat strain during informal unstructured outdoor physical activity in continental summer climate conditions, not only during formal organized sports, confirming that monitoring need extends beyond structured athletic contexts to the everyday outdoor play environments where the proposed system will primarily be deployed [3]. This finding directly supports the design decision to target the system at playground and community activity contexts rather than restricting its scope to formal school sports settings.  The physiological mechanisms linking dehydration and thermal strain to measurable cardiovascular biomarkers accessible through wrist wearable sensors form the core scientific justification for the proposed fusion approach. Carter et al. (2005) demonstrated that hydration status significantly influences heart rate variability following exercise heat stress, with dehydration producing measurable HRV suppression that persists in recovery periods and provides a detectable physiological signal of impaired hydration status [4]. Cheuvront et al. (2010) characterized the mechanisms of aerobic performance impairment with heat stress and dehydration, documenting the cardiovascular strain responses including elevated heart rate and reduced stroke volume that accompany dehydration under thermal load [5]. Périard et al. (2021) provided a comprehensive review of exercise under heat stress covering thermoregulation, hydration, performance implications, and mitigation strategies, establishing the full physiological context within which the proposed monitoring system operates [6]. Manning et al. (2023) specifically examined fluid replacement strategies and heart rate variability following exercise in heat, directly validating the utility of PPG- derived HRV proxies as accessible wearable biomarkers for monitoring hydration and recovery status [12].  Environmental context quantification for heat stress assessment has a well-established scientific and regulatory foundation. The ISO 7243 standard formalizes the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature index as the international standard for thermal environment assessment and heat-stress evaluation [7]. Brimicombe (2023) examined the practical utility of WBGT as an indicator of extreme heat risk to

humans, providing methodological context for the heat index integration approach adopted in the proposed system [8]. Eifling et al. (2024) updated Wilderness Medical Society clinical practice guidelines for the prevention and treatment of heat illness, reinforcing the importance of environment-aware prevention protocols that monitor both physiological and environmental indicators simultaneously [9]. The integration of weather-derived heat index as a contextual feature in the proposed fusion model is directly motivated by this body of evidence demonstrating that physiological indicators of heat strain and dehydration risk are most accurately interpreted when placed in the context of the environmental thermal load to which the child is exposed [8], [10].  Single-sensor limitations in consumer wearable health monitoring provide the direct technological motivation for the multi-sensor fusion approach. Accelerometer-only fall detection systems suffer from significant false alarm rates in free-living use where normal vigorous child activity generates motion profiles that overlap with fall signatures [3]. Generic heart rate alert systems lack the contextual awareness to distinguish physiologically appropriate heart rate elevation from physical exertion in warm conditions from pathological cardiovascular strain indicating dehydration or heat illness onset [4], [5]. The integration of multiple complementary sensing modalities with personalized baseline calibration and environmental context represents the motivated strategy for achieving the improved precision required for practical pediatric safety monitoring while maintaining the low false alarm rates necessary for sustained caregiver trust and system adoption.  1.2   Research Gap  Analysis of existing consumer wearable technology and academic research in pediatric health monitoring reveals a well-defined and practically significant research gap that the proposed system directly addresses across three interconnected dimensions.  The first dimension concerns the absence of proactive multi-modal dehydration early warning in consumer child safety wearables. All major commercial smartwatches and child-specific wearable products provide only single-signal monitoring features for health-related safety. Motion-based fall detection, generic heart rate ceiling alerts, and passive timed hydration reminders operate in complete isolation from one another, providing no mechanism for the integrated physiological risk assessment that meaningful early warning of dehydration onset requires [3], [5]. No commercial child safety wearable product currently combines motion, physiological vitals, and environmental heat load into a unified real-time risk score capable of detecting the compound physiological state of developing dehydration before clinical symptoms become apparent.  The second dimension concerns the absence of pediatric personalization in consumer health monitoring thresholds. Generic adult-derived heart rate and activity thresholds applied to children systematically misinterpret normal pediatric physiological profiles as pathological, generating false alarms that erode caregiver trust and lead to monitoring tool abandonment [2], [10]. Children's resting heart rate, heart rate variability characteristics, and thermoregulatory response patterns differ substantially from adult norms and vary meaningfully across the childhood age range, requiring individual baseline calibration rather than population-level threshold application for reliable risk discrimination [4], [6].  The third dimension concerns the absence of validated on-device implementations demonstrating real-world performance under wearable hardware constraints. Academic multi-sensor fusion approaches for health monitoring have largely been developed and evaluated in laboratory settings using research-grade hardware without demonstrating practical deployability within consumer

wearable power, memory, and latency constraints. The specific metrics of false alarms per hour, alert lead time, and battery impact under field conditions have rarely been reported for pediatric safety monitoring systems, leaving a critical gap between laboratory proof-of-concept and practical deployment validation [3], [8].  1.3   Research Problem  The fundamental research problem addressed in this study is that children engaged in outdoor physical activity under warm environmental conditions face meaningful and preventable risks of dehydration and heat strain that existing consumer wearable devices cannot proactively detect, because those devices rely on single-signal monitoring with generic adult-derived thresholds that lack the multi-modal physiological sensitivity, child-specific personalization, and environmental context integration required for early and reliable risk identification in pediatric populations.  Specifically, the problem requires designing and validating a multi-sensor fusion system for child wearables that combines accelerometer and gyroscope motion signals, heart rate, heart rate  variability proxies, skin temperature trends, and optional SpO₂ ph ysiological signals with weather- derived heat index environmental context to generate personalized, explainable early warnings for dehydration and compound events including dizzy falls, while operating within the battery, memory, and computation constraints of consumer Wear OS smartwatch hardware, maintaining false alarm rates low enough to sustain caregiver trust over extended deployment periods, and protecting the privacy of sensitive physiological data through edge-first processing and minimal cloud data transmission.  The consequences of failing to address this problem include children experiencing preventable escalation of dehydration and heat strain to clinical severity because early physiological warning signs go undetected, caregivers receiving either no alerts or excessive false alarms that undermine trust in monitoring technology, and the absence of validated child-specific early warning tools in the wearable technology ecosystem despite the existence of the sensor hardware and machine learning techniques required to build them.

1.4   Research Objectives  1.4.1   Main Objective  The primary objective of this research is to design, implement, and evaluate a lightweight on-device multi-sensor data fusion component that integrates accelerometer and gyroscope motion signals, heart rate, heart rate variability proxies, skin temperature   trend, and optional SpO₂ physiological  signals with weather-derived heat index environmental context to deliver personalized, explainable, and tiered early warnings for pediatric dehydration and compound safety events, demonstrating superior performance over motion-only and heart-rate-only single-modality baselines across AUROC, AUPRC, precision and recall at operational thresholds, false alarms per hour, alert lead time, and battery impact metrics, deployed as a functional component of the SafePlay smartwatch- based child safety ecosystem.  1.4.2   Specific Objectives  To integrate motion signals from the accelerometer and gyroscope with physiological signals  including heart rate, heart rate variability proxy, skin temperature trend, and optional SpO₂ alongside  activity state classification and weather-derived heat index context into a unified windowed feature extraction pipeline executing on the Wear OS smartwatch edge platform [3], [5].  To design and implement a lightweight on-device fusion classifier using logistic regression or gradient-boosted trees in a compact deployable format, personalized through a five to seven day individual baseline learning period that establishes each child's resting heart rate, heart rate variability range, and typical physiological responses to heat and activity, with threshold and model prior adjustments to minimize individual false alarm rates [4], [10].  To implement an explainable incident workflow incorporating haptic on-device check-in prompts, tiered risk assessment across Normal, Caution, and High states, explainable caregiver alert cards with physiological rationale, real-time location context, and escalation protocols to backup contacts when alerts go unacknowledged [1], [9].  To develop a privacy-preserving data architecture providing edge-first on-device processing, encrypted cloud summary synchronization, role-based caregiver dashboard access, and offline- tolerant store-and-forward synchronization ensuring no event data is lost during connectivity outages [7], [8].  To conduct a prospective field evaluation in school sports and playground contexts with appropriate ethical consent, measuring system performance against motion-only and heart-rate-only baselines using AUROC, AUPRC, precision and recall, false alarms per hour, median alert lead time, and battery delta, with ablation studies stratified by age, heat index band, and activity intensity [3], [12].

2.   METHODOLOGY  This chapter presents the comprehensive methodology adopted for the design, development, and implementation of the Pediatric Dehydration Early-Warning module within the SafePlay smartwatch-based child safety ecosystem. The methodology integrates multiple interdisciplinary domains including pediatric physiology, multi-sensor signal processing, lightweight machine learning for on-device inference, environmental context integration, explainable alert design, and privacy-preserving data architecture to develop a real-time early-warning system that is clinically grounded, technically deployable on consumer wearable hardware, and practically useful for non- specialist caregivers in real-world child monitoring contexts.  Pediatric dehydration and heat strain represent physiologically complex processes that do not manifest through any single measurable biomarker in isolation. The progressive cardiovascular and thermoregulatory responses to combined heat exposure and physical exertion interact across multiple physiological systems simultaneously, producing coordinated changes in heart rate dynamics, heart rate variability, skin temperature, motion patterns, and blood oxygenation that together constitute a more reliable and earlier indicator of developing risk than any individual signal alone [4], [5], [6]. The proposed methodology is designed to exploit this multi-modal physiological signature through systematic sensor fusion with environmental context integration, personalized baseline calibration, and intelligent alert management to produce an early-warning system that is both sensitive enough to detect genuine risk early and specific enough to maintain the low false alarm rates required for sustained caregiver engagement.  The overall methodology is organized into two primary phases. The first phase addresses the theoretical and conceptual foundations of the system, examining the core technological and scientific pillars including pediatric physiological responses to heat and dehydration, multi-sensor feature engineering, lightweight fusion model design, personalization through individual baseline learning, environmental context integration, explainable alert architecture, and privacy-preserving data handling. The second phase addresses practical implementation and evaluation, encompassing signal acquisition pipeline development, fusion model training and on-device deployment, caregiver application development, field pilot execution, and quantitative performance evaluation against defined baseline comparators and metric targets [3], [12].  2.1   Understanding Key Pillars of the Research Domain  2.1.1 Pediatric Physiology of Dehydration and Heat Strain  A thorough understanding of the pediatric physiological responses to dehydration and heat strain is foundational to the design of an effective early-warning system. Children's thermoregulatory systems differ from adults in several important ways that affect both the trajectory of physiological deterioration under heat and exertion stress and the measurable biomarker signatures that accompany it. Children have a higher surface area to body mass ratio that increases relative heat gain from the environment, a lower sweat rate per unit area that reduces evaporative cooling efficiency, and a cardiovascular system that responds to heat and exertion with proportionally larger heart rate increases relative to adults [2], [10].

Under conditions of progressive dehydration, the cardiovascular system responds with a characteristic pattern of compensatory adjustments. Plasma volume contraction reduces venous return and stroke volume, driving heart rate elevation to maintain cardiac output. Simultaneously, thermoregulatory demands increase skin blood flow to support heat dissipation, competing with exercising muscle for the reduced circulating volume and further amplifying cardiovascular strain. Heart rate variability, a measure of the beat-to-beat variability in cardiac cycle length that reflects autonomic nervous system modulation of cardiac function, is progressively suppressed as sympathetic nervous system activation increases to maintain cardiovascular output under the combined demands of exercise, heat, and dehydration [4], [12].  Skin temperature trends provide complementary physiological information that reflects both the thermoregulatory state and the adequacy of peripheral perfusion. During the early stages of heat strain, skin temperature typically rises as heat dissipation mechanisms are activated. As dehydration progresses and thermoregulatory capacity becomes strained, skin temperature trends may reflect reduced peripheral perfusion as the cardiovascular system prioritizes central organ perfusion over peripheral heat dissipation [5], [6]. These temperature dynamics, when tracked as trends over monitoring windows rather than as absolute values, provide meaningful physiological context that augments the heart rate and heart rate variability signals for risk assessment.  2.1.1   Multi Sensor Feature Engineering  Multi-sensor feature engineering transforms raw sensor data streams from the wearable's accelerometer, gyroscope, photoplethysmography sensor, skin temperature sensor, and optional pulse oximeter into a compact and informative feature vector that captures the physiological and motion characteristics relevant to dehydration and heat strain risk assessment. The feature engineering pipeline operates on windowed segments of sensor data, computing statistical and domain-specific features from each window that serve as the input representation for the fusion classifier [3], [5].  From the accelerometer and gyroscope data streams, activity state classification features are derived including magnitude statistics, dominant frequency components, and activity classification outputs distinguishing resting, walking, running, and vigorous play states. These activity features provide essential context for interpreting physiological signals, as heart rate and heart rate variability values that would indicate risk at rest may be entirely appropriate during vigorous physical exertion [3].  From the photoplethysmography sensor, heart rate is derived as the primary cardiovascular biomarker. Heart rate variability proxies are computed from the inter-beat interval series estimated from the PPG waveform, providing time-domain HRV features including the standard deviation of normal-to-normal intervals and the root mean square of successive differences that reflect autonomic nervous system state and cardiovascular strain [4], [12]. From the skin temperature sensor, trend features capturing the rate of change and trajectory of wrist temperature over monitoring windows provide thermoregulatory state information that complements the cardiovascular biomarkers.  Environmental context features derived from the weather API integration on the paired smartphone provide heat index or Wet Bulb Globe Temperature estimates that quantify the environmental thermal load experienced by the child. These features are critical for contextualizing physiological measurements, as the same heart rate value carries fundamentally different risk implications in a cool indoor environment versus a hot humid outdoor setting [7], [8].

2.1.2   Lightweight Fusion Model  The fusion model must satisfy a demanding set of joint requirements that reflect the practical constraints of wearable deployment: sufficient classification accuracy to support meaningful early warning, a computational footprint small enough to execute efficiently on watch-class processors, and sufficient interpretability to support explainable alert generation for non-specialist caregivers. These requirements favor compact, well-regularized discriminative classifiers over complex deep neural network architectures for the primary fusion task [3].  Logistic regression with carefully engineered feature representations provides a highly efficient baseline fusion approach that offers excellent interpretability through its coefficient structure, minimal computational overhead enabling real-time inference on constrained hardware, and straightforward personalization through prior adjustment and threshold shifting. Gradient-boosted tree ensembles provide a more expressive alternative that can capture non-linear feature interactions relevant to the complex physiological dynamics of dehydration onset, while remaining substantially more compact and computationally efficient than deep learning approaches for tabular feature inputs of the size generated by the proposed feature engineering pipeline [5], [10].  Both model architectures are evaluated comparatively in the proposed methodology, with the selection criterion being the model that best satisfies the joint objectives of AUROC performance, false alarm rate at the operational threshold, and inference latency on target hardware. Model serialization to a compact on-device format compatible with the Wear OS execution environment ensures that the selected model can be deployed and executed locally on the smartwatch without cloud inference dependency [3].

2.1.3   Model Compression  Deploying machine learning models on wearable hardware requires systematic application of model compression techniques that reduce parameter count, memory footprint, and computational complexity while preserving as much classification performance as possible. The proposed methodology applies a two-stage compression pipeline comprising structured pruning followed by quantization-aware training to produce TFLite models compatible with the XNNPACK delegate available on Wear OS platforms [4].  Structured pruning removes weights whose magnitude falls below a defined threshold, introducing sparsity into the weight matrices that can be exploited for computational savings during inference. Unlike unstructured pruning that removes individual weights, structured pruning removes entire filters or channels, enabling direct reduction in the number of operations executed during forward inference without requiring specialized sparse computation hardware. Progressive pruning schedules gradually increase sparsity during continued training, allowing the model to adapt its remaining weights to compensate for removed capacity [4].  Quantization-aware training simulates the effect of weight and activation quantization to 8-bit integer representations during the training process, enabling the model to develop weight distributions that are robust to the reduced numerical precision of integer arithmetic. The resulting TFLite int8 model achieves inference execution using integer operations that are significantly faster and more power-efficient on mobile processors than floating-point equivalents, targeting a compressed model size of approximately 500 KB and per-frame inference latency below 50 milliseconds on the target Snapdragon Wear 4100 processor [4].  2.1.4   Risk Fusion and Exponential Moving Average Smoothing  The mathematical framework for combining the outputs of the Global Danger Sound Model and the Personal Circle of Trust Model into a unified risk score represents a central design contribution of the proposed system. The risk fusion formula Risk = w_d · P(d istress) · (1 − P(trusted)) + δ_unknown encodes the intuitive safety  logic that risk is highest when distress probability is high and trusted voice probability is low, and that the presence of an unrecognized speaker in the acoustic environment constitutes an additional risk factor warranting a small positive penalty even in the absence of detected distress [3].  The weight parameter w_d, initialized to 1.0, controls the relative contribution of the distress probability to the risk score and may be adjusted through parental configuration or through on-device learning based on historical alert accuracy feedback. The   unknown speaker penalty δ_unknown, set in the range 0.05 to 0.15, is  applied when Voice Activity Detection confirms the presence of speech that does not match any enrolled trusted caregiver centroid above the verification threshold, reflecting the elevated risk associated with unidentified adult voices in the child's acoustic environment [3].  Raw per-window risk scores exhibit considerable variability due to the inherent uncertainty of single-frame audio classification and the natural acoustic dynamics of real-world environments. Exponential Moving  Average smoothing with factor α ≈ 0.3 is appli ed to the instantaneous risk sequence to produce a temporally stable smoothed risk estimate that suppresses alert responses to transient noise spikes while maintaining sensitivity to sustained threat conditions. The dwell time requirement that the smoothed risk must exceed the dynamic threshold continuously for one to two seconds before an alert is triggered provides a further layer of temporal filtering that eliminates spurious alerts from brief acoustic events [3].

2.1.5   Personalization Through Individual Baseline Learning  Personalization through individual baseline learning addresses the fundamental inadequacy of generic population-level thresholds for pediatric physiological monitoring. Children's resting heart rate, heart rate variability characteristics, and thermoregulatory response patterns vary substantially across individuals within the same age group, meaning that threshold values calibrated to population averages will systematically misclassify the physiological profiles of individuals whose normal resting state differs from the population mean [2], [4].  The proposed baseline learning approach accumulates five to seven days of monitoring data during normal daily activity to establish each child's individual physiological profile. From this baseline period, individual reference distributions are estimated for resting heart rate, heart rate variability indices across different activity states, and skin temperature ranges, providing a personalized reference against which subsequent monitoring windows are evaluated. Threshold and model prior adjustments derived from the individual baseline reduce false alarm rates by ensuring that the risk assessment reflects deviation from the specific child's normal physiological state rather than deviation from a population norm that may not accurately represent that child [10], [12].  The baseline learning period is designed to be minimally intrusive, operating passively from normal monitoring data without requiring any special calibration protocols or child participation beyond wearing the device. Progressive baseline updating through exponential smoothing allows the individual reference profile to evolve gradually as the child grows and their physiological characteristics change over time, maintaining personalization accuracy over extended deployment periods [4].  2.1.6   Heat Activity Detection  Environmental context integration through weather-derived heat index and Wet Bulb Globe Temperature data addresses one of the most significant sources of false alarms in physiological monitoring systems: the inability to distinguish pathological physiological responses from the normal adaptive responses to environmental heat and physical exertion [7], [8]. A child with elevated heart rate and suppressed heart rate variability in a hot outdoor environment during vigorous play may be exhibiting a physiologically appropriate response to high environmental thermal load and exercise intensity, or may be exhibiting the early signs of developing dehydration and heat strain. Without environmental context, these two scenarios are physiologically indistinguishable from wrist sensor data alone.  The weather API integration on the paired smartphone retrieves current temperature, humidity, and derived heat index values at configurable intervals, computing the effective environmental thermal load using established heat index formulations or WBGT approximations from readily available meteorological data. These environmental context features are incorporated into the fusion model's input feature vector alongside the physiological and motion features, enabling the classifier to learn the conditional relationship between physiological signals and risk given the environmental context [7], [10].

The practical effect of environmental context integration is a substantial reduction in false alarms during normal vigorous outdoor play in warm conditions, as the system correctly interprets elevated heart rate and reduced heart rate variability as contextually appropriate responses to high environmental load rather than pathological indicators. Conversely, the same physiological profile in a cool environment or at rest correctly receives elevated risk weighting, as the environmental context removes the benign explanation for the physiological elevation [8].  2.1.7   On-Device Learning and Adaptation  On-device learning provides the mechanism through which the proposed system improves its accuracy over deployment lifetime without requiring connectivity to external servers or transmission of sensitive audio data. Two complementary adaptation mechanisms are implemented to address the primary sources of false alarms in real-world child monitoring environments [3].  Trusted voice expansion addresses the practical reality that the initial enrollment of trusted caregivers may not capture all adults who regularly interact with the child in safe contexts, such as teachers, family friends, and extended family members. Unknown speaker embeddings encountered across multiple monitoring sessions are accumulated in an on-device buffer and clustered using Minibatch K-Means or DBSCAN algorithms to identify recurring speaker identities. When a cluster representing a recurring unknown speaker reaches a confidence threshold indicating consistent recurrence over multiple sessions, the parent application is prompted to review and optionally approve the addition of this speaker to the trusted registry. Upon parental approval, a speaker centroid is computed from the cluster embeddings and stored securely in the trusted registry [3].  Baseline noise adaptation addresses the challenge of false alarms arising from the normal acoustic characteristics of environments where children spend regular time, such as school playgrounds where elevated ambient noise levels and frequent shouting are typical rather than indicative of distress. Streaming statistics of ambient audio energy and spectral centroid are tracked through exponential smoothing, establishing a continuously updated baseline profile of the child's typical acoustic environment. When the current audio window's acoustic characteristics closely match the established baseline profile, a small conservative downward adjustment is applied to the instantaneous risk score to reflect the lower prior probability of genuine distress in the child's typical environment. These adjustments are designed to be conservative, ensuring that genuine threat signals are never suppressed by baseline adaptation [3].  2.1.8   Summary of Methodology  The proposed Privacy-Preserving Audio-Based Stranger Threat Detection Module is built upon a strong interdisciplinary foundation combining lightweight convolutional neural network design, speaker embedding and verification techniques, TFLite model compression, risk fusion mathematics, context-aware threshold modulation, Voice Activity Detection gating, on-device learning adaptation, and privacy-by-design architectural principles. Each of these components contributes a necessary capability to the system's overall function, and their integration produces a complete end-to-end acoustic threat detection pipeline that operates entirely within the computational, power, and privacy constraints of consumer Wear OS smartwatch hardware. The system represents a fundamental departure from cloud-dependent audio monitoring approaches and establishes on-device acoustic intelligence as a practically achievable and ethically appropriate approach to proactive child safety monitoring [1], [3], [4].

2.2   Approach  The proposed Privacy-Preserving Audio-Based Stranger Threat Detection Module follows a structured end-to-end approach that integrates continuous audio acquisition, lightweight on-device inference, contextual risk assessment, and intelligent alert delivery within a fully privacy-preserving architecture. The approach is designed to ensure real-time threat detection capability, minimal false alarm generation in normal child activity contexts, and practical deployability within the battery and memory constraints of Wear OS smartwatch hardware [3], [4].  The overall processing workflow begins with continuous microphone capture into a ring buffer on the Wear OS smartwatch, followed by Voice Activity Detection gating to determine whether downstream model inference is warranted for each one-second window. Log-Mel spectrogram feature extraction is performed locally using optimized C++ and TFLite routines. The Global Danger Sound Model estimates P(distress) from the spectrogram input, while the Circle of Trust Model computes speaker embeddings and estimates P(trusted) for windows where speech is detected. The risk fusion engine combines these probabilities with the unknown speaker penalty and applies context-based threshold modulation from geofencing and Bluetooth Low Energy signals. Exponential Moving Average smoothing and dwell time enforcement filter the risk stream before alert generation, and confirmed alerts are transmitted as metadata-only payloads to the guardian companion application [1], [3].  2.2.1   Data Collection  Data collection for the proposed system encompasses two complementary streams: assembly and curation of publicly available audio datasets for model training, and collection of a consented watch- microphone dataset for device-specific fine-tuning and field evaluation.  The publicly available dataset assembly combines seven primary sources covering the target audio classification categories. Positive distress examples are drawn from the Women and Children Danger dataset providing 19,375 one-second segments across child danger, woman danger, and normal classes, and from the AudioSet Screaming subset providing approximately 1,000 screaming segments [7], [9]. Negative background examples representing normal acoustic environments are drawn from UrbanSound8K with 8,732 segments across ten urban sound categories and ESC-50 with 2,000 segments across fifty environmental categories [8], [12]. Emotional and threatening speech examples for training the anger and threat speech detection capability are sourced from CREMA-D with 7,442 segments from 91 performers and RAVDESS with 7,356 recordings across eight emotional states, as well as the FSD50K collection providing over 51,000 segments across 200 sound classes for extended category coverage [10], [11], [13]. The SAVEE and TESS datasets provide additional phonetically balanced emotional speech across seven emotion categories from British English and Canadian English speakers respectively [14].  The consented watch-microphone dataset is recorded under ethical clearance and institutional review board approval, comprising approximately 500 segments capturing distress vocalizations and normal play sounds recorded through the target Wear OS smartwatch microphone in representative acoustic environments. This device-specific dataset is essential for fine-tuning the trained models to the specific acoustic characteristics of the watch microphone, which differs from studio recording equipment in frequency response, sensitivity, and noise floor characteristics. Caregiver speech

samples for Circle of Trust Model evaluation are collected separately under a consent protocol that clearly explains the enrollment procedure and data handling to all participants [3].  All collected audio is resampled to mono 16 kHz, segmented into one-second windows with 50% overlap, amplitude-normalized, and converted to log-Mel spectrograms with 64 Mel bands as the standard feature representation for model training and evaluation [15].

2.2.2   Methodology  2.2.2 Methodology  The methodology of the proposed module consists of six main stages: audio capture and VAD gating, feature extraction, Global Danger Sound Model inference, Circle of Trust Model inference, risk fusion and context modulation, and alert generation and transmission.  In the first stage, the Wear OS audio capture service maintains a continuous ring buffer of microphone samples at 16 kHz mono. Each one-second frame with 0.5-second hop is passed to the Voice Activity Detection module, which determines whether the frame contains speech or a sufficiently loud acoustic event to warrant downstream model activation. Frames classified as silence or low-energy ambient noise are discarded without further processing, conserving battery by preventing unnecessary model inference [3].  In the second stage, frames passing the VAD gate are processed through the log-Mel spectrogram computation pipeline implemented in optimized C++ and TFLite, producing a 64-by-96 time- frequency feature tensor that serves as the shared input representation for both downstream model inference paths [15].  In the third stage, the Global Danger Sound Model processes the log-Mel spectrogram tensor through the compressed MobileNet-V2 or V3-Small TFLite int8 model to produce a scalar probability estimate P(distress) representing the likelihood that the current audio window contains a distress event such as a scream, cry, or threatening vocalization [4].  In the fourth stage, executed only when VAD additionally confirms the presence of speech rather than a non-speech loud event, the Circle of Trust Model processes the speech segment through the speaker encoder to produce a 256-dimensional embedding vector. Cosine similarity is computed against all enrolled caregiver centroids in the trusted registry, and the maximum similarity value is passed through a calibrated sigmoid to produce P(trusted) [6].  In the fifth stage, the risk fusion engine computes the instantaneous risk score from P(distress) and P(trusted), applies the unknown speaker penalty where applicable, and retrieves the current geofence status and Bluetooth Low Energy parent proximity measurements to compute the dynamically modulated alert threshold T'. Exponential Moving Average smoothing is applied to the instantaneous  risk stream with α ≈ 0.3 to produce the smoothed risk estimate [3], [17].  In the sixth stage, the alert manager monitors the smoothed risk stream against the dynamic threshold T' and triggers an alert when continuous exceedance is maintained for the dwell period of one to two seconds. Alert payloads containing only the event label, confidence score, timestamp, and coarse location are transmitted to the guardian application via Bluetooth or cellular connection, and the event is logged in the on-device metadata log for diagnostic purposes [3].  2.2.3   Multi-Sensor Fusion vs. Single-Modality Monitoring  The fundamental architectural choice between cloud-based audio processing and fully on-device processing represents the most significant design decision in the proposed system and directly determines its privacy properties, latency characteristics, connectivity requirements, and practical

deployability in real-world child monitoring contexts.  Cloud-based audio processing architectures transmit raw or compressed audio streams from the wearable device to remote servers where computationally intensive inference operations are performed using server-grade hardware. This approach enables the deployment of significantly larger and more accurate models than can be accommodated on wearable hardware and simplifies the development process by decoupling model complexity from device constraints. However, it introduces unacceptable privacy risks through the transmission of raw audio containing sensitive personal conversations, creates alert latency dependencies on network connectivity quality that may result in delays of several seconds in poor coverage areas, renders the system non-functional during network outages, and imposes ongoing bandwidth and server infrastructure costs [1].  Fully on-device processing, as adopted in the proposed system, performs all inference operations locally on the wearable device using models specifically optimized for the device's computational and memory constraints. This approach eliminates raw audio transmission entirely, providing strong privacy guarantees that are not dependent on server security practices or data retention policies. It ensures consistent alert latency regardless of network conditions, maintains functionality during connectivity outages, and eliminates ongoing server processing costs. The trade-off is the necessity for systematic model compression to meet device constraints, which requires careful architectural design and optimization to minimize accuracy loss [4].  In this research, fully on-device processing is adopted as the definitively superior architectural approach for child safety audio monitoring, where privacy requirements are paramount, network connectivity cannot be assumed in all monitoring contexts, and the latency overhead of cloud round- trips is unacceptable for safety-critical alert delivery [1], [3].  2.3   High Level System Architecture Diagram  The proposed Privacy-Preserving Audio-Based Stranger Threat Detection Module is designed as a modular, single-device-primary architecture that performs all audio intelligence operations on the Wear OS smartwatch, with the cloud layer limited to alert relay and configuration synchronization functions that do not involve audio data. The architecture is structured to ensure real-time processing capability, graceful degradation under connectivity loss, and strict enforcement of the privacy-by- design principles that define the system's data handling approach.  At a high level, the system consists of four primary layers: the audio processing layer, the inference layer, the risk management layer, and the communication layer. The audio processing layer resides entirely on the child's smartwatch and encompasses the microphone capture ring buffer, the Voice Activity Detection module, and the log-Mel spectrogram feature extraction pipeline. This layer operates continuously during system active state and is responsible for the real-time acoustic monitoring function that enables proactive threat detection [3].  The inference layer, also residing on the smartwatch, contains the Global Danger Sound Model and the Circle of Trust Model as separate TFLite runtime instances. The Global Danger Sound Model processes all VAD-activated frames to produce P(distress), while the Circle of Trust Model is invoked only for speech-containing frames to produce P(trusted). Both models execute using the XNNPACK delegate for accelerated integer arithmetic on the watch processor [4].  The risk management layer integrates the inference outputs with the context sensing subsystems comprising the geofencing status monitor using the Android Location Services API and the

Bluetooth Low Energy parent proximity scanner. This layer executes the risk fusion formula, applies Exponential Moving Average smoothing, evaluates the dynamic threshold condition, enforces the dwell time requirement, and manages the on-device learning adaptation processes including unknown speaker clustering and ambient baseline tracking [3], [17].  The communication layer handles transmission of alert metadata payloads and configuration synchronization to the guardian companion application through Bluetooth or cellular connections, and manages the on-device secure storage subsystem using the Android Keystore for encryption of voice embeddings, trusted centroids, and configuration parameters. This layer enforces the strict no- raw-audio transmission constraint that defines the system's privacy architecture [3].

2.3.1   Functional Requirements  Continuous Multi-Sensor Acquisition  The system implements continuous acquisition of accelerometer and gyroscope motion data, PPG- derived heart rate and inter- beat interval series, wrist skin temperature trend, and optional SpO₂ from  the wearable sensor hardware, processed through a windowed feature extraction pipeline that computes the complete physiological and motion feature vector for each monitoring window at configurable intervals [5], [12].  On-Device Fusion and Risk Tiering  The lightweight fusion classifier executes on-device on the Wear OS platform, integrating the complete feature vector with the child's personalized baseline profile to compute a calibrated real- time risk score mapped to the three-tier Normal, Caution, and High risk assessment framework. All classifier inference operates locally without cloud connectivity dependency [3], [10].  Explainable Alert and Check-In Workflow  Haptic check-in prompts on the child's smartwatch, explainable caregiver alert cards with physiological rationale, location context, and recommended actions, and graduated escalation protocols to backup contacts for unacknowledged alerts are all implemented within the alert management subsystem [1], [9].  Environmental Context and Geofencing  Weather API integration on the paired smartphone provides real-time heat index and WBGT-proxy environmental context features at configurable retrieval intervals. Geofencing provides location context for alert metadata and supports context-specific threshold adjustment for known high-risk environments [7], [8].  Privacy-Preserving Logging and Synchronization  Edge-first processing retains all raw sensor data on-device. Encrypted event summaries are synchronized to the cloud backend through the offline-tolerant store-and-forward mechanism. End- to-end encryption and role-based access control protect all stored and transmitted data [3].  2.3.2   Non-Functional Requirements  Performance  The system targets per-frame inference latency below 50 milliseconds for the Global Danger Sound Model on target Wear OS hardware, end-to-end alert delivery latency below 2 seconds, distress recall above 90%, and false alarm rate below 5% in field testing conditions. Battery consumption is targeted below 10% per day under typical monitoring conditions including continuous VAD operation and periodic Bluetooth Low Energy scanning [3], [4].  Reliability  The system maintains basic threat detection and emergency alert functionality during network connectivity loss through local alert storage and on-device boundary checking. Edge-only operation mode using cached parameters ensures continuous monitoring without cloud dependency, with alert

transmission queued for delivery upon connectivity restoration [3].  Security  All voice embeddings, trusted centroids, and configuration parameters are stored using hardware- backed Android Keystore encryption. All data transmission to the guardian application employs TLS encryption. Enrollment and configuration operations require authenticated parental authorization. No raw audio is stored or transmitted under any operating condition [3].  Privacy  The system enforces raw audio non-retention and non-transmission as absolute architectural constraints. Alert payloads contain only minimal metadata. Telemetry is limited to anonymized performance diagnostics. Consent workflows are implemented for all enrollment and configuration operations affecting child data [3].  2.3.3   Other Requirements  Offline Functionality  All threat detection, risk fusion, and alert generation operations function without network connectivity using on-device models and cached context parameters. Alerts generated during offline periods are stored locally with timestamps and transmitted to the guardian application upon connectivity restoration, ensuring no safety events are lost due to network outages [3].  Portability  The system architecture is designed for primary deployment on Wear OS with the Android SDK and TFLite runtime, with architectural provisions for future adaptation to watchOS using Core ML as the inference runtime, requiring no changes to the underlying model architectures or risk fusion logic [3].  Accessibility  The guardian companion application implements high-contrast visual design, readable typography at appropriate sizes for mobile viewing, and haptic feedback for alert notifications to ensure accessibility across diverse user populations including those with visual or auditory impairments.  2.4   Consideration of Aspects of the System  2.4.1   Social Aspects  The deployment of audio-based monitoring technology for child safety carries significant social implications that extend beyond technical performance metrics. In Sri Lanka, where documented rates of child abuse and stranger-related incidents create genuine and well-founded parental concern, a system that proactively detects acoustic distress without requiring the child to consciously activate an alert addresses a critical gap in existing safety technologies that current commercial products have not resolved [1], [2].  The privacy-preserving design philosophy of the proposed system addresses one of the most

significant social barriers to adoption of audio monitoring technology. Parents who are aware of the privacy risks associated with continuous audio transmission to cloud servers may understandably resist deploying such technologies despite their potential safety benefits. By keeping all raw audio on the device and transmitting only minimal metadata, the system provides meaningful safety assurance without requiring parents to accept surveillance-level audio access to their children's acoustic environments [1], [3].  The on-device learning adaptation mechanism that reduces false alarms in normal play environments directly addresses the social risk of alert fatigue. Systems that generate frequent false alarms from children's natural play sounds including shouting, laughing, and energetic physical activity rapidly lose parental trust and are abandoned, leaving children unmonitored. By intelligently distinguishing between normal play acoustics and genuine distress signals through context-aware baseline adaptation, the system maintains its practical utility over extended deployment periods [3].  2.4.2   Security Aspects  Security considerations in a child audio monitoring system extend beyond standard data protection requirements to encompass the specific risks associated with unauthorized access to a system monitoring a child's acoustic environment. Hardware-backed Android Keystore encryption protects all stored voice embeddings and trusted speaker centroids against extraction from lost or stolen devices, ensuring that even physical device compromise does not expose sensitive voice identity data [3].  The authentication requirement for all enrollment and configuration operations prevents unauthorized modification of the trusted speaker registry or alert threshold parameters by individuals who gain temporary access to the smartwatch or the guardian application. Role-based access control distinguishes between primary guardian permissions that allow full system configuration and secondary caregiver permissions that allow alert acknowledgment only [3].  The Bluetooth Low Energy parent proximity scanning implementation uses filtered scanning with parent MAC address or UUID specification to prevent false proximity detections from unrelated Bluetooth devices, ensuring that the threshold modulation mechanism cannot be manipulated by positioning arbitrary Bluetooth devices near the child [18].  2.4.3   Ethical Aspects  The ethical dimensions of a system that continuously monitors the acoustic environment surrounding a child are both complex and consequential. Transparency is a foundational ethical requirement, demanding that all caregivers and children of sufficient maturity are clearly informed that acoustic monitoring is active, what types of sounds trigger processing, and how the resulting data is handled. The distinction between audio-triggered metadata generation and continuous audio surveillance must be clearly communicated to all parties [3].  The collection of caregiver voice samples for Circle of Trust enrollment requires explicit informed consent from all enrolled individuals, who must understand that their voice embeddings will be stored on the child's device and used for speaker verification purposes. The consent workflow implemented in the guardian application documents this agreement and provides mechanisms for enrolled speakers to request removal from the trusted registry [3].

The age-appropriateness of audio monitoring raises important ethical questions about children's privacy and autonomy that intensify as children mature. While young children have limited expectation of acoustic privacy and clear need for proactive safety protection, older children and pre- teenagers may reasonably expect greater privacy in their conversations and social interactions. Future iterations of the system should incorporate age-adaptive monitoring intensity that reduces acoustic surveillance scope as children mature toward adolescence [3].  2.4.4   Limitations  While the proposed system represents a significant advancement over existing static geofencing approaches, several limitations must be acknowledged. The system's adaptive accuracy is dependent on the quality and quantity of historical behavioral data available for each child, meaning that newly enrolled users experience a learning period during which boundary adaptation may be less precise than for established users with rich behavioral histories [10].  The system's performance in dense urban environments with significant GPS signal attenuation, such as areas with tall buildings or underground spaces, remains constrained by fundamental hardware limitations of current GPS technology despite the multi-sensor fusion mitigation strategies employed [7]. Continuous GPS and cloud communication impose battery consumption on the smartwatch that may require daily charging, which may limit adoption for families whose children are not accustomed to wearable devices.  Initial deployment costs including smartwatch hardware, cloud infrastructure, and API service subscriptions represent a financial barrier that may limit accessibility for lower-income families in developing markets, despite the significant safety benefits the system provides [5].  2.5   Commercialization Aspects of the Product  2.5.1   Revenue Earning  The Privacy-Preserving Audio-Based Stranger Threat Detection Module demonstrates strong commercialization potential within the rapidly growing child wearable safety market, projected to expand from 1.2 billion USD in 2024 to 3.5 billion USD by 2033. The system's unique combination of proactive acoustic threat detection, on-device privacy preservation, and contextual intelligence addresses capability gaps in existing commercial products that represent the most significant unmet need among parents seeking comprehensive child safety monitoring solutions [2].  The privacy-preserving architecture represents a particularly compelling commercial differentiator in a market increasingly sensitized to data privacy concerns following high-profile incidents involving children's data. Parents who have been unwilling to adopt cloud-based audio monitoring solutions due to privacy concerns represent a substantial addressable market segment that the proposed system is specifically designed to serve [1], [3].

2.1.1   Target Audience  The primary target audience comprises parents and caregivers of children aged five to thirteen who seek proactive safety monitoring beyond location tracking, particularly those who have concerns about stranger danger in contexts where the child has limited independent mobility including school routes, outdoor play, and community activities. Secondary target audiences include schools and childcare institutions seeking to enhance duty of care monitoring for students in outdoor and transit contexts, and child safety advocacy organizations interested in deploying technology-based protection tools in community settings [2].  2.1.1   Market Space  The proposed system occupies a distinctive position within the child safety wearable market at the intersection of three growing technology segments: wearable AI, privacy-preserving edge computing, and proactive safety monitoring. Current market offerings in the child safety wearable category address only the location monitoring and manual alert segments, leaving the proactive acoustic monitoring segment entirely unserved by commercial products [2]. The growing mainstream awareness of on-device AI capabilities, driven by the proliferation of features like on- device speech recognition and photography AI on smartphones, creates a favorable context for consumer acceptance of on-device acoustic monitoring as a credible and trustworthy privacy- preserving technology approach [1].  2.1.1   Revenue Earning  The primary revenue model comprises a hardware bundle combining a certified child smartwatch with the pre-installed Stranger Threat Detection application, supplemented by a subscription tier providing access to the guardian companion application's advanced analytics features including alert history, false alarm rate reporting, and trusted voice management. An institutional licensing model for schools and childcare facilities enables large-scale deployment with centralized management capabilities and volume pricing. Future revenue opportunities include licensing the on-device audio AI technology stack to other wearable device manufacturers seeking to add proactive safety monitoring capabilities to their product lines [4].  2.2   Testing and Implementation  The implementation and testing phase of the Privacy-Preserving Audio-Based Stranger Threat Detection Module encompasses the complete development lifecycle from model training and compression through Wear OS application integration, component-level validation, and end-to-end system evaluation under both controlled laboratory conditions and representative field scenarios. Given the safety-critical nature of the application and the hard performance constraints governing inference latency, battery consumption, recall, and false alarm rate, rigorous and systematic testing at every level of the system is essential to validate practical deployability [3], [4].  A modular software architecture is adopted throughout the implementation to enable independent development, testing, and optimization of individual pipeline components before integration into the unified system. This approach facilitates targeted debugging of performance issues, enables component-level benchmarking against hardware constraint targets, and supports future maintenance

and model update deployment through over-the-air update mechanisms [3].  2.2.1   Code Implementation of the Research Part  Alert Management System Implementation  Pediatric Physiology of Dehydration and Heat Strain  A thorough understanding of the pediatric physiological responses to dehydration and heat strain is foundational to the design of an effective early-warning system. Children's thermoregulatory systems differ from adults in several important ways that affect both the trajectory of physiological deterioration under heat and exertion stress and the measurable biomarker signatures that accompany it. Children have a higher surface area to body mass ratio that increases relative heat gain from the environment, a lower sweat rate per unit area that reduces evaporative cooling efficiency, and a cardiovascular system that responds to heat and exertion with proportionally larger heart rate increases relative to adults [2], [10].  Under conditions of progressive dehydration, the cardiovascular system responds with a characteristic pattern of compensatory adjustments. Plasma volume contraction reduces venous return and stroke volume, driving heart rate elevation to maintain cardiac output. Simultaneously, thermoregulatory demands increase skin blood flow to support heat dissipation, competing with exercising muscle for the reduced circulating volume and further amplifying cardiovascular strain. Heart rate variability, a measure of the beat-to-beat variability in cardiac cycle length that reflects autonomic nervous system modulation of cardiac function, is progressively suppressed as sympathetic nervous system activation increases to maintain cardiovascular output under the combined demands of exercise, heat, and dehydration [4], [12].  Skin temperature trends provide complementary physiological information that reflects both the thermoregulatory state and the adequacy of peripheral perfusion. During the early stages of heat strain, skin temperature typically rises as heat dissipation mechanisms are activated. As dehydration progresses and thermoregulatory capacity becomes strained, skin temperature trends may reflect reduced peripheral perfusion as the cardiovascular system prioritizes central organ perfusion over peripheral heat dissipation [5], [6]. These temperature dynamics, when tracked as trends over monitoring windows rather than as absolute values, provide meaningful physiological context that augments the heart rate and heart rate variability signals for risk assessment.  Circle of Trust Model Implementation  The Circle of Trust speaker encoder is implemented using the Resemblyzer library for initial development and evaluation, with comparative evaluation of the SpeechBrain ECAPA-TDNN model for potential deployment. The enrollment workflow is implemented as a Wear OS application screen that guides the caregiver through recording three to five speech utterances, computes embeddings for each utterance, averages them to form the speaker centroid, and stores the centroid in the Android Keystore encrypted storage. Inference-time embedding computation and cosine similarity comparison are implemented in Python and compiled to TFLite format for on-device deployment, with the calibrated sigmoid conversion parameters estimated from a held-out enrollment dataset [6].  Wear OS Application Integration  The complete end-to-end pipeline is integrated into a Wear OS application using Kotlin and the Android SDK. The audio capture service runs as a foreground service maintaining the ring buffer and VAD processing loop. TFLite model inference is executed using the XNNPACK delegate for accelerated integer arithmetic. The Android Location Services API provides geofencing status through DWELL transition callbacks, and the Bluetooth LE Scanner API performs parent proximity

scanning with configurable duty cycle. The on-device learning adaptation module maintains embedding buffers and baseline statistics in local encrypted storage and executes clustering operations during device idle periods to minimize interference with real-time monitoring [3].  The guardian companion mobile application is developed using React Native for cross-platform compatibility, implementing real-time alert display with contextual information, alert history and acknowledgment, trusted voice enrollment management, geofence configuration, and Bluetooth Low Energy pairing management [3].  2.2.2   Testing  Unit Testing  Unit testing validates individual pipeline components in isolation against their specified performance targets. The VAD module is tested against a dataset of silent, speech-containing, and loud non-speech audio windows to measure gate accuracy and the fraction of silent windows correctly suppressed without model activation. The Global Danger Sound Model is evaluated on a held-out test partition of the training dataset measuring precision, recall, F1 score, and false alarm rate across all distress and non-distress audio categories. The Circle of Trust Model is evaluated on held-out speaker pairs measuring equal error rate and the accuracy of P(trusted) calibration [3], [4], [6].  Integration Testing  Integration testing validates the data flow between pipeline components under realistic processing conditions. The complete inference chain from VAD gate through feature extraction, Global Danger Sound Model inference, Circle of Trust Model inference, and risk fusion is tested with representative audio inputs measuring end-to-end per-frame processing latency against the 50 millisecond target. Geofence status and Bluetooth Low Energy proximity signal integration with risk fusion threshold modulation is tested against simulated context state sequences to verify correct threshold adjustment behavior [17], [18].  System Testing  System testing evaluates the complete integrated prototype under controlled acoustic conditions representing the primary use case scenarios including playground environments with elevated ambient noise and child vocalization, school settings with classroom and corridor acoustic characteristics, residential environments with typical domestic background sounds, and outdoor public spaces with traffic and crowd noise. Simulated distress events including screams, cries, and threatening speech are introduced into each acoustic context at varying distances from the watch microphone to measure recall and false alarm rate across conditions [3].  Performance Evaluation  The system is evaluated against five primary performance indicators. Distress recall is measured as the fraction of true distress events that generate alert responses within the two-second end-to-end latency target. False alarm rate is measured as the fraction of non-distress audio windows that generate spurious alerts across all tested acoustic contexts. End-to-end latency from the onset of a distress event to guardian alert delivery is measured across ten repeated trials per acoustic context. Battery consumption is measured across eight-hour continuous monitoring sessions on the target hardware. Model memory footprint is measured against the 500 KB TFLite model size target [3], [4].

Guardian Usability Evaluation  Guardian usability evaluation collects qualitative feedback from parent participants on alert clarity, contextual information utility, enrollment workflow usability, and subjective assessment of nuisance alert frequency. Participants are asked to rate the system's alert presentation against a comparative static threshold baseline system to assess the perceived improvement in alert relevance and actionability delivered by the context-aware risk fusion approach [3].  2.3   Tools and Technologies  The development of the Adaptive Geofencing Module required the integration of a carefully selected set of tools, frameworks, libraries, hardware platforms, and external services.
