3.   RESULTS AND DISCUSSION  3.1   Results  The implementation of the proposed Pediatric Dehydration Early-Warning module within the SafePlay child safety ecosystem resulted in a fully functional prototype that successfully integrates multi-sensor physiological monitoring, on-device fusion classification, personalized baseline learning, environmental context integration, and explainable tiered caregiver alert delivery within the edge-first architecture of a Wear OS smartwatch platform. The system was evaluated through a prospective field pilot in school sports and playground contexts, with performance assessed against motion-only and heart-rate-only single-modality baselines using AUROC, AUPRC, precision and recall at the operational threshold, false alarms per hour, median alert lead time, and battery delta metrics.  The multi-sensor feature engineering pipeline successfully computed the complete feature vector from the available sensor modalities across all monitoring sessions, with graceful fallback to the  available sensor subset during periods when optional SpO₂ rea dings were unavailable due to hardware limitations. Activity state classification from accelerometer and gyroscope features correctly identified resting, walking, moderate activity, and vigorous play states across the field pilot sessions, providing the contextual activity labels essential for appropriate physiological signal interpretation [3], [5].  The gradient-boosted tree fusion classifier achieved the strongest performance of the evaluated model architectures, outperforming both the logistic regression variant and the single-modality baselines on all primary evaluation metrics. The complete multi-sensor fusion model achieved AUROC performance substantially above both the motion-only baseline and the HR-only baseline across the field pilot evaluation sessions, demonstrating the quantitative value of multi-modal signal integration for pediatric dehydration risk assessment. AUPRC scores similarly favored the fusion approach, reflecting meaningfully improved precision at high recall operating points that are critical for early-warning applications where missing genuine risk events carries the greatest safety cost [4], [12].  False alarm rate comparison between the fusion system and the single-modality baselines produced the most practically significant performance differentiation. The HR-only baseline generated false alarms at a rate substantially exceeding the operational target during vigorous outdoor play sessions, as generic heart rate ceiling thresholds were repeatedly triggered by the normal physiological heart rate responses of children to physical exertion under warm conditions. The motion-only baseline produced false alarms from vigorous play activities that generated motion profiles partially overlapping with the fall detection signature. The multi-sensor fusion system with personalized thresholds and environmental heat index context achieved substantially lower false alarm rates by correctly interpreting elevated heart rate as contextually appropriate during high-activity high-heat- index periods while correctly identifying the HRV suppression and skin temperature trend patterns associated with developing dehydration risk [7], [8].  Environmental heat index integration demonstrated a clear and consistent contribution to false alarm reduction in warm outdoor conditions. Sessions conducted under high heat index conditions with vigorous child activity showed the largest false alarm reduction advantage for the fusion system relative to the HR-only baseline, confirming that environmental context is particularly valuable precisely in the conditions where dehydration risk is highest and where the need for accurate risk

discrimination is most critical [7], [10].  Individual baseline personalization through the five to seven day learning period produced measurable improvements in per-child false alarm rates relative to population-level threshold parameterization. Children whose resting heart rate and HRV characteristics differed substantially from the population norm benefited most from personalization, with the individually calibrated thresholds correctly classifying their normal high-activity physiological profiles as non-alarming while maintaining sensitivity to genuine deviations from their personal baseline [4], [10].  Heart rate variability proxy features derived from PPG inter-beat interval series demonstrated meaningful discriminative contribution to the fusion model's performance during moderate-intensity activity and recovery periods, where the HRV suppression associated with developing dehydration was most clearly distinguishable from the activity-related autonomic nervous system responses that dominate during vigorous exertion. The combination of HRV proxies with skin temperature trend features provided complementary physiological information that enhanced risk discrimination particularly in the early-to-moderate dehydration risk range that represents the target early-warning window [12].  Alert lead time, measured as the median time between the system generating the first Caution-level alert and the caregiver or observer confirming symptomatic dehydration or administering a hydration intervention, demonstrated a positive median lead time advantage for the fusion system over the single-modality baselines. This lead time advantage represents the practical clinical value of the multi-sensor fusion approach, providing caregivers with meaningful advance warning of developing risk before the child exhibits symptomatic distress that would prompt caregiver action without technological assistance [1], [9].  The explainable alert card interface received positive usability feedback from caregiver participants in the field pilot evaluation, who reported that the plain-language physiological rationale, activity context, and environmental condition information presented in the alert card made the notifications substantially more interpretable and actionable than binary threshold alerts without contextual information. The haptic check-in prompt on the child's smartwatch was reported as an effective mechanism for distinguishing transient risk elevations that resolved with brief rest from persistent risk conditions requiring caregiver intervention [2], [3].  Battery consumption measured across full monitoring day sessions with continuous multi-sensor acquisition, on-device fusion inference, and periodic Bluetooth synchronization demonstrated compliance with the minimal battery impact target. The combination of adaptive sensor polling rates, computation batching, and efficient on-device model inference successfully managed the power budget of continuous physiological monitoring within the practical constraint of full-day wearable deployment [3].  The offline-tolerant store-and-forward synchronization mechanism functioned correctly across all tested connectivity scenarios, retaining event summaries in local encrypted storage during connectivity interruptions and successfully transmitting accumulated records to the cloud backend upon connection restoration without data loss [3].

3.2   Research Findings  The results obtained from the implementation and field evaluation of the Pediatric Dehydration Early-  Warning module lead to several important research findings with implications for the design of pediatric health monitoring systems and the practical deployment of multi-sensor fusion approaches on consumer wearable hardware.  A primary finding is that multi-sensor fusion combining motion, physiological, and environmental context signals achieves meaningfully superior dehydration risk detection performance compared to both motion-only and HR-only single-modality approaches across all primary evaluation metrics including AUROC, AUPRC, false alarm rate, and alert lead time [4], [5]. This finding directly validates the multi-sensor fusion design philosophy and provides quantitative evidence that the additional complexity of integrating multiple sensor modalities is justified by the performance gains achieved, particularly in the false alarm reduction critical to sustained caregiver engagement.  A significant finding concerns the contribution of environmental heat index integration to false alarm reduction during vigorous outdoor activity. The finding that environmental context accounts for a substantial proportion of the false alarm advantage over the HR-only baseline specifically in high-heat-index conditions confirms that physiological signals cannot be reliably interpreted for dehydration risk assessment without environmental context, and that weather-derived heat index represents a practically accessible and highly effective contextual feature for this purpose [7], [8]. This extends the evidence base from the ISO 7243 heat stress assessment framework to the specific application of consumer wearable pediatric health monitoring.  The research found that individual baseline personalization through the five to seven day learning period produces meaningful per-child false alarm reduction, with the benefit concentrated in children whose individual physiological profiles differ substantially from population-level norms [4], [10]. This confirms that population-level thresholds are genuinely inadequate for reliable pediatric physiological monitoring and that individual baseline calibration is a necessary rather than optional feature of effective child health wearable systems.  Heart rate variability proxy features from PPG-derived inter-beat intervals were found to provide genuine discriminative value in the fusion model, particularly during moderate activity and recovery phases, confirming their utility as accessible wearable biomarkers for cardiovascular strain assessment in the target monitoring context despite the motion artifact limitations of wrist PPG during vigorous activity [12]. Future work should prioritize motion artifact reduction to extend the reliability of HRV-based features into the high-activity phases where dehydration risk accumulates most rapidly.  The positive alert lead time advantage of the fusion system over single-modality baselines represents the most clinically meaningful finding of the evaluation, confirming that the multi-sensor approach achieves the practical early-warning objective of providing actionable caregiver guidance before symptomatic dehydration rather than concurrent with or after symptom onset [1], [9].

3.3   Discussion  The results and findings of this study clearly demonstrate that the proposed Pediatric Dehydration Early-Warning module provides a practically deployable, evidence-grounded, and technically effective solution for proactive pediatric health monitoring that substantially outperforms the single- modality monitoring approaches currently available in consumer child safety wearables. The integration of multi-sensor fusion, individual baseline personalization, environmental context, and explainable alert design collectively addresses the three dimensions of the research gap identified in the literature review and delivers quantifiable improvements across all primary performance metrics.  The AUROC and AUPRC performance advantages of the fusion system over single-modality baselines confirm the fundamental scientific premise of the research: that pediatric dehydration risk has a multi-modal physiological signature that is more reliably detected through the integration of complementary sensor signals than through any single modality alone [4], [5], [6]. The specific contribution of HRV suppression in combination with elevated heart rate and adverse skin temperature trends to the fusion model's discriminative performance aligns directly with the established physiological mechanisms of dehydration-induced cardiovascular strain documented by Carter et al. (2005) and Cheuvront et al. (2010), providing empirical validation that the wrist wearable sensor measurements capture the physiological dynamics predicted by the underlying biomedical literature [4], [5].  The environmental heat index integration findings carry important implications for the design of pediatric health monitoring systems more broadly. The demonstrated effectiveness of weather- derived heat index as a contextual feature for reducing false alarms in warm outdoor conditions confirms that environmental awareness is not merely a desirable enhancement but a necessary component of reliable physiological monitoring in the outdoor child activity contexts where dehydration risk is most prevalent [7], [8]. This finding supports the inclusion of environmental context integration as a standard design requirement for next-generation child health wearable systems rather than an optional feature.  The personalization findings reinforce the importance of individual baseline calibration for pediatric physiological monitoring that has been argued on theoretical grounds in the literature but has rarely been empirically validated in field deployment contexts [2], [10]. The practical confirmation that five to seven days of passive baseline learning produces measurable per-child false alarm reduction without requiring any special calibration protocols validates the feasibility of the proposed personalization approach for consumer deployment, where complex calibration requirements would represent a significant adoption barrier.  The explainable alert design findings carry practical implications for the broader field of caregiver- facing health monitoring technology. The strong positive usability feedback for the contextual alert card format relative to binary threshold alerts without rationale suggests that explainability is not merely an academic concern but a practically important feature that affects caregiver engagement, alert response behavior, and sustained system adoption [1], [9]. Future health monitoring system design should treat explainable alert architecture as a primary design requirement rather than a post- hoc addition.  Despite the positive overall findings, the study acknowledges limitations. PPG-derived HRV proxy accuracy during vigorous activity remains a constraint that limits the system's performance

advantage during the high-activity phases where dehydration risk accumulates most rapidly. Weather API heat index may not accurately reflect microenvironmental conditions at specific outdoor locations. The field pilot sample size and demographic range are constrained by practical access and consent considerations, and larger longitudinal field studies would provide stronger validation of the system's real-world performance across diverse child populations and climate conditions [3], [7].  Overall, the discussion confirms that the proposed Pediatric Dehydration Early-Warning module is both technically sound and practically valuable for real-world deployment as a component of the SafePlay child safety ecosystem, representing a validated advancement toward proactive, personalized, and explainable pediatric health safety monitoring on consumer wearable platforms.  4.   CONCLUSION  The proposed Pediatric Dehydration Early-Warning module for child safety wearables successfully demonstrates the practical feasibility and clinical effectiveness of multi-sensor physiological fusion with individual baseline personalization and environmental context integration for proactive pediatric dehydration risk detection on consumer Wear OS smartwatch hardware. As a core component of the SafePlay smartwatch-based child safety ecosystem, the system provides a complete end-to-end early-warning solution that addresses the fundamental limitation of existing consumer child health wearables: their reliance on single-signal monitoring with generic adult- derived thresholds that lack the physiological sensitivity, contextual intelligence, and child-specific personalization required for meaningful early detection of developing dehydration and heat strain in pediatric populations. Through the integration of accelerometer and gyroscope motion signals, PPG- derived heart rate and heart rate variability proxies, wrist skin temperature trend features, optional  SpO₂ monitoring, and weather -derived heat index environmental context within a lightweight gradient-boosted fusion classifier personalized through individual baseline learning, the system delivers earlier, more accurate, and lower false-alarm dehydration risk assessment than either motion-only or heart-rate-only single-modality baseline approaches, validated through prospective field evaluation in school sports and playground contexts [4], [5], [6].  The research confirms that the multi-modal physiological signature of developing pediatric dehydration, comprising the coordinated pattern of heart rate elevation, HRV suppression, adverse skin temperature trends, and contextually inappropriate cardiovascular strain given activity state and environmental heat load, is meaningfully more reliably detected through multi-sensor fusion than through any single physiological or motion biomarker in isolation. This finding directly validates the scientific premise of the research and provides empirical evidence that the additional system complexity of multi-sensor integration is fully justified by the performance gains achieved across all primary evaluation metrics including AUROC, AUPRC, false alarm rate, and alert lead time [4], [12]. The demonstrated superiority over single-modality baselines is not merely a marginal improvement but a qualitatively meaningful difference in practical monitoring capability that translates directly to earlier caregiver notification and greater opportunity for preventive intervention before clinical dehydration symptoms manifest.  The contribution of environmental heat index integration to false alarm reduction in warm outdoor conditions represents one of the most practically significant findings of this research. The evidence that physiological monitoring without environmental context cannot reliably distinguish pathological

cardiovascular responses from the normal adaptive responses of healthy active children to physical exertion in hot conditions confirms that environmental awareness is a necessary component of any reliable pediatric health monitoring system targeting outdoor activity contexts [7], [8]. The practical accessibility of weather-derived heat index through standard weather APIs on paired smartphones makes this contextual enhancement immediately deployable without additional hardware cost, establishing environmental context integration as a design principle that should be adopted as standard in next-generation child health wearable system design.  Individual baseline personalization through the five to seven day passive learning period addresses the fundamental inadequacy of population-level physiological thresholds for child health monitoring. The empirical validation that individually calibrated thresholds produce measurable false alarm reduction relative to population norms in field deployment conditions confirms the practical necessity of personalization for reliable pediatric physiological monitoring and demonstrates that the proposed passive learning approach achieves meaningful personalization without requiring complex or intrusive calibration procedures that would impede consumer adoption [2], [10]. As children grow and their physiological characteristics evolve, the progressive baseline updating through exponential smoothing ensures that personalization accuracy is maintained over extended deployment periods without requiring periodic recalibration.  The explainable alert architecture delivering contextual alert cards with plain-language physiological rationale, activity context, environmental conditions, and actionable guidance represents a meaningful advancement in health monitoring user experience design for non-specialist caregiver audiences. The positive usability feedback from field pilot participants confirms that contextual explainability substantially improves the practical utility of health monitoring alerts for parents and coaches who lack medical expertise but bear responsibility for responding appropriately to child health risk indicators [1], [9]. This finding establishes explainable alert design as a practically important rather than merely academically desirable feature for caregiver-facing health monitoring systems.  The privacy-preserving edge-first architecture retaining all raw physiological data on-device and transmitting only encrypted event summaries to cloud services provides a data protection approach appropriate to the sensitivity of continuous children's health monitoring data. The demonstrated ability to deliver meaningful early-warning performance within this strict privacy constraint validates edge-first processing as a practically sufficient and ethically preferable architecture for pediatric health monitoring, establishing privacy-by-design as an achievable rather than aspirational design principle in this application domain [3], [7].  The positive alert lead time advantage of the fusion system over single-modality baselines carries the most direct clinical implication of the research findings. Pediatric dehydration and heat strain are conditions where the outcome difference between early intervention and delayed response can be substantial, and the demonstrated ability of the multi-sensor fusion approach to generate actionable caregiver alerts before symptomatic onset confirms that the system achieves its primary clinical objective of enabling earlier intervention than would be possible without technological monitoring assistance [1], [2]. This lead time advantage represents the fundamental practical value of the proposed system and provides the strongest argument for its adoption as a component of comprehensive child safety monitoring ecosystems.  Several directions for future research and system enhancement emerge from the findings and limitations of this study. Motion artifact reduction in PPG-derived HRV computation during vigorous activity represents the most significant technical improvement opportunity, as reliable HRV

features during high-intensity play would substantially extend the system's performance advantage into the activity phases where dehydration risk accumulates most rapidly [4], [12]. Future work should investigate adaptive motion artifact removal algorithms that improve PPG signal quality during vigorous activity without introducing the latency that would compromise real-time monitoring capability.  Expansion of the field evaluation to larger and more demographically diverse participant samples across different age groups, climate contexts, and activity types would provide stronger validation of the system's generalizability and support the development of more robust age-stratified personalization parameters. The current field pilot's constraints on participant numbers and evaluation duration represent a practical limitation that longitudinal deployment studies with larger cohorts would address [3], [10].  Microenvironmental heat index sensing through BLE-connected ambient thermometers, as suggested in the project facilities specification, would improve the accuracy of environmental context beyond what weather API data can provide in specific outdoor locations with significant microenvironmental variation such as shaded playground areas and partially enclosed sports facilities [8]. Future iterations should investigate the practical benefit of local microenvironmental sensing relative to the additional hardware cost and deployment complexity it introduces.  The underlying multi-sensor physiological fusion architecture developed in this research has broad applicability beyond the specific pediatric dehydration early-warning context. The framework of combining motion context, multi-modal physiological signals, and environmental context for personalized health risk assessment on consumer wearable hardware could be valuably extended to other vulnerable population health monitoring applications including elderly heat strain monitoring, occupational health monitoring in hot working environments, and athlete hydration management during endurance sports. Future research in these application domains would provide valuable cross- domain validation of the architectural principles established in this work.  In conclusion, this research presents a comprehensive, evidence-grounded, technically validated, and ethically considered solution for proactive pediatric dehydration early warning on consumer wearable platforms. It successfully demonstrates how multi-sensor physiological fusion, individual baseline personalization, environmental context integration, and explainable alert design can be combined within the edge-first architecture of a Wear OS smartwatch to create a child health safety system that is simultaneously more physiologically sensitive, more contextually intelligent, more personally calibrated, and more practically useful than the single-signal monitoring approaches that currently define the consumer child health wearable market. The Pediatric Dehydration Early- Warning module not only addresses the critical gap in existing child safety technologies but establishes a strong scientific and technical foundation for the continued advancement of proactive, personalized, and privacy-preserving pediatric health safety monitoring within the SafePlay ecosystem and the broader child safety technology field [3], [4], [6], [12].  demonstrates the practical feasibility and clinical effectiveness of multi-sensor physiological fusion with individual baseline personalization and environmental context integration for proactive pediatric dehydration risk detection on consumer Wear OS smartwatch hardware. 1. INTRODUCTION  In undergraduate group projects, the formation of project groups and the selection of the topic for those projects are two of the most critical initial decisions to made at the process of group project life cycle. Those two decisions directly determine whether a group have the necessary technical skills to deliver a better output, whether individual group members  have equal workloads and whether the group’s collective effort is enough for meet the  demands of the chosen topic. Except for this, team formation and topic validation in most institutions including SLIIT still remain entirely informal which relying on random assignment, self-grouping or brief supervisor interviews with no data driven process of team balance or topic readiness.  This research addresses the first most layer of the Intelligent Project Management System: the Intelligent Team Formation and Topic Feasibility Analysis component. While other members handles the project planning (Lekamge R.M.D.), risk monitoring (Kulathunga S.A.I.K.), quality assessment (Rashmika R.M.D.). This component is responsible for ensuring every group project begins with a group that is composed mathematically validated for skill balance, personality diverse and ready for the chosen topic effectively by eliminating the foundational problems introduced by ad hoc team assignment.  This system directly supports UN Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by ensuring that every undergraduate, regardless of their social network or self-sufficient skills is placed in a group that maximizes their probability equation of project success through evidence-based, algorithmic matching.  1.1 Background and Context  The results of poor group formation in undergraduate group projects are well documented and significant, Oakley et al. (2004) established that improper unbalanced team formations which those where high performing students are clustered or where critical skills are no where to be found are in the main structural predictors of project failure and the free rider  phenomenon, which is low contributing members get benefit from high performers’ efforts  without commencing any Contribution for the project [1].Studies of multiple institutions have shown that randomly formed groups perform significantly worse in average than the groups formed through structured, skill matching processes [2].  Other than a balanced group, the deeper challenge is aligning the topic to the group. Which is also known as the cold start problem of group projects. A certain group can be internally balanced in terms of skills yet collectively lack the specific technical skill that regard to the topic that is chosen by the group. For example, a group building a ML system with no member experienced in python or data preprocessing is structurally set up to fail from the day one. No existing student facing tool validates this alignment before project begins. Supervisors typically discover such mistakes only two weeks into the project, in that point significant time and effort has been wasted already.  The combination of Sentence Transformers and multi objective evolutionary algorithms has uncovered new possibilities for data driven group formation. Reimers and Gurevych

(2019) have demonstrated that Sentence-BERT produces semantically meaningful vector representations of the text that get skill relatedness more accurately that keyword matching [3]. Also, Deb et al. (2002) established NSGA-II as the gold standard algorithm for multi objective optimization problems where multiple competing criteria must be parallelly optimized accurately the structure of group formation problem [4]. Chen and Guestrin (2016) showed the superiority of XGBoost for tubular classification tasks including predicting of the outcome form structured feature vectors [5], establishing its suitability for the Feasibility Prediction module.  1.2 Literature Review  A detailed review of existing literature was conducted across the domains of automated team formation, multi objective optimization, semantic skill profiling and educational outcome prediction.  1.2.1 Automated and Constraint-Based Team Formation  The issue of algorithmically forming balanced groups has been studied extensively in both educational and professional contexts. Borrego et al. (2013) reviewed group formation strategies in engineering education and found out that structured skill based matching consistently outperformed random assignment on project quality [6]. The CATME system (Layton et al. 2010) is the most widely deployed automated group formation tool in higher education, using student self-reported skills and schedule availability to suggest group compositions. [7]. However, CATME relies on ordinal self-assessment scales that are highly susceptible to dunning-Kruger bias, does not incorporate semantic skill profiling and has no process to validating group readiness against a specific topic. Its group formation objective is also single dimensional with no consideration of personality diversity or multi objective tradeoffs.  More capable multi objective approaches have been found in the software engineering group   formation   literature.   Gutiérrez-Rodríguez   et   al.   (2016)   applied   evolutionary algorithms to form development teams that parallelly optimize technical skill coverage and collaboration potential [8]. That shows the feasibility of evolutionary team formation but does not point out the cold start feasibility dimension that is core to this research.  1.2.2 Semantic Skill Profiling with Sentence Transformers  Former skill profiling platforms shows skills as discrete labels or ordinal scores, losing the semantic relationships between related skills. Reimers and Gurevych (2019) introduced Sentence-BERT (SBERT), which produces rich vector representations of sentences and short documents that capture semantic similarity with mostly higher accuracy than prior methods [3]. The all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model used in this component makes 384 dimensional embeddings optimized for semantic textual similarity tasks with low computational overhead, making it suitable for real-time student profiling at cohort scale.  The application of SBERT to student skill profiling has been explored by Ramos et al. (2022), who demonstrated that SBERT-encoded competency descriptions align well with expert judgments of skill relatedness in professional competency frameworks [9]. This

validates the core embedding approach of the Student Vector Profiling Engine proposed in this component.  1.2.3 Multi-Objective Optimization for Team Composition  Deb et al. (2002) introduces NSGA-II an elitist non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm that process a variety of Pareto-optimal front of solutions for multi-objective optimization problems [4]. NSGA-II became the mostly cited multi-objective evolutionary algorithm in engineering optimization literature. The pymoo library (Blank and Deb 2020) provides a high grade Python Implementation NSGA-II with well structured APIs for custom objective function definition and constraint specification [10], making that directly suitable for the group formation optimization formulated in this component.  The three objective formulation used in this component maximizing skill coverage, minimizing skill redundancy and maximizing personality diversity in novel in the educational group formation context and draws inspiration from the workforce diversity optimization literature for similar multi objective formulations have showed superior group performance outcomes over single object approaches [11].  1.2.4 Predictive Modelling for Educational Outcomes  Chen and Guestrin (2016) introduced XGBoost, a gradient boosting framework which has consistently gained state of the art performance on tubular classification tasks across a wide range of domains [5]. In educational data mining, Romero and Ventura (2010) showed that gradient boosting models applied to student academic performances can predict project outcome with much accuracy than ever before [12]. Most recent work by Lundberg and Lee (2017) introduced SHAP values as a theoretically grounded framework for explaining individual predictions of complex models [13] enabling the transparency that wanted for an academic decision support tool where supervisors must be able to understand and  question the system’s recommendations.  The mix of XGBoost for outcome prediction and SHAP for explanation is now considered best practice in high stakes educational prediction systems [14] and it is the initial approach adopted in the Topic Feasibility Predictor in this component.  1.2.5 Existing Tools and Their Limitations  A proper survey of already existing team formation and topic validation tools uncovers consistent and critical gaps. CATME (Layton et al. 2010) addresses group balance via self report but has no NLP based profiling, no multi objective optimization and no topic feasibility validation. TeamMaker and similar tools apply ruler based matching but are they are rely on certain domains and lack semantic understanding of skill content. Random or self-selection paths, skill the norm at SLIIT and most institutions have introduce systematic bias towards homogeneous groups. No existing tool in the world combines the semantic kill profiling, multi objective evolutionary group optimization and ML based topic feasibility validation in a single integrated pipeline and confirming the novelty and the necessity of this research component.

3. METHODOLOGY  This research adopts a Design Science Research (DSR) methodology (Hevner et al., 2004), which is well-suited for projects that create and evaluate an innovative IT artifact solving a unaddressed clearly defined practical problem [15]. The methodology proceeds through five structured phases: Problem Definition, System Design, Prototype Development, Evaluation, and Iteration.  3.1 Research Approach  The DSR approach is applied like this. The research problem is the absence of data-driven, skill-aware group formation and topic feasibility validation in undergraduate projects is formally defined through literature review and stakeholder analysis. A solution artifact (the Intelligent Team Formation and Topic Feasibility Analysis system) is designed and constructed   through   development   cycles.   The   artifact   is   evaluated   against   defined performance metrics using empirical methods, and iterative refinements are made based on evaluation outcomes. This ensures the system is both technically rich and practically useful within the SLIIT undergraduate research ecosystem.  Dataset   Selection   and   Acquisition:   Three   publicly   available   Kaggle   datasets   are employed to support the training, calibration, and validation of the system's machine learning components. The Students' Academic Performance Dataset (xAPI-Edu-Data, Aljarah et al., Kaggle, 2016) contains 480 university student records across 16 features including grade level, section, topic, engagement metrics (raised hands, visited resources, discussion participation), and a three-class academic performance label (Low / Medium / High) which is binarized to a project success outcome label (pass / fail) for XGBoost feasibility predictor training, and used to validate SBERT-encoded skill vector cosine similarity against expert-assigned performance levels. The Higher Education Students Performance Evaluation Dataset (Kaggle, 2022) provides multi-module GPA scores, demographic attributes, and academic engagement indicators for university students across multiple semesters, used to calibrate the Student Vector Profiling Engine and to verify the L2-normalised skill vector construction against externally validated student capability rankings. The Student Performance Factors Dataset (Kaggle, 2024) contains 6,607 student records with GPA, study habits, extracurricular participation, parental involvement, and exam   scores,   used   to   generate   realistic   synthetic   cohort   populations   for   NSGA-II population initialization experiments and to validate that the three-objective Pareto-front correctly identifies diverse, balanced team configurations relative to traditional ground- truth human-assigned team quality ratings.  3.2 Technical Methods and Algorithms  Student Vector Profiling Engine:   Each student's profile is encoded in two stages. First, academic signals (normalized module grades and GPA) are concatenated as a structured numeric vector, with normalization parameters derived from the Higher Education Students Performance Evaluation Dataset (Kaggle, 2022), which provides multi-semester GPA distributions used to establish cohort-level normalization bounds. Second, free-text skill

survey responses are processed by the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 SBERT model to produce a 384- dimensional semantic embedding. Cosine similarity validation of the SBERT encoder is performed against skill-pair ground-truth labels derived from the xAPI-Edu-Data dataset (Kaggle, 2016), where students in the same topic section and grade tier are treated as positively similar pairs and cross-topic, cross-tier pairs as negatively dissimilar confirming  a mean cosine similarity of ≥ 0.80 on held -out validation pairs. The two representations are concatenated and L2-normalized to produce the final student skill vector S   ∈   R^384. Big Five personality trait scores are encoded separately as a 5-dimensional vector and appended during team formation objective computation.  NSGA-II Optimization Engine:   Group formation is modelled as a combinatorial multi- objective optimization problem. Given a cohort of N students and a target team size of k (default: 4), the search space is all valid k-partitions of N students. The three objective functions are: (1) Skill Coverage: the fraction of unique skill dimensions covered by at least one team member above a threshold; (2) Skill Redundancy: the mean pairwise cosine similarity between member vectors (to be minimized); and (3) Personality Diversity: the mean Euclidean distance between member Big Five vectors (to be maximized). NSGA-II with population size 200 and 500 generations is applied using pymoo 0.6. Population initialization experiments use synthetic cohort populations generated from the Student Performance Factors Dataset (Kaggle, 2024), where each student's GPA, study habits, extracurricular score, and exam performance are mapped to skill vector dimensions, enabling controlled validation of the Pareto-front quality across cohort sizes of 40, 60, 80, and   100   students.   The   engine   produces   a   Pareto-front   of   non-dominated   team configurations from which the top-ranked solution per group is selected.  Topic Feasibility Predictor:   For each student team-topic pairing, a feature vector is constructed comprising: the L2-normalised aggregated team skill vector (element-wise mean of member vectors), the SBERT-encoded topic requirement vector, the cosine similarity scalar between the two, the GPA variance across team members, and the team size. A XGBoost classifier (max depth 6, learning rate 0.05, 300 estimators) is trained on binary outcome labels derived from the xAPI-Edu-Data dataset (Aljarah et al., Kaggle, 2016), where the three-class academic performance label (Low / Medium / High) is binarized low mapped to failure (0), Medium and High mapped to success (1)   —   producing 480 labelled team-topic pairing records across 16 features. The dataset's topic and section attributes are used as proxy topic-requirement identifiers, and student engagement features (raised hands, visited resources, discussion participation) are mapped to skill coverage dimensions within the 384-dimensional vector space. Training uses 5-fold stratified cross- validation. Class imbalance (127 Low vs 353 Medium+High) is addressed using SMOTE oversampling on the training folds. Probability outputs are calibrated via Platt scaling (CalibratedClassifierCV with sigmoid method). SHAP TreeExplainer computes per- feature contributions for every prediction.  Cold-Start Skill Validator:   The aggregated team skill vector is compared against the topic requirement vector using element wise subtraction to identify specific skill dimensions where the team falls below the required threshold. Dimensions with a gap magnitude

exceeding a configurable threshold (default: 0.3 on the normalized scale) are flagged as critical gaps. The validator generates a structured skill-gap report listing each flagged dimension, its current team coverage score, the required score, and the magnitude of the gap. Teams with a predicted feasibility score below 60% are automatically flagged for supervisor review.  3.3 Tools and Platforms  •   Programming Language: Python 3.11 (ML/NLP backend), JavaScript/TypeScript (React frontend)  •   NLP Framework: HuggingFace Sentence-Transformers (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), spaCy v3  •   Multi-Objective Optimization: pymoo 0.6 (NSGA-II implementation)  •   Machine Learning: XGBoost 2.x, scikit-learn (Platt scaling, SMOTE via imbalanced-learn), SHAP  •   Backend API: FastAPI (Python), OpenAPI 3.0 documentation  •   Frontend Dashboard: React 18, Recharts (radar charts, bar charts), Tailwind CSS  •   Database: PostgreSQL 15 (student profiles, team configurations, feasibility scores)  •   Cloud: AWS EC2 (model serving), AWS S3 (profile data storage)  •   Version Control: GitHub (integrated with parent IPMS contribution analytics module)  •   Testing: Pytest (unit/integration), Locust (load testing)  3.4 Data Collection and Ethical Considerations  Primary model training and validation data is sourced from three publicly available Kaggle datasets: the Students' Academic Performance Dataset (xAPI-Edu-Data, Aljarah et al., Kaggle, 2016) for XGBoost feasibility predictor training and SBERT profiling validation, the Higher Education Students Performance Evaluation Dataset (Kaggle, 2022) for student skill vector normalization calibration and the Student Performance Factors Dataset (Kaggle, 2024) for NSGA-II population initialization experiments across controlled cohort sizes. All three datasets are publicly licensed, anonymized, and contain no personally identifiable information. In addition to these external datasets, supplementary institutional data will be collected from two sources: (1) anonymized historical student academic records and project outcome labels from past IT4010 cohorts at SLIIT, with written permission from the Department of Information Technology, used to fine tune the XGBoost model to the SLIIT academic context and (2) a pilot study involving current IT4010 students who voluntarily consent to complete the skill survey and personality assessment instruments. All SLIIT student data will be fully anonymized prior to processing. No personally identifiable information will be retained in the system after the anonymization. Ethical clearance will be obtained from the SLIIT Ethics Review Committee before any institutional data collection begins. Ground-truth labels for the XGBoost feasibility model

will be derived from supervisor-assigned final project grades, with a binary success threshold set at a grade of C or above.  3.5 Validation Strategy and Performance Metrics  •   SBERT Profiling Accuracy: Mean cosine similarity ≥ 0.80 against expert - validated skill pairings; validated using positive/negative pairs derived from xAPI-Edu-Data topic and grade tier groupings  •   Dataset Representativeness: Overlap between xAPI-Edu-Data feature space and SLIIT student profile schema evaluated via Jaccard similarity on feature label  sets; score ≥ 0.70 required before XGBoost training proceeds on the external  dataset  •   NSGA- II Team Quality: Expert quality rating ≥ 4.0/5.0 on balance and diversity  criteria; Pareto-front quality validated across synthetic cohorts of 40 – 100 students generated from Student Performance Factors Dataset (Kaggle, 2024)  •   XGBoost Feasibility Predictor: F1- score ≥ 0.82 and AUC - ROC ≥ 0.85 on held -out test set; class imbalance (127 Low vs 353 Medium+High in xAPI-Edu-Data) addressed via SMOTE; performance reported separately on external Kaggle test split and SLIIT institutional holdout  •   System Throughput: Team formation for 100 students completed within 60 seconds on standard server hardware  •   Supervisor Satisfaction: Satisfaction score ≥ 4.0/5.0 from dashboard usability  evaluation

4. HIGH-LEVEL SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE  The Intelligent Group Formation and Topic Feasibility Analysis component follows a modular, pipeline-based architecture consisting four primary subsystems: the Student Vector Profiling Engine, the NSGA-II Optimization Engine, the Topic Feasibility Predictor and Cold-Start Validator, and the IPMS Integration API and Dashboard. This component interfaces directly with the broader IPMS architecture, receiving student profile data and research topic submissions as input, and returning validated team configurations, feasibility scores, and skill-gap reports to the supervisor and student dashboards.  4.1 Component Overview  Input Layer:   Student academic records, skill survey responses, and personality assessment data are submitted via the IPMS onboarding interface. Research topic proposal documents (PDF/DOCX) are submitted by student groups via the IPMS proposal submission module. All inputs are validated and pre-processed using spaCy before entering the profiling pipeline.  Student Vector Profiling Engine:   Each student's multi-modal profile data is processed by the SBERT encoding pipeline to produce a 384-dimensional skill vector. Vectors are stored in the PostgreSQL profile store and made available for batch retrieval during the optimization phase.  NSGA-II Optimization Engine:   When a team formation request is received (e.g., at the start of the academic project cycle), the optimization engine retrieves all student vectors for the cohort and runs NSGA-II to generate Pareto-optimal team configurations. The top- ranked configuration per group is selected and stored.  Topic Feasibility Predictor:   Once a team-topic pairing is submitted, the XGBoost model computes a Success Probability score and the SHAP explainer generates feature level attributions. The Cold-Start Validator performs element wise skill gap analysis and generates the structured gap report.  Dashboard Layer:   All outputs are rendered on the IPMS supervisor dashboard (React 18) with radar charts showing per-team skill coverage, feasibility score badges, SHAP waterfall explanation views, and skill-gap heatmaps. Students have access to their own skill profile and gap report.

Figure 1: High-Level System Architecture of the Intelligent Team Formation and Topic Feasibility Analysis Component  4.2 Component Interactions and Data Flow  The data flow is conitous from profile ingestion to team output and then branching through the feasibility prediction pipeline. Student profiles enter the Input Layer, pass through the Profiling Engine, and their vectors are stored in the PostgreSQL profile store. The NSGA- II engine then operates on the full cohort vector set to generate team configurations. Once teams are formed, each team-topic pairing is submitted to the Feasibility Predictor, which returns a Success Probability score, SHAP explanations, and a skill-gap report. All outputs are exposed via the IPMS REST API and rendered on the React dashboard. Integration with the parent IPMS is achieved via RESTful APIs: the parent system sends a team formation request with the cohort student ID list; this component returns a team configuration object containing member assignments, skill-coverage matrices, and feasibility assessments in JSON format.  Figure 2: Student Vector Profiling and NSGA-II Team Optimization Pipeline  4.3 Scalability and Security Considerations

•   The FastAPI backend is containerized using Docker with horizontal scaling for peak formation periods (e.g., start of academic year).  •   NSGA-II optimization is computationally intensive for large cohorts; parallelization is implemented using Python multiprocessing for population evaluation.  •   All inter service communication is encrypted via HTTPS/TLS 1.3; student profile data is encrypted at rest using AES-256.  •   Role-based access control (RBAC) ensures students can access only their own skill profile and gap report and supervisors see cohort-level team configurations and feasibility dashboards.  •   The XGBoost model is version-controlled and retrainable on each new cohort's outcome data to improve prediction accuracy over time.

Figure 3: Topic Feasibility Analysis and Cold-Start Validation Workflow

5. USER REQUIREMENTS  5.1 Stakeholder Identification  •   Students: Primary users who complete the skill survey and personality assessment, view their skill profile vectors, and receive skill-gap reports for their assigned topic.  •   Supervisors: Secondary users who initiate team formation cycles, review and optionally override AI-generated team configurations, and access cohort level feasibility dashboards.  •   System Administrator (IPMS): Manages cohort enrollment, configures team size and feasibility thresholds, and monitors model retraining cycles.  5.2 Functional Requirements  FR#   Requirement Name  Description  FR1   Student Profile Intake  The system shall accept student academic grades, GPA, skill survey responses, and personality assessment answers as profile inputs via the IPMS onboarding interface.  FR2   SBERT Skill Vector Generation  The system shall encode each student's profile into a 384- dimensional semantic skill vector using the Sentence-BERT all- MiniLM-L6-v2 model.  FR3   Team Formation Request  The system shall accept a cohort level group formation request specifying the cohort student list and target team size (default: 4).  FR4   NSGA-II  Optimization  The system shall run NSGA-II multi-objective   optimization   to generate Pareto-optimal team configurations   maximizing   skill coverage,   minimizing   redundancy, and   maximizing   personality diversity.  FR5   Team Configuration Output  The system shall return a ranked list of Pareto-optimal team configurations with per-team skill-coverage matrices and diversity scores.  FR6   Topic Submission   The system shall accept research topic proposal documents (PDF/DOCX) and encode topic requirements using SBERT for feasibility analysis.  FR7   Feasibility Prediction  The system shall compute an XGBoost-based Success Probability score (0–100%) for each team-topic pairing with Platt-calibrated confidence.  FR8   SHAP Explanation   The system shall generate SHAP-based feature attribution explanations for each feasibility score prediction.  FR9   Skill-Gap Report   The system shall generate a structured skill-gap report for each team- topic pairing identifying concept level gaps and flagging teams below the configured threshold.  FR10   Supervisor Override  The system shall allow supervisors to manually adjust AI-generated team configurations and log all overrides with timestamps and justification notes. Accuracy   The SBERT profiling engine shall achieve mean cosine similarity ≥ 0.80; the XGBoost predictor shall achieve F1-score ≥ 0.82 and AUC-ROC ≥ 0.85.  Usability   The supervisor dashboard shall achieve a satisfaction score of ≥ 4.0/5.0 from supervisor evaluation panels. 6. COMMERCIALIZATION PLAN  6.1 Target Market and Customer Persona  The initial market for this system consists of higher education institutions in Sri Lanka and the broader South and Southeast Asian region that run project-based undergraduate programs in STEM and IT disciplines. The immediate target is SLIIT, with potential expansion to the University of Moratuwa, NSBM Green University, the Informatics Institute of Technology, and regionally to universities in India, Malaysia, and Singapore that operate comparable undergraduate research frameworks. Secondary markets include corporate graduate development programs and EdTech platforms providing solid project management services.  6.2 Value Proposition  The system offers three core value propositions: (1) it eliminates the free rider problem by ensuring every team begins with a mathematically balanced, skill-diverse composition, reducing the structural inequity that random assignment introduces; (2) it prevents wasted project effort by identifying team-topic mismatches before work begins, enabling early intervention and topic reselection where necessary and (3) it provides institutional administrators with a fully auditable, data-driven record of every team formation decision, supporting accreditation requirements for fair and transparent assessment practices.  6.3 Revenue Model  •   Institutional Licensing: Annual per-institution licensing fee based on active student enrollment (e.g., LKR 500,000 – 2,000,000 per year for institutions of 500 –  5,000 students).  •   SaaS API Access: Per-formation API pricing for EdTech platforms integrating the NSGA-II formation engine and feasibility predictor into their own products.  •   Premium Analytics Module: Cohort level longitudinal analytics dashboard tracking the relationship between team formation quality scores and final project outcomes over multiple academic years.  •   Model Retraining Services: Annual model retraining contracts to update the XGBoost feasibility predictor on each institution's latest students outcome data.  6.4 Competitive Advantage  Unlike   CATME   (ordinal   self-report,   single-objective,   no   feasibility   validation), TeamMaker (rule-based, no NLP), or random/self-selection (no data), this system is the only   solution   that   mix   semantic   NLP-based   student   profiling   with   multi-objective evolutionary team optimization and ML-based topic feasibility prediction in a single integrated pipeline. Its XGBoost model improves in accuracy with every new cohort of outcome data creating a compounding predictive advantage that is structurally difficult for competitors to replicate. Its deep integration with the IPMS parent system creates a significant institutional switching cost.

APPENDICES  Appendix A: Skill Survey Instrument  The skill survey used to generate SBERT input text comprises 20 questions across five domain categories: (1) Programming and Software Development (e.g., "Describe your experience with Python, including the types of projects you have built"); (2) Data Science and Machine Learning (e.g., "What ML algorithms or frameworks have you applied in academic or personal projects?"); (3) Database Systems and Backend Development; (4) Frontend and User Interface Development; and (5) Research and Academic Writing Skills. Each response is a free-text entry of 50 – 200 words. The concatenated responses from all five categories form the SBERT encoding input. A separate 16-item Big Five Inventory (BFI-10 variant adapted for academic context) captures Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism on a 5-point Likert scale. DECLARATION  I declare that this is my own work, and this proposal does not knowingly incorporate any material previously submitted for a degree or diploma at any other university or higher education institution, nor does it contain any material that has been previously published or written by another person apart from where proper acknowledgment is given in the text. ABSTRACT  There   are   two   foundational   but   unaddressed   challenges   in   undergraduate   project management. The formation of balanced, skill-full project teams and early validation of topic feasibility. Previous approaches to the group projects at any institution rely on random group allocation, self-selection or purely manual supervisor decisions without no proper  consideration of the idea of team members’ skills, member’s personality diversity or alignment between the team’s collective performance and the requirements of the chosen  topic. This research is to propose an AI   powered Intelligent Team Formation and Topic Feasibility Analysis system as the first component of the broader Intelligent Project Management System for Undergraduate Students.  The research gap that we have identified lies in the absence of any system that simultaneously optimizes group composition across multiple competing objectives and validates the readiness of that group for a specific research topic or any other project topic  before the work begins; There by solving the cold start problem that reduces the project’s  outcomes from the very first day of the project. The proposed solution suggests a four stage pipeline: (1) an SBERT based student Vector Profiling Engine that encodes each student's academic grades (GPA), survey reported skills and personality traits into a unified 384 dimensional semantic skill vector; (2) An NSGA-II multi objective optimization engine that generates optimal group configuration by simultaneously maximizing skill coverage and minimizing skill redundancy and maximizing personality diversity; (3) An XGBoost based Topic Feasibility Predictor that measures a Success Probability score (0   –   100%) for each group-topic pairing using cosine similarity betwee n the group’s aggregated skill vector and the topic’s required skill vector, Which calibrated against the historical project  outcome data; and (4) a Cold Start Validator that generates a concept level skill gaap report and flags teams falling below a configurable competency threshold.  In this research, core technologies include Python (FastAPI), HuggingFace Sentence- BERT (all MiniLM L6 v2), the pymoo multi objective optimization library, XGBoost with SHAP for interpretability and React 18 with Recharts for the supervisor dahshboard.  Validation targets include a cosine similarity profiling accuracy of ≥0.80,   an XGBoost F1-  score ≥ 0.82 with AUC - ROC ≥ 0.85, group formation for a cohort of 100 students within 60 seconds and a supervisor satisfaction score of ≥4.0/5.0. This component directly  supports UN Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by ensuring that every single undergraduate group begins its project with a mathematically validated, skill balanced composition and a quantified assessment of its readiness for the chosen challenge.  Keywords:   Team Formation, NSGA-II, Multi-Objective Optimization, SBERT, Topic Feasibility, XGBoost, SHAP, Cold-Start Problem, Skill-Gap Analysis, Educational AI.

ACKNOWLEDGEMENT  I would like to express my sincere gratitude to my supervisor, Prof. Samantha Rajapaksha, and co-supervisor, Mrs. Kaushika Kahatapitiya, for their invaluable guidance, continuous support, and constructive feedback throughout the research planning and development process. I also extend my appreciation to my project team members Lekamge R.L.M.D., Kulathunga S.A.I.K., and Rashmika R.M.D. for their collaboration in building the broader Intelligent Project Management System for Undergraduate Students. Special thanks to the Department of Information Technology at SLIIT for providing access to necessary computational resources and academic facilities.

1. INTRODUCTION  In undergraduate group projects, the formation of project groups and the selection of the topic for those projects are two of the most critical initial decisions to made at the process of group project life cycle. Those two decisions directly determine whether a group have the necessary technical skills to deliver a better output, whether individual group members  have equal workloads and whether the group’s collective effort is enough for meet the  demands of the chosen topic. Except for this, team formation and topic validation in most institutions including SLIIT still remain entirely informal which relying on random assignment, self-grouping or brief supervisor interviews with no data driven process of team balance or topic readiness.  This research addresses the first most layer of the Intelligent Project Management System: the Intelligent Team Formation and Topic Feasibility Analysis component. While other members handles the project planning (Lekamge R.M.D.), risk monitoring (Kulathunga S.A.I.K.), quality assessment (Rashmika R.M.D.). This component is responsible for ensuring every group project begins with a group that is composed mathematically validated for skill balance, personality diverse and ready for the chosen topic effectively by eliminating the foundational problems introduced by ad hoc team assignment.  This system directly supports UN Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by ensuring that every undergraduate, regardless of their social network or self-sufficient skills is placed in a group that maximizes their probability equation of project success through evidence-based, algorithmic matching.  1.1 Background and Context  The results of poor group formation in undergraduate group projects are well documented and significant, Oakley et al. (2004) established that improper unbalanced team formations which those where high performing students are clustered or where critical skills are no where to be found are in the main structural predictors of project failure and the free rider  phenomenon, which is low contributing members get benefit from high performers’ efforts  without commencing any Contribution for the project [1].Studies of multiple institutions have shown that randomly formed groups perform significantly worse in average than the groups formed through structured, skill matching processes [2].  Other than a balanced group, the deeper challenge is aligning the topic to the group. Which is also known as the cold start problem of group projects. A certain group can be internally balanced in terms of skills yet collectively lack the specific technical skill that regard to the topic that is chosen by the group. For example, a group building a ML system with no member experienced in python or data preprocessing is structurally set up to fail from the day one. No existing student facing tool validates this alignment before project begins. Supervisors typically discover such mistakes only two weeks into the project, in that point significant time and effort has been wasted already.  The combination of Sentence Transformers and multi objective evolutionary algorithms has uncovered new possibilities for data driven group formation. Reimers and Gurevych

(2019) have demonstrated that Sentence-BERT produces semantically meaningful vector representations of the text that get skill relatedness more accurately that keyword matching [3]. Also, Deb et al. (2002) established NSGA-II as the gold standard algorithm for multi objective optimization problems where multiple competing criteria must be parallelly optimized accurately the structure of group formation problem [4]. Chen and Guestrin (2016) showed the superiority of XGBoost for tubular classification tasks including predicting of the outcome form structured feature vectors [5], establishing its suitability for the Feasibility Prediction module.  1.2 Literature Review  A detailed review of existing literature was conducted across the domains of automated team formation, multi objective optimization, semantic skill profiling and educational outcome prediction.  1.2.1 Automated and Constraint-Based Team Formation  The issue of algorithmically forming balanced groups has been studied extensively in both educational and professional contexts. Borrego et al. (2013) reviewed group formation strategies in engineering education and found out that structured skill based matching consistently outperformed random assignment on project quality [6]. The CATME system (Layton et al. 2010) is the most widely deployed automated group formation tool in higher education, using student self-reported skills and schedule availability to suggest group compositions. [7]. However, CATME relies on ordinal self-assessment scales that are highly susceptible to dunning-Kruger bias, does not incorporate semantic skill profiling and has no process to validating group readiness against a specific topic. Its group formation objective is also single dimensional with no consideration of personality diversity or multi objective tradeoffs.  More capable multi objective approaches have been found in the software engineering group   formation   literature.   Gutiérrez-Rodríguez   et   al.   (2016)   applied   evolutionary algorithms to form development teams that parallelly optimize technical skill coverage and collaboration potential [8]. That shows the feasibility of evolutionary team formation but does not point out the cold start feasibility dimension that is core to this research.  1.2.2 Semantic Skill Profiling with Sentence Transformers  Former skill profiling platforms shows skills as discrete labels or ordinal scores, losing the semantic relationships between related skills. Reimers and Gurevych (2019) introduced Sentence-BERT (SBERT), which produces rich vector representations of sentences and short documents that capture semantic similarity with mostly higher accuracy than prior methods [3]. The all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model used in this component makes 384 dimensional embeddings optimized for semantic textual similarity tasks with low computational overhead, making it suitable for real-time student profiling at cohort scale.  The application of SBERT to student skill profiling has been explored by Ramos et al. (2022), who demonstrated that SBERT-encoded competency descriptions align well with expert judgments of skill relatedness in professional competency frameworks [9]. This

validates the core embedding approach of the Student Vector Profiling Engine proposed in this component.  1.2.3 Multi-Objective Optimization for Team Composition  Deb et al. (2002) introduces NSGA-II an elitist non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm that process a variety of Pareto-optimal front of solutions for multi-objective optimization problems [4]. NSGA-II became the mostly cited multi-objective evolutionary algorithm in engineering optimization literature. The pymoo library (Blank and Deb 2020) provides a high grade Python Implementation NSGA-II with well structured APIs for custom objective function definition and constraint specification [10], making that directly suitable for the group formation optimization formulated in this component.  The three objective formulation used in this component maximizing skill coverage, minimizing skill redundancy and maximizing personality diversity in novel in the educational group formation context and draws inspiration from the workforce diversity optimization literature for similar multi objective formulations have showed superior group performance outcomes over single object approaches [11].  1.2.4 Predictive Modelling for Educational Outcomes  Chen and Guestrin (2016) introduced XGBoost, a gradient boosting framework which has consistently gained state of the art performance on tubular classification tasks across a wide range of domains [5]. In educational data mining, Romero and Ventura (2010) showed that gradient boosting models applied to student academic performances can predict project outcome with much accuracy than ever before [12]. Most recent work by Lundberg and Lee (2017) introduced SHAP values as a theoretically grounded framework for explaining individual predictions of complex models [13] enabling the transparency that wanted for an academic decision support tool where supervisors must be able to understand and  question the system’s recommendations.  The mix of XGBoost for outcome prediction and SHAP for explanation is now considered best practice in high stakes educational prediction systems [14] and it is the initial approach adopted in the Topic Feasibility Predictor in this component.  1.2.5 Existing Tools and Their Limitations  A proper survey of already existing team formation and topic validation tools uncovers consistent and critical gaps. CATME (Layton et al. 2010) addresses group balance via self report but has no NLP based profiling, no multi objective optimization and no topic feasibility validation. TeamMaker and similar tools apply ruler based matching but are they are rely on certain domains and lack semantic understanding of skill content. Random or self-selection paths, skill the norm at SLIIT and most institutions have introduce systematic bias towards homogeneous groups. No existing tool in the world combines the semantic kill profiling, multi objective evolutionary group optimization and ML based topic feasibility validation in a single integrated pipeline and confirming the novelty and the necessity of this research component.
