1. INTRODUCTION  In undergraduate group projects, the formation of project groups and the selection of the topic for those projects are two of the most critical initial decisions to made at the process of group project life cycle. Those two decisions directly determine whether a group have the necessary technical skills to deliver a better output, whether individual group members  have equal workloads and whether the group’s collective effort is enough for meet the  demands of the chosen topic. Except for this, team formation and topic validation in most institutions including SLIIT still remain entirely informal which relying on random assignment, self-grouping or brief supervisor interviews with no data driven process of team balance or topic readiness.  This research addresses the first most layer of the Intelligent Project Management System: the Intelligent Team Formation and Topic Feasibility Analysis component. While other members handles the project planning (Lekamge R.M.D.), risk monitoring (Kulathunga S.A.I.K.), quality assessment (Rashmika R.M.D.). This component is responsible for ensuring every group project begins with a group that is composed mathematically validated for skill balance, personality diverse and ready for the chosen topic effectively by eliminating the foundational problems introduced by ad hoc team assignment.  This system directly supports UN Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by ensuring that every undergraduate, regardless of their social network or self-sufficient skills is placed in a group that maximizes their probability equation of project success through evidence-based, algorithmic matching.  1.1 Background and Context  The results of poor group formation in undergraduate group projects are well documented and significant, Oakley et al. (2004) established that improper unbalanced team formations which those where high performing students are clustered or where critical skills are no where to be found are in the main structural predictors of project failure and the free rider  phenomenon, which is low contributing members get benefit from high performers’ efforts  without commencing any Contribution for the project [1].Studies of multiple institutions have shown that randomly formed groups perform significantly worse in average than the groups formed through structured, skill matching processes [2].  Other than a balanced group, the deeper challenge is aligning the topic to the group. Which is also known as the cold start problem of group projects. A certain group can be internally balanced in terms of skills yet collectively lack the specific technical skill that regard to the topic that is chosen by the group. For example, a group building a ML system with no member experienced in python or data preprocessing is structurally set up to fail from the day one. No existing student facing tool validates this alignment before project begins. Supervisors typically discover such mistakes only two weeks into the project, in that point significant time and effort has been wasted already.  The combination of Sentence Transformers and multi objective evolutionary algorithms has uncovered new possibilities for data driven group formation. Reimers and Gurevych

(2019) have demonstrated that Sentence-BERT produces semantically meaningful vector representations of the text that get skill relatedness more accurately that keyword matching [3]. Also, Deb et al. (2002) established NSGA-II as the gold standard algorithm for multi objective optimization problems where multiple competing criteria must be parallelly optimized accurately the structure of group formation problem [4]. Chen and Guestrin (2016) showed the superiority of XGBoost for tubular classification tasks including predicting of the outcome form structured feature vectors [5], establishing its suitability for the Feasibility Prediction module.  1.2 Literature Review  A detailed review of existing literature was conducted across the domains of automated team formation, multi objective optimization, semantic skill profiling and educational outcome prediction.  1.2.1 Automated and Constraint-Based Team Formation  The issue of algorithmically forming balanced groups has been studied extensively in both educational and professional contexts. Borrego et al. (2013) reviewed group formation strategies in engineering education and found out that structured skill based matching consistently outperformed random assignment on project quality [6]. The CATME system (Layton et al. 2010) is the most widely deployed automated group formation tool in higher education, using student self-reported skills and schedule availability to suggest group compositions. [7]. However, CATME relies on ordinal self-assessment scales that are highly susceptible to dunning-Kruger bias, does not incorporate semantic skill profiling and has no process to validating group readiness against a specific topic. Its group formation objective is also single dimensional with no consideration of personality diversity or multi objective tradeoffs.  More capable multi objective approaches have been found in the software engineering group   formation   literature.   Gutiérrez-Rodríguez   et   al.   (2016)   applied   evolutionary algorithms to form development teams that parallelly optimize technical skill coverage and collaboration potential [8]. That shows the feasibility of evolutionary team formation but does not point out the cold start feasibility dimension that is core to this research.  1.2.2 Semantic Skill Profiling with Sentence Transformers  Former skill profiling platforms shows skills as discrete labels or ordinal scores, losing the semantic relationships between related skills. Reimers and Gurevych (2019) introduced Sentence-BERT (SBERT), which produces rich vector representations of sentences and short documents that capture semantic similarity with mostly higher accuracy than prior methods [3]. The all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model used in this component makes 384 dimensional embeddings optimized for semantic textual similarity tasks with low computational overhead, making it suitable for real-time student profiling at cohort scale.  The application of SBERT to student skill profiling has been explored by Ramos et al. (2022), who demonstrated that SBERT-encoded competency descriptions align well with expert judgments of skill relatedness in professional competency frameworks [9]. This

validates the core embedding approach of the Student Vector Profiling Engine proposed in this component.  1.2.3 Multi-Objective Optimization for Team Composition  Deb et al. (2002) introduces NSGA-II an elitist non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm that process a variety of Pareto-optimal front of solutions for multi-objective optimization problems [4]. NSGA-II became the mostly cited multi-objective evolutionary algorithm in engineering optimization literature. The pymoo library (Blank and Deb 2020) provides a high grade Python Implementation NSGA-II with well structured APIs for custom objective function definition and constraint specification [10], making that directly suitable for the group formation optimization formulated in this component.  The three objective formulation used in this component maximizing skill coverage, minimizing skill redundancy and maximizing personality diversity in novel in the educational group formation context and draws inspiration from the workforce diversity optimization literature for similar multi objective formulations have showed superior group performance outcomes over single object approaches [11].  1.2.4 Predictive Modelling for Educational Outcomes  Chen and Guestrin (2016) introduced XGBoost, a gradient boosting framework which has consistently gained state of the art performance on tubular classification tasks across a wide range of domains [5]. In educational data mining, Romero and Ventura (2010) showed that gradient boosting models applied to student academic performances can predict project outcome with much accuracy than ever before [12]. Most recent work by Lundberg and Lee (2017) introduced SHAP values as a theoretically grounded framework for explaining individual predictions of complex models [13] enabling the transparency that wanted for an academic decision support tool where supervisors must be able to understand and  question the system’s recommendations.  The mix of XGBoost for outcome prediction and SHAP for explanation is now considered best practice in high stakes educational prediction systems [14] and it is the initial approach adopted in the Topic Feasibility Predictor in this component.  1.2.5 Existing Tools and Their Limitations  A proper survey of already existing team formation and topic validation tools uncovers consistent and critical gaps. CATME (Layton et al. 2010) addresses group balance via self report but has no NLP based profiling, no multi objective optimization and no topic feasibility validation. TeamMaker and similar tools apply ruler based matching but are they are rely on certain domains and lack semantic understanding of skill content. Random or self-selection paths, skill the norm at SLIIT and most institutions have introduce systematic bias towards homogeneous groups. No existing tool in the world combines the semantic kill profiling, multi objective evolutionary group optimization and ML based topic feasibility validation in a single integrated pipeline and confirming the novelty and the necessity of this research component.

1.3 Research Gap  The analysis of existing systems and literature review reveals a clear and well-defined research gap that this component addresses directly. The following table will summarize this gap.  Aspect   Existing: Random / Self- Select  Existing: CATME  Proposed System  Team Formation Basis  No data — purely social  Ordinal self-report scales  SBERT semantic skill vectors  Skill Profiling Accuracy  None   Low (Dunning- Kruger bias)  Cosine sim ≥ 0.80 (validated)  Optimization  Approach  None   Single-objective heuristic  NSGA-II 3-objective Pareto-optimal  Personality Diversity   Not considered   Not considered   Big Five diversity  maximization  Topic Feasibility Check  None   None   XGBoost Success Probability (0–100%)  Cold-Start Validation   None   None   Skill-gap report + threshold flagging  Explainability   None   None   SHAP feature-level explanation  Table 2: Research Gap Analysis   –   Existing Systems vs. Proposed System  The main objective of the novelty of this research lies in simultaneously solving two previously separate issues, team composition and topic readiness validation within a single integrated and mathematically accurate pipeline. By coupling NSGA-II based multi objective group formation with SBERT based semantic profiling and XGBoost based feasaibblity prediction, this component eliminates the cold start gap that has initially been found only after project work has begun and when it is too late to restructure teams without  much cost to student ‘s wellbeing and project quality.

2. OBJECTIVES  2.1 Main Objective  To design and implement an AI powered Intelligent Group Formation and Topic Feasibility Analysis   System   that   uses   Sentence-BERT   semantic   profiling   to   construct   multi- dimensional student skill vectors, applies NSGA-II multi objective optimization to generate Pareto optimal group configuration that simultaneously maximize skill coverage, minimize redundancy and maximize personality diversity, and validates each team-topic paring through a XGBoost based Feasibility Predictor and Cold Start Skill Validator before project Start.  2.2 Specific Objectives  Specific Objective 1: To Build the SBERT Student Vector Profiling Engine  •   Specific: Develop an NLP-based profiling pipeline using the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 Sentence-BERT model to encode each student's academic module grades (normalized to [0,1]), GPA, free-text skill survey responses (20 questions), and Big Five personality assessment responses into a unified 384-dimensional semantic skill vector S   ∈   R^384 per student.  •   Measurable: Achieve a mean cosine similarity of ≥ 0.80 between SBERT -encoded skill descriptions and expert-validated ground-truth skill pairings on a held out validation set of 50 student profiles.  •   Achievable: Leverages HuggingFace all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (pre-trained) with a lightweight concatenation and normalization layer; no task-specific fine tuning required.  •   Realistic: Feasible using anonymized academic records from SLIIT IT4010 cohorts with appropriate ethical clearance.  •   Time-bound: Expected completion within Months 2 – 4 of implementation.  Specific Objective 2: To Implement NSGA-II Multi-Objective Team Optimization Engine  •   Specific: Develop a multi-objective team formation engine using the NSGA-II algorithm (pymoo 0.6) that optimizes three simultaneous objectives for a given cohort: (1) maximize team skill coverage (breadth of unique skill dimensions covered), (2) minimize intra-team skill redundancy (overlap penalty), and (3) maximize personality trait diversity (Big Five Euclidean distance). The engine shall output a ranked list of Pareto-optimal team configurations.  •   Measurable: Team formation for a cohort of 100 students into groups of 4 shall complete within 60 seconds; generated teams shall achieve a mean expert quality  rating of ≥ 4.0/5.0 on balance and diversity criteria.  •   Achievable: pymoo 0.6 provides production-ready NSGA-II with configurable population size (200) and generation count (500).  •   Realistic: 500-generation NSGA-II optimization for a cohort of 100 is computationally tractable on standard server hardware.  •   Time-bound: Expected completion within Months 3 – 5 of implementation.

Specific Objective 3: To Develop XGBoost Topic Feasibility Predictor and Cold- Start Validator  •   Specific: Train an XGBoost classifier on historical SLIIT project outcome data (binary: success / failure) using the following features per team-topic pairing: aggregated team skill vector, topic requirement vector (SBERT-encoded), cosine similarity between team and topic vectors, GPA variance across team members, and team size. Apply Platt scaling for probability calibration; use SHAP for per- prediction explanation. Implement a Cold-Start Validator that generates a concept- level skill-gap report and flags teams below a configurable threshold (default: 60% Success Probability).  •   Measurable: XGBoost classifier achieves F1- score ≥ 0.82 and AUC - ROC ≥ 0.85  on a held-out test set of 100 historical team-topic pairings.  •   Achievable: XGBoost 2.x and SHAP are mature, well-documented libraries; Platt scaling is implemented via scikit-learn CalibratedClassifierCV.  •   Realistic: Sufficient historical outcome data (at least 3 prior cohorts) is available from the SLIIT Department of Information Technology.  •   Time-bound: Expected completion within Months 4 – 6 of implementation.  Specific Objective 4: To Develop IPMS Integration API and Supervisor Dashboard  •   Specific: Design and expose a REST API (FastAPI) that makes team compositions, skill-coverage matrices, feasibility scores, and skill-gap reports available to the Project Planning module (Lekamge R.L.M.D.) and Risk Monitoring module (Kulathunga S.A.I.K.) within the broader IPMS. Implement a React 18 supervisor dashboard with Recharts-based radar skill charts and SHAP explanation views.  •   Measurable: API response time ≤ 500ms for team and feasibility retrieval under standard load (≤ 50 concurrent requests); supervisor satisfaction score ≥ 4.0/5.0  from usability evaluation.  •   Achievable: FastAPI async framework supports required throughput; Recharts provides production-quality charting components.  •   Realistic: API contract definitions agreed with partner modules in future; dashboard co-designed with supervisor focus groups.  •   Time-bound: API endpoints stable and documented by Month 7; dashboard validated by Month 8.  Specific Objective 5: To Evaluate System Performance and Validate Outcomes  •   Specific: Conduct end-to-end system evaluation comparing AI-formed teams against historically random assignments using project outcome records, and measure supervisor and student usability of the dashboard and feasibility reports.  •   Measurable: SBERT profiling cosine sim ≥ 0.80; NSGA - II team quality ≥ 4.0/5.0 expert rating; XGBoost F1 ≥ 0.82, AUC - ROC ≥ 0.85; formation speed ≤ 60s for 100 students; supervisor satisfaction ≥ 4.0/5.0.  •   Achievable: Evaluation uses historical cohort data for retrospective validation and a live pilot for prospective assessment.  •   Realistic: Pilot testing is feasible.

•   Time-bound: Expected completion within Month 9 of implementation.

3. METHODOLOGY  This research adopts a Design Science Research (DSR) methodology (Hevner et al., 2004), which is well-suited for projects that create and evaluate an innovative IT artifact solving a unaddressed clearly defined practical problem [15]. The methodology proceeds through five structured phases: Problem Definition, System Design, Prototype Development, Evaluation, and Iteration.  3.1 Research Approach  The DSR approach is applied like this. The research problem is the absence of data-driven, skill-aware group formation and topic feasibility validation in undergraduate projects is formally defined through literature review and stakeholder analysis. A solution artifact (the Intelligent Team Formation and Topic Feasibility Analysis system) is designed and constructed   through   development   cycles.   The   artifact   is   evaluated   against   defined performance metrics using empirical methods, and iterative refinements are made based on evaluation outcomes. This ensures the system is both technically rich and practically useful within the SLIIT undergraduate research ecosystem.  Dataset   Selection   and   Acquisition:   Three   publicly   available   Kaggle   datasets   are employed to support the training, calibration, and validation of the system's machine learning components. The Students' Academic Performance Dataset (xAPI-Edu-Data, Aljarah et al., Kaggle, 2016) contains 480 university student records across 16 features including grade level, section, topic, engagement metrics (raised hands, visited resources, discussion participation), and a three-class academic performance label (Low / Medium / High) which is binarized to a project success outcome label (pass / fail) for XGBoost feasibility predictor training, and used to validate SBERT-encoded skill vector cosine similarity against expert-assigned performance levels. The Higher Education Students Performance Evaluation Dataset (Kaggle, 2022) provides multi-module GPA scores, demographic attributes, and academic engagement indicators for university students across multiple semesters, used to calibrate the Student Vector Profiling Engine and to verify the L2-normalised skill vector construction against externally validated student capability rankings. The Student Performance Factors Dataset (Kaggle, 2024) contains 6,607 student records with GPA, study habits, extracurricular participation, parental involvement, and exam   scores,   used   to   generate   realistic   synthetic   cohort   populations   for   NSGA-II population initialization experiments and to validate that the three-objective Pareto-front correctly identifies diverse, balanced team configurations relative to traditional ground- truth human-assigned team quality ratings.  3.2 Technical Methods and Algorithms  Student Vector Profiling Engine:   Each student's profile is encoded in two stages. First, academic signals (normalized module grades and GPA) are concatenated as a structured numeric vector, with normalization parameters derived from the Higher Education Students Performance Evaluation Dataset (Kaggle, 2022), which provides multi-semester GPA distributions used to establish cohort-level normalization bounds. Second, free-text skill

survey responses are processed by the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 SBERT model to produce a 384- dimensional semantic embedding. Cosine similarity validation of the SBERT encoder is performed against skill-pair ground-truth labels derived from the xAPI-Edu-Data dataset (Kaggle, 2016), where students in the same topic section and grade tier are treated as positively similar pairs and cross-topic, cross-tier pairs as negatively dissimilar confirming  a mean cosine similarity of ≥ 0.80 on held -out validation pairs. The two representations are concatenated and L2-normalized to produce the final student skill vector S   ∈   R^384. Big Five personality trait scores are encoded separately as a 5-dimensional vector and appended during team formation objective computation.  NSGA-II Optimization Engine:   Group formation is modelled as a combinatorial multi- objective optimization problem. Given a cohort of N students and a target team size of k (default: 4), the search space is all valid k-partitions of N students. The three objective functions are: (1) Skill Coverage: the fraction of unique skill dimensions covered by at least one team member above a threshold; (2) Skill Redundancy: the mean pairwise cosine similarity between member vectors (to be minimized); and (3) Personality Diversity: the mean Euclidean distance between member Big Five vectors (to be maximized). NSGA-II with population size 200 and 500 generations is applied using pymoo 0.6. Population initialization experiments use synthetic cohort populations generated from the Student Performance Factors Dataset (Kaggle, 2024), where each student's GPA, study habits, extracurricular score, and exam performance are mapped to skill vector dimensions, enabling controlled validation of the Pareto-front quality across cohort sizes of 40, 60, 80, and   100   students.   The   engine   produces   a   Pareto-front   of   non-dominated   team configurations from which the top-ranked solution per group is selected.  Topic Feasibility Predictor:   For each student team-topic pairing, a feature vector is constructed comprising: the L2-normalised aggregated team skill vector (element-wise mean of member vectors), the SBERT-encoded topic requirement vector, the cosine similarity scalar between the two, the GPA variance across team members, and the team size. A XGBoost classifier (max depth 6, learning rate 0.05, 300 estimators) is trained on binary outcome labels derived from the xAPI-Edu-Data dataset (Aljarah et al., Kaggle, 2016), where the three-class academic performance label (Low / Medium / High) is binarized low mapped to failure (0), Medium and High mapped to success (1)   —   producing 480 labelled team-topic pairing records across 16 features. The dataset's topic and section attributes are used as proxy topic-requirement identifiers, and student engagement features (raised hands, visited resources, discussion participation) are mapped to skill coverage dimensions within the 384-dimensional vector space. Training uses 5-fold stratified cross- validation. Class imbalance (127 Low vs 353 Medium+High) is addressed using SMOTE oversampling on the training folds. Probability outputs are calibrated via Platt scaling (CalibratedClassifierCV with sigmoid method). SHAP TreeExplainer   computes per- feature contributions for every prediction.  Cold-Start Skill Validator:   The aggregated team skill vector is compared against the topic requirement vector using element wise subtraction to identify specific skill dimensions where the team falls below the required threshold. Dimensions with a gap magnitude

exceeding a configurable threshold (default: 0.3 on the normalized scale) are flagged as critical gaps. The validator generates a structured skill-gap report listing each flagged dimension, its current team coverage score, the required score, and the magnitude of the gap. Teams with a predicted feasibility score below 60% are automatically flagged for supervisor review.  3.3 Tools and Platforms  •   Programming Language: Python 3.11 (ML/NLP backend), JavaScript/TypeScript (React frontend)  •   NLP Framework: HuggingFace Sentence-Transformers (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), spaCy v3  •   Multi-Objective Optimization: pymoo 0.6 (NSGA-II implementation)  •   Machine Learning: XGBoost 2.x, scikit-learn (Platt scaling, SMOTE via imbalanced-learn), SHAP  •   Backend API: FastAPI (Python), OpenAPI 3.0 documentation  •   Frontend Dashboard: React 18, Recharts (radar charts, bar charts), Tailwind CSS  •   Database: PostgreSQL 15 (student profiles, team configurations, feasibility scores)  •   Cloud: AWS EC2 (model serving), AWS S3 (profile data storage)  •   Version Control: GitHub (integrated with parent IPMS contribution analytics module)  •   Testing: Pytest (unit/integration), Locust (load testing)  3.4 Data Collection and Ethical Considerations  Primary model training and validation data is sourced from three publicly available Kaggle datasets: the Students' Academic Performance Dataset (xAPI-Edu-Data, Aljarah et al., Kaggle, 2016) for XGBoost feasibility predictor training and SBERT profiling validation, the Higher Education Students Performance Evaluation Dataset (Kaggle, 2022) for student skill vector normalization calibration and the Student Performance Factors Dataset (Kaggle, 2024) for NSGA-II population initialization experiments across controlled cohort sizes. All three datasets are publicly licensed, anonymized, and contain no personally identifiable information. In addition to these external datasets, supplementary institutional data will be collected from two sources: (1) anonymized historical student academic records and project outcome labels from past IT4010 cohorts at SLIIT, with written permission from the Department of Information Technology, used to fine tune the XGBoost model to the SLIIT academic context and (2) a pilot study involving current IT4010 students who voluntarily consent to complete the skill survey and personality assessment instruments. All SLIIT student data will be fully anonymized prior to processing. No personally identifiable information will be retained in the system after the anonymization. Ethical clearance will be obtained from the SLIIT Ethics Review Committee before any institutional data collection begins. Ground-truth labels for the XGBoost feasibility model

will be derived from supervisor-assigned final project grades, with a binary success threshold set at a grade of C or above.  3.5 Validation Strategy and Performance Metrics  •   SBERT Profiling Accuracy: Mean cosine similarity ≥ 0.80 against expert - validated skill pairings; validated using positive/negative pairs derived from xAPI-Edu-Data topic and grade tier groupings  •   Dataset Representativeness: Overlap between xAPI-Edu-Data feature space and SLIIT student profile schema evaluated via Jaccard similarity on feature label  sets; score ≥ 0.70 required before XGBoost training proceeds on the external  dataset  •   NSGA- II Team Quality: Expert quality rating ≥ 4.0/5.0 on balance and diversity  criteria; Pareto-front quality validated across synthetic cohorts of 40 – 100 students generated from Student Performance Factors Dataset (Kaggle, 2024)  •   XGBoost Feasibility Predictor: F1- score ≥ 0.82 and AUC - ROC ≥ 0.85 on held -out test set; class imbalance (127 Low vs 353 Medium+High in xAPI-Edu-Data) addressed via SMOTE; performance reported separately on external Kaggle test split and SLIIT institutional holdout  •   System Throughput: Team formation for 100 students completed within 60 seconds on standard server hardware  •   Supervisor Satisfaction: Satisfaction score ≥ 4.0/5.0 from dashboard usability  evaluation

4. HIGH-LEVEL SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE  The Intelligent Group Formation and Topic Feasibility Analysis component follows a modular, pipeline-based architecture consisting four primary subsystems: the Student Vector Profiling Engine, the NSGA-II Optimization Engine, the Topic Feasibility Predictor and Cold-Start Validator, and the IPMS Integration API and Dashboard. This component interfaces directly with the broader IPMS architecture, receiving student profile data and research topic submissions as input, and returning validated team configurations, feasibility scores, and skill-gap reports to the supervisor and student dashboards.  4.1 Component Overview  Input Layer:   Student academic records, skill survey responses, and personality assessment data are submitted via the IPMS onboarding interface. Research topic proposal documents (PDF/DOCX) are submitted by student groups via the IPMS proposal submission module. All inputs are validated and pre-processed using spaCy before entering the profiling pipeline.  Student Vector Profiling Engine:   Each student's multi-modal profile data is processed by the SBERT encoding pipeline to produce a 384-dimensional skill vector. Vectors are stored in the PostgreSQL profile store and made available for batch retrieval during the optimization phase.  NSGA-II Optimization Engine:   When a team formation request is received (e.g., at the start of the academic project cycle), the optimization engine retrieves all student vectors for the cohort and runs NSGA-II to generate Pareto-optimal team configurations. The top- ranked configuration per group is selected and stored.  Topic Feasibility Predictor:   Once a team-topic pairing is submitted, the XGBoost model computes a Success Probability score and the SHAP explainer generates feature level attributions. The Cold-Start Validator performs element wise skill gap analysis and generates the structured gap report.  Dashboard Layer:   All outputs are rendered on the IPMS supervisor dashboard (React 18) with radar charts showing per-team skill coverage, feasibility score badges, SHAP waterfall explanation views, and skill-gap heatmaps. Students have access to their own skill profile and gap report.

Figure 1: High-Level System Architecture of the Intelligent Team Formation and Topic Feasibility Analysis Component  4.2 Component Interactions and Data Flow  The data flow is conitous from profile ingestion to team output and then branching through the feasibility prediction pipeline. Student profiles enter the Input Layer, pass through the Profiling Engine, and their vectors are stored in the PostgreSQL profile store. The NSGA- II engine then operates on the full cohort vector set to generate team configurations. Once teams are formed, each team-topic pairing is submitted to the Feasibility Predictor, which returns a Success Probability score, SHAP explanations, and a skill-gap report. All outputs are exposed via the IPMS REST API and rendered on the React dashboard. Integration with the parent IPMS is achieved via RESTful APIs: the parent system sends a team formation request with the cohort student ID list; this component returns a team configuration object containing member assignments, skill-coverage matrices, and feasibility assessments in JSON format.  Figure 2: Student Vector Profiling and NSGA-II Team Optimization Pipeline  4.3 Scalability and Security Considerations

•   The FastAPI backend is containerized using Docker with horizontal scaling for peak formation periods (e.g., start of academic year).  •   NSGA-II optimization is computationally intensive for large cohorts; parallelization is implemented using Python multiprocessing for population evaluation.  •   All inter service communication is encrypted via HTTPS/TLS 1.3; student profile data is encrypted at rest using AES-256.  •   Role-based access control (RBAC) ensures students can access only their own skill profile and gap report and supervisors see cohort-level team configurations and feasibility dashboards.  •   The XGBoost model is version-controlled and retrainable on each new cohort's outcome data to improve prediction accuracy over time.

Figure 3: Topic Feasibility Analysis and Cold-Start Validation Workflow

FR5   Team Configuration Output  The system shall return a ranked list of Pareto-optimal team configurations with per-team skill-coverage matrices and diversity scores. 6. COMMERCIALIZATION PLAN  6.1 Target Market and Customer Persona  The initial market for this system consists of higher education institutions in Sri Lanka and the broader South and Southeast Asian region that run project-based undergraduate programs in STEM and IT disciplines. The immediate target is SLIIT, with potential expansion to the University of Moratuwa, NSBM Green University, the Informatics Institute of Technology, and regionally to universities in India, Malaysia, and Singapore that operate comparable undergraduate research frameworks. Secondary markets include corporate graduate development programs and EdTech platforms providing solid project management services.  6.2 Value Proposition  The system offers three core value propositions: (1) it eliminates the free rider problem by ensuring every team begins with a mathematically balanced, skill-diverse composition, reducing the structural inequity that random assignment introduces; (2) it prevents wasted project effort by identifying team-topic mismatches before work begins, enabling early intervention and topic reselection where necessary and (3) it provides institutional administrators with a fully auditable, data-driven record of every team formation decision, supporting accreditation requirements for fair and transparent assessment practices.  6.3 Revenue Model  •   Institutional Licensing: Annual per-institution licensing fee based on active student enrollment (e.g., LKR 500,000 – 2,000,000 per year for institutions of 500 –  5,000 students).  •   SaaS API Access: Per-formation API pricing for EdTech platforms integrating the NSGA-II formation engine and feasibility predictor into their own products.  •   Premium Analytics Module: Cohort level longitudinal analytics dashboard tracking the relationship between team formation quality scores and final project outcomes over multiple academic years.  •   Model Retraining Services: Annual model retraining contracts to update the XGBoost feasibility predictor on each institution's latest students outcome data.  6.4 Competitive Advantage  Unlike   CATME   (ordinal   self-report,   single-objective,   no   feasibility   validation), TeamMaker (rule-based, no NLP), or random/self-selection (no data), this system is the only   solution   that   mix   semantic   NLP-based   student   profiling   with   multi-objective evolutionary team optimization and ML-based topic feasibility prediction in a single integrated pipeline. Its XGBoost model improves in accuracy with every new cohort of outcome data creating a compounding predictive advantage that is structurally difficult for competitors to replicate. Its deep integration with the IPMS parent system creates a significant institutional switching cost.

4 | P a g e  ABSTRACT  This paper addresses a hard problem in contemporary educational institutions: grading  students’ assignments and providing structured, useful feedback is still largely a human -centric task. Most current tools are geared towards grading and rubric systems, b ut they don’t provide  actionable, conceptual advice that helps instructors target exactly what students are missing. To address this problem, this paper introduces an AI-based system for Automated Quality Assessment and Adaptive Mentorship. This system is conceptualized as an integral part of a broader project: The Intelligent Project Management System for Undergraduate Students (R26- IT-095). The problem statement is evident: there are no systems that go beyond grading to identify exactly where students are weak in their understanding. Rubric-based grading systems are labor-intensive, subjective, and unreliable. Computerized grading tools are mostly geared towards catching surface-level mistakes without providing instructors with actionable advice on how to   improve students’   understanding. Our system will employ a multi-step system: an NLP- based Semantic Grading Engine that will analyze how well a student’s report is  structured, how deep its technical content is, and how well it aligns with a given rubric system by using transformer models; An AI-driven Resource Recommendation Engine, which connects the identified gaps to relevant learning materials, e.g., academic papers and tutorials; An   Automated   Feedback   Generation   module,   which   produces   structured,   personalized improvement reports for each student. This shifts the focus of the grading process to intelligent mentorship, thus bridging the loop between grading and learning.  The key technologies used here include Python, BERT/Sentence Transformers for semantic analysis, spacey for NLP, a Neo4j-based knowledge graph for concept mapping, and a React.js- based dashboard. This system is intended to integrate well with the GitHub contribution and project planning features of the parent platform. It is expected that the system results will be a reduction in manual grading time by over 60 percent, concordance under 80 percent with the expert evaluator, and a demonstration of the improved report quality of students with repeat of the system. This element of the system is a direct contribution towards the attainment of the UN Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) through provision of fair, transparent and data balanced academic mentorship.  Keywords:   Automated Quality Assessment, NLP, Semantic Grading, Adaptive Mentorship, Resource Recommendation, Feedback Generation, Educational AI, BERT.  .

10 | P a g e  1. INTRODUCTION  Feedback and assessment is one of the key factors that a university can impact students at undergraduate level. Students working on research projects want timely, constructive and  relevant feedback to their work. It’s no good just getting a mark at the bottom of a page and  being told that is all the lecturers has to say. Currently, most universities including SLIIT are using manual methods for assessing and providing feedback to students. This is a very time- consuming task and the method of assessment and marking of the project is highly dependent on the lecturer.  This project is related to the subcomponent of R26-IT-095 Intelligent Project Management System; in this project, the subcomponent aims at developing an application to assess and evaluate the student research reports and to translate the assessment into valuable information that benefits the students. In other words, this part focuses on the written work in the  students’ reports and aims at delivering useful assessment comments that contribute to real  learning for the students as opposed to merely indicating mistakes. This project is hence related to UN SDG 4   –   Quality Education. In particular, it aims at ensuring that every student receives the adequate academic support in a timely manner that benefits the students, regardless of the workload facing the supervisor.  It is SDBI’s contribution to achieving the UN’s Sustainable Development Goal 4, to ensure  inclusive and effective quality education for all. It provides immediate, structured and meaningful feedback to students regarding their performance in a data-informed way. It indicates performance in relation to achievement for each learning outcome as well as highlighting gaps in relation to the expected level of achievement for the student in relation to the learning outcome. Ultimately it seeks to improve student performance to the highest standard of education possible, even when a Field Supervisor has heavy caseloads and cannot provide the required individual attention.  1.1 Background and Context  Marking research reports is genuinely time-consuming work. A supervisor looking after several groups has to go through each report, check the structure, the academic language, how well the student understands the topic, and whether it actually follows the rubric   all while juggling deadlines. Research consistently shows that the quality and speed of feedback is one of the strongest factors in whether students actually improve [1], yet in practice feedback tends to arrive late, stay quite general, and often have little connection to the specific problems in a student's work [2].  What is more significant is what occurs after the mark has been given. In the case that a student scores poorly on their literature review or their methodology section, what they actually require is not simply to know the score that they need to know what to read, what to revisit and how to correct it. Tools like Moodle and Blackboard can record grades and show rubric comments, but they cannot look at a student's work and figure out what the student still does not understand, or point them towards something that would actually help [3].  The integration of NLP and machine learning into academic assessment has started to change what is possible here. Models like BERT have shown they can compare student writing against reference content with real accuracy [4], and knowledge graphs offer a way to connect concepts so that when a weakness is detected, you can trace back what underlying understanding might be missing [5]. The idea behind this project is to bring those pieces together to build something that does not just score a report, but actually uses that score to help the student learn. This work

11 | P a g e  is also aligned with SDG 4 and the CoEAI research cluster at SLIIT, applying AI directly to improve the fairness and consistency of academic feedback.  This research proposes combining these technologies into a unified Automated Quality Assessment and Adaptive Mentorship system. The system will evaluate student reports using semantic   NLP,   map   identified   weaknesses   to   academic   concepts,   and   automatically recommend learning resources to guide improvement   effectively acting as a personal AI research mentor for every student in the program.  This element is also consistent with SDG 4 (Quality Education) and Co EAI research cluster (Centre of Excellence for AI) in SLIIT because it directly implements the progressive AI to enhance the equity, regularity, and achievement of education.  1.2 Literature Review  A fair amount of work has been done on using NLP and AI for educational assessment, though most of it stops short of what this project is trying to do. The following review goes through the key existing approaches and what each one is missing.  Rani and Sujatha [6] built an automated evaluation system for descriptive answers using keyword extraction and semantic similarity. It got reasonable accuracy but was designed for short answers only and did not give any structured feedback or try to identify what the student actually did not understand.  Ramachandran et al. [7] took things further with a BERT-based rubric grading system for essays, which lined up well with human graders on overall scores. The problem is it could not point to a specific weak section in the report or suggest anything for the student to do about it.  Cui et al. [8] showed that GNN-based models trained on knowledge graphs could predict student performance across connected concepts a useful insight for diagnosing learning gaps. But that work never connected to a practical feedback system, so there was no way for it to actually help a student act on those gaps.  Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, developed by Corbett and Anderson [9], has been widely used in tutoring systems to track student mastery over time, and more recent work has extended this with graph-based propagation [10]. These approaches work well for structured exercises but were never designed for evaluating long-form academic writing like research reports.  The ACORN system [11] tried something different by using multimodal analysis of classroom recordings to assess teacher performance. It is an interesting approach, but it looks at the teacher side only and has nothing to do with evaluating what students actually submit.  Liu et al. [12] built a recommendation system for academic resources using citation networks and reading history it worked well for personalized suggestions but was not connected to any assessment pipeline, so it could not react to what a specific student actually got wrong in their work.  Commercial tools, Turnitin and Grammarly, as to commercial tools, can identify the surface- level writing problems but not assess the technical depth, the rubric requirements, or the fact that the student comprehends the material he/she is writing about [2].They also do not generate any kind of improvement plan tied to learning resources.  Taken together, the gap is clear: there is no existing system that combines proper rubric-based semantic evaluation of research reports, knowledge graph-based weakness diagnosis, and

12 | P a g e  automated personalized resource recommendations in one place. That is exactly what this project is trying to build.  1.3 Research Gap  Looking at what is out there, the gap becomes fairly obvious. Existing tools either grade without explaining, or explain without diagnosing the actual problem. The table below sets out how the proposed system compares against what is currently available:  Aspect   Existing: Turnitin/LMS  Existing: Rubric Graders (BERT)  Proposed System  Grading Capability  Surface-level (plagiarism/grammar)  Holistic score, limited rubric  Section-by-section rubric compliance with semantic depth analysis  Weakness Identification  None   Score deduction only   Concept-level mapping to knowledge graph nodes  Feedback Generation  Generic comments   Rubric scores only   Structured, personalized improvement reports  Resource Recommendation  None   None   Targeted papers, tutorials, and examples based on identified gaps  Adaptive Learning Loop  None   None   Tracks improvement across submission iterations  Table 2: Research Gap Analysis   –   Existing Systems vs. Proposed System  What makes this project different is not just that it grades it is that it tries to understand why a student is struggling and does something about it. No existing tool currently combines semantic NLP-based   assessment   with   knowledge   graph   diagnosis   and   automated   resource recommendations for research report evaluation in an undergraduate setting. That is the gap this work is filling.

15 | P a g e  3. METHODOLOGY  This research adopts a Design Science Research (DSR) methodology, which is particularly well-suited for projects that aim to create and evaluate an innovative IT artifact that solves a clearly defined practical problem [13]. The methodology proceeds through five structured phases: Problem Definition, System Design, Prototype Development, Evaluation, and Iteration.  3.1 Research Approach  This project is being approached using a Design Science Research methodology. The overall goal of the research is to design and implement an innovative solution that can be validated against the problems identified. This approach as opposed to a theoretical approach is fitting to this problem because rather than being purely descriptive, the goal of the research is to be prescriptive and provide actionable solutions to students and educators while improving the assessment process. In this project, the problems of current assessment processes are clearly identified, with manual, inconsistent assessment not providing students with any tangible output. A working solution is then designed and implemented, validated through measurable metrics and then iteratively refined through the testing process.  3.2 Technical Methods and Algorithms  Semantic Grading Engine   Using Sentence-BERT (SBERT), the core grading module converts the rubric descriptors and the student report sections into the semantic space through the embedding of the semantic vectors using cosine similarity, providing a continuous score. For cases where the rubric compliance is categorical (e.g., Excellent/Good/Adequate/Poor), a classification head is added on top of the BERT encoder and the model is then fine-tuned on the training dataset of the annotated student reports along with the grades provided by the knowledgeable instructors.  Knowledge Graph Construction : The IT research domain The Knowledge Graph for the IT research domain is constructed by applying a semi-automated ontology extraction technique. The syllabi of Computer Science courses, general authoring guidelines for academic papers and a collection of   IT research papers are processed by applying spaCy’s NER (Named Entity  Recognition) and dependency parsing to derive concept entities and relationships. The derived entities and relationships are stored in a Neo4j graph database where node labels represent academic concepts (e.g., Machine Learning, Research Gap, Literature Review Structure) and the edges between the nodes represent the prerequisite/dependency relationship.  Weakness Propagation and Mapping   : They work on graded report sections corresponding to concepts located on Knowledge Graph for which the score is below the minimum threshold. From these report sections, they identify the essential concepts required to pass the skills that are analyzed through graph traversal algorithms and carry out the root-cause analysis of the weaknesses identified for each student who has been assessed.  Resource Recommendation :   The Resource Recommendation algorithm is a content-based recommendation algorithm. It takes the semantic representation of the identified concept gaps and matches them against a knowledge base built from academic resources we index from Semantic Scholar, arXiv and institutional repositories. The matched resources are then ranked based on the semantic similarity to the concept gaps, the publication date of the resource and the citation count.

16 | P a g e  Feedback Generation   : This block generates an improvement report based on templates and a large language model. Templates contain section feedback for each assignment and are populated based on the score given to each criterion, as well as the skills and knowledge gaps discovered, and recommended by the AI. For narrative summary sections, it utilizes GPT-4o via API to produce well-explained feedback for students .  3.3 Tools and Platforms  •   Programming languages: We use Python 3.10+ for the ML/NLP part, and JavaScript/TypeScript for the frontend.  •   NLP tools: We use HuggingFace Transformers for BERT and SBERT, and spaCy v3 for NLP  •   Knowledge Graph: Neo4j (graph database), NetworkX (graph algorithms), PyVis (visualization)  •   ML libraries: We use PyTorch and scikit-learn for machine learning.  •   Backend API tech stack: We use FastAPI in Python, along with Node.js/Express.js for integration with the parent system.  •   Frontend dashboard tech stack: We use React.js for the frontend, along with D3.js for graph visualization.  •   External API tech stack: We use the Semantic Scholar Academic Graph API and OpenAI GPT-4o API.  •   Databases: We use MongoDB for document-based data and PostgreSQL for relational databases.  •   Cloud hosting: We use AWS EC2 for model serving and AWS S3 for report storage.  •   Version control: We use GitHub, along with an integration with the parent system’s  contribution analytics.  3.4 Data Collection and Ethical Considerations  The following method has been proposed for data collection. Instead of collecting reports from SLIIT students, the dataset for this research will be obtained from the Kaggle platform, which provides publicly available datasets for research and machine learning development. Kaggle hosts a wide range of academic writing datasets, essays, and report-style documents that can be used for training and evaluating automated assessment systems.   The selected dataset will consist of report-like or essay-based academic documents that are already publicly available and permitted for research use. Since the data is publicly shared for research purposes, no personal identifiable information (PII) will be collected or stored in the proposed system. Any potential identifiers present in the dataset will be removed to ensure that all data used in the analysis remains fully anonymized. Even though the data is collected from a public dataset platform, the research will still follow ethical research practices and comply with relevant academic data protection standards. Ethical clearance will be requested before starting the research to ensure that the study follows proper research governance and ethical guidelines. To prepare a dataset of ground truth labels for training the automated grading system, a subset of 100 reports will be randomly selected from the collected dataset. These reports will then be evaluated   independently   by   three   experienced   academic   supervisors   with   significant  experience in assessing academic reports. After grading, the Cohen’s Kappa value will be  calculated to measure the level of agreement among the evaluators. Only the samples that show

17 | P a g e  a strong level of agreement (Kappa value greater than 0.70) will be selected for the final training dataset. This process ensures that the ground truth labels used for training the system are reliable and consistent. The final dataset will consist of the 100 samples with the highest agreement scores among the evaluators, ensuring the quality and accuracy of the training data used for the classification model.  3.5 Validation Strategy and Performance Metrics  •   Grading Accuracy: Cohen's Kappa ≥ 0.80 against expert grader consensus  •   Concept Mapping Accuracy: ≥ 85% precision in mapping to correct KG nodes (expert  validation)  •   Recommendation Relevance: ≥ 80% relevance score by academic supervisors  •   Feedback Report Usability: SUS Score ≥ 85 from student and supervisor evaluations  •   Learning Outcome Improvement: ≥ 15% improvement in mean report quality between  iterations

18 | P a g e  4. HIGH-LEVEL SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE  A new component has been developed as a pipeline of four individual modules. The main functionality of the component is grading received reports, identifying weaknesses and linking them to the relevant concepts, suggesting learning materials and summarizing all data in a student feedback report. The component integrates with IPMS system by receiving received reports, grading, identifying weaknesses, linking them to concepts, suggesting learning materials and sending back graded and marked report with recommended learning materials to student and academic advisor pages.  4.1 Component Overview  Input Layer:   The source document in PDF or DOCX format is inputted by the student through the IPMS portal. The source document is parsed for structured text, headings and metadata by the document parsing module. Pre-processing activities are carried out by utilising spaCy for sentence splitting, tokenization and entity recognition.  Semantic Grading Engine : The output of this block is fed into the Semantic Grading Engine, where each subsection is embedded using Sentence-BERT and compared against the rubric descriptions stored in the Semantic Grading Engine. This results in a score vector and a compliance flag for each subsection, and a list of sections that do not meet the threshold are marked as weaknesses.  Knowledge Graph Concept Mapper:   The marked sections and the concepts related to them are mapped to the nodes of the IT Research Knowledge Graph in Neo4j. The traversal in the graph gives the prerequisites which the students are not aware of, hence multi layered weakness detection.  Resource Recommendation Engine:   The identified weakness concepts are then inputted into the recommendation engine, which uses the Semantic Scholar API and an in-house curated resources database to generate a ranked list of relevant papers, tutorials, and examples for each concept.  Feedback Generation Module:   This module uses the grading results, weakness concepts and recommended resources to output a feedback report in an agreed structural format. The NLG (Natural Language Generation) component then generates detailed prose sentences to produce a concise and meaningful summary of the feedback given and the action required from the learner IPMS .  Dashboard Layer:   This deliverable will implement a complete feedback report for students on their IPMS student dashboard. This will be based on a dynamic Knowlege Graph that graphically represents for each student (as well as for the class by the supervisor, through an aggregate classroom view) the concepts and associated items they are strong and weak on

20 | P a g e  4.2 Component Interactions and Data Flow  All our workflow does is move in one direction, from the starting point (submission) to the ending point (feedback). A report comes in, it is graded by the Grading Engine, and this grading results in the Knowledge Graph Mapper output which in turn gives us the list of weaknesses for the student. These weaknesses are then used by the Recommendation Engine and the outputs of the three components are then provided to the Feedback Generation module before reaching the dashboard. As the reporting is done asynchronously, the system is able to process many reports at the same time without slowing down the grading.  Parent IPMS connection is implemented through REST API. The parent application sends a submission event including the student ID, group ID and document URL, and the component returns a JSON response with grade vector, weaknesses, suggested resources and full feedback. 24 | P a g e  6. COMMERCIALIZATION PLAN  6.1 Target Market and Customer Persona  The most immediate market for this system is universities in Sri Lanka and the wider South and Southeast Asian region that run research-based undergraduate programs, particularly in IT and STEM. SLIIT is the natural starting point, but the system could reasonably expand to other local   universities   like   University   of   Moratuwa,   NSBM,   and   Informatics   Institute   of Technology, and eventually to international institutions with similar program structures. There is also a secondary market in private EdTech platforms that offer research supervision services, and in corporate training programs that need to evaluate technical reports at scale.  Secondary markets include private EdTech platforms that provide research supervision support services and corporate training programs that require technical report evaluation at scale.  6.2 Value Proposition  The system has three things that are significant to institutions. First, it offloads supervisors up to 60% of the time on marking which liberates them to the type of mentoring dialogue that actually requires a human. Second, it ensures that each student receives equal and rubric- based feedback irrespective of supervisor workload and the size of the classes. Third, it proactively monitors how students are getting better with time by associating feedback with the particular learning materials and quantifying the improvement per submission which provides institutions with something quantifiable to actually refer to in regards to learning outcomes.  6.3 Revenue Model  •   Institutional Licensing: Annual per-institution licensing fee based on student enrollment size (e.g., LKR 500,000 – 2,000,000 per year for institutions of 500 – 5,000 students).  •   SaaS API Access: Per-evaluation API pricing for EdTech platforms integrating the grading engine into their own products (e.g., USD 0.10 – 0.50 per report evaluation).  •   Premium Analytics Module: Additional subscription for advanced cohort analytics, benchmarking, and accreditation reporting.  6.4 Competitive Advantage  Turnitin checks for plagiarism. Gradescope handles structured problem sets. General LMS tools record grades. None of them do what this system does combine semantic research report evaluation, knowledge graph-based weakness diagnosis, and automated adaptive resource recommendation in a single pipeline. 1  Intelligent Dyslexia Support Device  R26-IT-069  Project Proposal Report  Abekoon I.L- IT22175670  B.Sc. (Hons) Degree in Information Technology Specialized in  Information Technology  Department of Information Technology  Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology Sri Lanka  March 2026

2

3  ABSTRACT  Affects about 10% of the global population and Sri Lanka has seen a similar trend. Children in our Bilingual (Sinhala-English) schools already navigate two scripts or writing systems. Our study showed that that 22% of children in the semi-urban areas of Sri Lanka are struggling significantly with reading and spelling. Incorrect pronunciation is one of the core causes of problems with reading and spelling. Children spend huge amounts of time trying to work out how to change what they see on a page of print into what the word sounds like. If they cannot accomplish this, then their reading speed is dramatically slowed down, and comprehension can be very poor. However the applications currently available are designed for the developed countries and have expensive technology dependent on the artificial intellience and speech recognition technology. These are affordable to those with the ability to pay in developed and upper-middle class developing economies, but are completely unaffordable in lower income countries such as Sri Lanka.This entry is about my individual work for the Smart Reading Buddy (SRB) project. I have developed a Pronunciation Verification module based on speech verification using the matching technique between audio samples. Unlike using a full automatic speech recognition (ASR) approach, here I used Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) to compare the child’s speech recording with a reference clean audio sample for each word attempted by the child. The attempt is marked as OK, ALMOST or WRONG and is accompanied by a specific lighting, vibration and audio feedback provided by the Buddy hardware.  Three features in this module are unique:  1.   Visual Mouth Guide – Simple animated lip movement of each word is displayed before it is read by the child (especially important where the sound is not found in Sinhala)  2.   Multi-Attempt Learning Strategy – The child gets increasing assistance from the Buddy over up to three attempts. First, a retry message is given; secondly a listen reminder is given; thirdly, the audio is replayed at a slower rate and the lip movement guide is replayed.  3.   The Pronunciation Error Pattern Analysis (PEPA) which records which sound(s) a child is having trouble with and builds over time a picture of the individual’s speech difficulties.  The entire system is implemented in Flutter/Dart, and works offline on a standard Android device. The data is sent to the Buddy device via Bluetooth Low Energy. Local data is stored per session and synced to the analytics server. Our work is aligned with the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals - SDG 4: Quality Education and SDG 10: Reduced Inequalities.  . Keywords: Dyslexia, Pronunciation Verification, Dynamic Time Warping, Visual Mouth Guide, Error Pattern Analysis, Multisensory Feedback, Assistive Technology, Bilingual Education, Sri Lanka.

4  ACKNOWLEDGEMENT  I want to start by thanking my supervisor and co-supervisor. Their input genuinely helped me think more clearly about what I was building and why. I also want to thank my teammates this kind of group project only works when everyone pulls their weight, and they did. I’m grateful to SLIIT for the support and resources throughout. And I’d like to acknowledge the educators and researchers in Sri Lanka who have been raising awareness about how little help dyslexic children actually receive that work is part of what motivated this project.
