7  1. INTRODUCTION  1.1 Background and Context  Dyslexia is a learning disability that affects the ability of the person to recognize words correctly, spell, and decode written words. The phonological processing is the primary problem. Simply put, the brain is not coordinated to manipulate individual sounds which constitute words. Approximately, every ten percent of the global population is impacted and without prompt assistance these may continue to haunt a child into his or her adulthood. This is even more complicated in Sri Lanka. The children who are in Sinhala- medium and bilingual schools must learn to deal with two systems of writing at the same time. The alpha syllabic script of Sinhalese is very consistent in terms of letters and sounds. Conversely, the spelling system of the English language is mostly irregular and the letters have varying sounds with the same letter having various sounds at their usage in words. This complicates learning particularly to the dyslexic children. Sandyanganie et al. (2016) have discovered that more than 22 percent of ten-year-olds in semi-urban Sri Lanka have severe reading and spelling problems. This is even aggravated by low family income, little education of parents and the fact that many teachers have never been trained to identify and support dyslexic learners. The ramifications of the same are severe. In under-resourced environments, dyslexic children face a greater risk of school dropout, poor chances of acquiring secure employment, depression, or low self-esteem. Although the challenge is common, very few available tools are affordable to mitigate on the problem in Sri Lanka.  Majority of the assistive technology available in the commercial market is targets the English speaking population, needs a strong internet connection or expensive hardware, and it is inaccessible to the very families who are in the greatest need. The centre of this problem lies in pronunciation. Inability to associate a written word and its sound leads to poor reading fluency and understanding in a child. A basic application where people can instantly have a response on if they are pronouncing their words correctly and can operate offline on a basic smartphone might get the children learning on a higher level. The project will contribute to SDG 4 (Quality Education), especially 4.1, 4.5 and 4.a that focus on the inclusive education of all people, including those with disabilities. It is also associated with SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) and SDG 9 (Innovation and Infrastructure). The work is included in the AIMS research cluster of SLIIT and is affiliated to the EdTech and HealthTech research domains.1.2 Literature Review. A lot of studies have been conducted on the use of technology in assisting dyslexic students, especially phonological training and pronunciation. This section discusses three aspects that are most pertinent to this project; what the research has to say about dyslexia and phonological processing, how computer-based pronunciation aids have evolved and what is available in low-resource context.  1.2.1 Dyslexia and Phonological Processing  According to the International Dyslexia Association (2020), phonological awareness is one of the fundamental impairments of dyslexia, and the structured phonics teaching method is one of the most supported means of intervention [1]. Indrarathne (2019) focused on Sri Lankan learners in particular and discovered that dyslexic students learning English as a foreign language are struggling with a twofold problem which they are attempting to map the sounds having a phonological system that functions in a much different way in Sinhala [2]. The University of York research on the case of teacher awareness in Sri Lanka draws an equally worrying image: the gap between teachers’ knowledge on dyslexia and the support they offer is indeed vast [3].

8  1.2.2 Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training (CAPT)  Neri et al. (2002) established that CAPT systems have the ability to provide an effective feedback in pronunciation especially when the correction is provided immediately to the attempt [A]. The traditional method involves a complete Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) pipeline to identify errors but it has actual disadvantages. ASR systems demand a lot of processing, usually trained on adult speech, and do not work in noisy conditions [B] none of which are applicable to a child with a cheap Android phone in a busy classroom.  There has been an increase in the usage of lighter options. MFCC feature-vector-based DTW-based pronunciation scoring has shown reasonable accuracy without a full ASR pipeline, a significant difference that makes it much more practical in the context of an offline mobile application [C]. Visual feedback of lip and mouth position has been studied as an articulation-centred tool in speech therapy to enable learners to relate written symbols to the actual process of making a sound, providing an articulation-centred perspective that adds further useful opinion to the tool [D]. That is the concept of Visual Mouth Guide of this module.  1.2.3 Assistive Technology for Dyslexia  Al-Lamki and Al-Lamki (2012) have discovered that multisensory interventions (those involving auditory, visual, and kinesthetic components) are always better than single channel interventions on dyslexic learners [4]. The design of this module was based on that discovery. Cost and accessibility were identified by Jayawardena and Abeyawickrama (2016) as the primary obstacles to introducing the assistive technology to the Sri Lankan classroom [5], which explains why maintaining the hardware at LKR 3,500 was a difficult limit at the beginning. Considering what is currently available in the market: such tools as Nessy Reading & Spelling, Claro ScanPen, or Prizmo are English-based and have subscription fees, which are too expensive to afford by a typical family in Sri Lanka. Free software such as NVDA and Bookshare is text based and has no touch with pronunciation whatsoever. The reality is that there is no other product that can perform the bilingual Sinhala-English pronunciation checking, offline functioning, multisensory feedback, time tracking error trends, and is below LKR 4000.  1.2.4 Summary of Limitations in Existing Work  •   Full ASR is computationally expensive and performs poorly with child voices in noisy environments  •   All tools reviewed focus on English only there is nothing designed for Sinhala-English bilingual learners  •   High cost and internet dependency make existing tools inaccessible to low-income Sri Lankan families  •   Multisensory feedback combining haptic, visual, and audio cues is largely absent from affordable tools  •   No existing solution tracks pronunciation error patterns to build a personalised speech difficulty profile  •   No affordable tool provides visual articulation guidance (mouth/lip animations) for bilingual dyslexic learners

9  1.3 Research Gap  After reviewing literature and seeing what is available, one fact is evident there is a gap: there is no low priced offline off-the-shelf outand capable bilingual pronunciation checker system that can be used by dyslexic kids studying in primary schools in Sri Lanka. This is the divide that this element should close.  The disparity breaks down into three dimensions. The available tools are technically founded on full ASR pipelines that cannot be used on low-end devices offline. The methods founded on DTW have proved in the research laboratories, but they have never been constructed into a child-oriented, bilingual application that includes a layered adaptive coaching. Contextually speaking, there is no tool that has been designed or experimented within a Sinhalese-English bilingual learning environment where the phonological attributes of both scripts present some challenges and where English only tools simply cannot explain the challenges. As concerns the access, everything that is currently available is sold at the Western market not at LKR 30, 000-70, 000 a months  Sealing of those gaps is not the only thing in this module. It has three unique original contributions that are not found elsewhere: a Visual Mouth Guide that shows animated articulation cues before each attempt, a Multi-Attempt Learning Strategy that gradually increases support based on three attempts, and a Pronunciation Error Pattern Analysis system that builds up an individual phoneme-based speech difficulty pattern based on the data of the session.  2. OBJECTIVES  2.1 Main Objective  To create and develop a lightweight, fully offline, augmented pronunciation verification module with dyslexic primary school children (age 615) in Sri Lanka (both Sinhala and English) based on DTW- based audio similarity scoring, to provide real-time multisensory feedback on the Smart Reading Buddy hardware and companion mobile application, with embedded Visual Mouth Guide animations, adaptive multi-attempt coaching and customised pronunciation error pattern analysis.  2.2 Specific Objectives  1.To create and construct a bilingual word display module whereby the Sinhalese and English packs of words are used under a simple and easy to use child friendly interface with audio-visual prompts.  2.To introduce a Visual Mouth Guide (VMG) illustrating animated movements of lips and mouth with each word, so that children will be able to observe the formation of a sound with the help of their bodies and then strive to do it.  3.In order to create a preprocessing pipeline and audio recording with Hold-to-Speak, silence- removal, and MFCC feature-extractor resistant to child voices in noisy conditions.  4.To apply a DTW based similarity scoring algorithm which compares the recording of a child with a reference audio sample and classifies the output as OK, ALMOST and WRONG based on the measurement of the accuracy.  5.In order to create a Multi-Attempt Learning Strategy that will transition to Buddy coaching of as many as three attempts per word -retry prompt on the first attempt, a listen-carefully cue on the second attempt, and slowed-down reference audio with VMG replay on the third attempt.

10  6.To create a Pronunciation Error Pattern Analysis (PEPA) module incorporating per-sound accuracy data per session into an individualised pattern of speech difficulty, it is necessary to know what a child is always having trouble with.  7To incorporate Buddy hardware feedback control in such a way that the device reacts to every classification result by corresponding to the right LED lights, vibration pattern, and audio prompt.  8.To create an interaction logging system, which documents the pronunciation accuracy, the count of attempts, error rates per sound, and the session completion rate on the Personalized Progress Analytics Hub.  9.In order to test the system on supervised testing with primary school children, in order to measure classification accuracy, user interaction and usability under the real-life conditions.  SO1 Bilingual Word Display Module  Q: What is the objective?   To design a word display module that displays Sinhala and English words in a child-friendly manner with audio-visual cues.  Q: Why is this objective important or needed?   There is no tool that currently offers the facility of presenting bilingual Sinhala and English words to dyslexic children in Sri Lanka. Children should be able to see the word, hear the word, and attempt the word.  Q: How will you measure it?   By verifying that the word pack contains a minimum of 50 words across both languages, reviewed and approved by a language expert before testing begins.  Q: How does it align with the research problem?   The research problem identifies the absence of any bilingual pronunciation tool for Sri Lankan dyslexic learners. This objective directly addresses that gap by building the content delivery foundation of the module.  SO2 Visual Mouth Guide (VMG)  Q: What is the objective?   To design a word display module that displays Sinhala and English words in a child-friendly manner with audio-visual cues.  Q: Why is this objective important or needed?   There is no tool that currently offers the facility of presenting bilingual Sinhala and English words to dyslexic children in Sri Lanka. Children should be able to see the word, hear the word, and attempt the word.  SO3 Audio Recording and Preprocessing Pipeline  Q: What is the objective?  The objective is to develop an audio recording and preprocessing pipeline with Hold-to-Speak, silence removal, and MFCC feature extraction for handling child voices in noisy classroom environments.  Q: Why is this objective needed?  The objective is needed because the ASR system is not feasible with child voices in noisy environments, which is one of the research gaps identified in the problem statement. A clean preprocessing pipeline is required for the DTW scoring to be feasible in the ASR system on a basic smartphone.

11  Q : How will you measure it?  The objective is measured by testing the pipeline in noisy environments and checking the false positive rate, which should be less than or equal to 10%, i.e., the system should not accept a wrong pronunciation more than 10% of the time.  Q: How does it align with the research problem?  The research problem is not feasible for the ASR system in offline mobile devices with child voices. The objective is the preprocessing part of the problem.  SO4 DTW Based Similarity Scoring Engine  Q:   What is the objective?  To develop a DTW-based similarity scoring algorithm, where the recorded pronunciation of the child would be compared to a reference audio and classified as OK, ALMOST, or WRONG, and measured for its accuracy.  Q: Why is the objective important?  Currently, there is no light-weight, offline pronunciation scoring system for bilingual Sinhala/English- speaking children. While the DTW approach has been shown to be a feasible alternative to ASR systems, its application to a bilingual scenario, particularly for children, has never been explored.  Q: How would you measure it?  The proposed system would measure its effectiveness by comparing its output to a set of ground truth recordings, where the classification accuracy of the system would be at least 80%.  Q: How does it relate to the research problem?  The proposed SO4 system addresses the technical part of the research problem, as there currently exists no feasible offline pronunciation scoring system.  .

12  3. METHODOLOGY  The research will be conducted by following a design science research approach. DSR is an appropriate method for this research because the whole purpose of this research is to design a thing (an IT system that solves a real problem) and then evaluate if it actually works. DSR has six steps: problem identification, specifying the objectives of the solution, designing and building the artefact, demonstrating the artefact, evaluating the artefact, and writing up  3.1 Research Approach  I'm taking an iterative build-measure-learn approach. The idea is to build an initial working prototype, run it with a small group of primary school children who have reading difficulties, always in the presence of a parent or teacher, measure the results, and then improve before the next round. I will measure both quantitative results (such as classification accuracy, system latency, and rates of errors per sound) and qualitative results (such as how easy it was for the child to use the program, how useful it was for the teacher).  3.2 Technical Methods and Algorithms  Audio Preprocessing: When the child stops recording, the audio from the mobile’s microphone is cleaned before anything else is done. Silence is removed from the start and end of the audio, the audio is normalized, and a pre-emphasis filter is applied to compensate for the high-frequency roll-off that is characteristic of cheap microphones. After that, the MFCC features are extracted with 13 coefficients, a window of 25ms, and a step of 10ms.  Pronunciation Similarity Scoring: Then, the DTW algorithm is used to compute the similarity between the MFCCs of the child’s audio and the reference audio. The advantage of the DTW algorithm is that it “stretches and shrinks the time axis to find the best alignment between two signals.” This is important because “children vary their speaking rates.” After that, the result is normalized and compared with thresholds to produce one of the following: OK, ALMOST, or WRONG. These thresholds will be established based on the testing with real children rather than guessed.  BLE Communication: After that, the application sends a command code to the Buddy device via Bluetooth Low Energy.  3.3 Visual Mouth Guide (VMG)  One of the more innovative parts of this module is the Visual Mouth Guide. Research shows that dyslexic learners often have trouble mapping written symbols to the physical movements needed to produce a sound [D]. Hearing a word is helpful, but it does not always tell you what your mouth is supposed to be doing. The VMG bridges that gap by showing a short-animated lip-movement sequence before each pronunciation attempt.  The animation is deliberately simple a cartoon mouth outline cycling through the key positions for the target phoneme. The child can replay it as many times as they want before pressing the record button. The table below shows how different sounds are handled:

13  Target Sound   Mouth Animation Cue   Supporting Cue  "B" /   බ   Lips close tightly, then release   Vibration pulse when lips should close  "S" /   ස   Teeth together, slight smile position  High-pitched audio tone cue  "TH"   Tongue lightly touching upper front teeth  Slow-motion reference audio  "R" /   ර   Tongue curled slightly back, lips neutral  Side-by-side child vs reference waveform  The VMG frames are stored as lightweight SVG sequences inside the app bundle, so there is no internet dependency and the storage overhead is minimal. Every sound in both the Sinhala and English word packs has a corresponding VMG entry. This feature is especially valuable for sounds like English ‘TH’ and ‘R’ that have no equivalent in Sinhala — children need explicit visual guidance for those, not just audio. Figure 3 in the Appendix shows a storyboard of the VMG animation for three common phonemes.  3.4 Multi-Attempt Learning Strategy  Rather than just letting a child retry indefinitely without any change in feedback, this module uses a graduated coaching strategy. The idea is grounded in scaffolded learning — the amount of support increases with each attempt, but only as much as is actually needed. On the first attempt, the child is on their own. If they are still struggling by the third, they get full guided support.  The strategy works as follows:  Attempt   DTW Result   Buddy Response   Support Level  1st attempt   ALMOST or WRONG  Green/yellow/red light + vibration Buddy says: “Try again!”  Minimal — child tries independently  2nd attempt   ALMOST or WRONG  Red light + longer vibration Buddy says: “Listen carefully first” + plays normal-speed reference audio  Moderate — audio reminder provided  3rd attempt   Any result   Slowed-down reference audio (70% speed) Buddy says: “Watch and listen” + VMG replay  Maximum — full guided support  The session continues immediately with a positive Buddy reaction if the youngster becomes comfortable at any stage. The term is marked in the session log and added to the child's error fingerprint for the teacher or parent to check if the results of all three attempts are incorrect. The Flutter app's logic is constructed as a simple state machine; no intricate branching is required, and the attempt counter resets for every new word. There is no requirement for real-time processing

14  during the session because the 70%-speed audio is pre-generated during content creation and saved with the standard reference.  3.5 Pronunciation Error Pattern Analysis (PEPA)  The PEPA module is probably the strongest research contribution in this component. On its own, per- word feedback tells a child how they did in the moment. PEPA takes a longer view it looks across all sessions and identifies which sounds a child consistently gets wrong, turning that data into a structured speech difficulty profile.  The mechanism is simple: every time a word is attempted, the result (OK, ALMOST, or WRONG) is logged alongside the phoneme(s) associated with that word. At the end of each session, PEPA aggregates the logs and recalculates an error rate per sound. If a sound’s error rate exceeds a set threshold across multiple sessions, it gets flagged as a persistent difficulty.  Table 7 shows the kind of output PEPA produces:  Sound / Phoneme   Total Attempts   Incorrect Attempts   Error Rate (%)  R ( ර )   20   9   45%  L ( ල )   18   7   38%  TH (English)   15   9   60%  B ( බ )   22   3   14%  S ( ස )   20   4   20%  In this example, R, L, and TH are all flagged because their error rates are high enough to suggest a persistent problem. The Analytics Hub uses those flags to prioritise those sounds in the child’s daily micro-plan. A teacher looking at the weekly report can immediately see where each child needs the most practice without needing any technical knowledge to read the data.  PEPA uses pure rule-based logic no machine learning models are involved. The phoneme-to-word mapping is stored in the word pack JSON file. Error rates are recalculated at the end of each session and stored in SQLite. The profile is displayed as a simple bar chart in the app’s progress dashboard. From a research standpoint, the aggregated PEPA data across a sample of children would give us a picture of common phonological error patterns in dyslexic Sinhala-English bilingual learners data that simply does not exist in published literature right now.

17  4. HIGH-LEVEL SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE  The pronunciation verification module is one of four components in the Smart Reading Buddy ecosystem. Figure 1 (to be added in the final submission) will show the overall system architecture. This section focuses on the internal structure of the pronunciation module and how it fits in with the rest of the system.  4.1 Component Overview  The module breaks down into seven parts.   The first three are all about setting the child up before they even try to say the word. The last four kick in after they speak.  •   Word Display   is the starting point — it puts the word on screen in both languages and gives the child a button to hear it pronounced first.  •   Visual Mouth Guide   comes next. Before recording starts, it plays a short animation showing exactly how to position the lips and mouth for the target sound — so the child isn't just guessing.  •   Audio Capture   is what handles the actual recording interaction. There's a hold-to-speak button, and once the child lets go, the system trims any silence from the edges and normalizes the sample rate to keep things consistent.  •   Once audio is captured,   Signal Processing   takes over. It runs the clip through pre-emphasis, splits it into frames, applies a window function, and extracts the MFCC features — essentially turning the raw audio into something the scoring engine can work with.  •   The   DTW Scoring Engine   then compares the child's MFCC vectors against a reference recording using Dynamic Time Warping. The normalized distance it gets back maps to one of three labels: OK, ALMOST, or WRONG.  •   Multi-Attempt Controller   keeps track of how many times the child has tried the current word. Based on that count, it decides which type of coaching response to fire — so a first attempt gets different feedback than a third.  •   Finally,   Feedback Dispatch and Logging   ties everything together. It sends the result over BLE to the physical Buddy device, triggers the right on-screen animation, and writes the full session record to SQLite — including the per-phoneme breakdown that feeds into PEPA.  4.2 Data Flow  The flow is linear and entirely on-device: the child watches the VMG animation and listens to the reference → presses Hold-to-Speak and says the word → audio is captured and cleaned → MFCC features extracted → DTW scoring runs → the Multi-Attempt Controller checks the attempt number and picks the right coaching response → the result is sent to the Buddy via BLE and shown on screen → everything is logged to SQLite, including phoneme-level data for PEPA. No network call happens at any stage.  4.3 Integration with the SRB Ecosystem  The pronunciation module connects to the rest of the SRB system in two ways. First, it uses the same BLE protocol as the Timed Reading and Stylus Writing modules all three send command codes to the same physical Buddy device. Second, the session logs it generates accuracy rates, retry counts, DTW scores, and PEPA phoneme error rates   are fed into the Personalized Progress Analytics Hub, which uses them to build the child’s error fingerprint and create daily practice micro-plans.

18  4.4 Scalability and Security Considerations  Word packs and VMG animation mappings are stored in JSON, so new vocabulary or mouth guide frames can be added without touching the application code. Both the normal-speed and 70%-speed reference audio files are stored in compressed format within the app bundle. All data stays on the device the SQLite schema stores session IDs, not names or school information. BLE pairing uses address- based authentication to block unauthorised device connections.

26  APPENDICES  Appendix A: Sample Word Pack Structure (JSON Schema)  {   "language": "sinhala",   "level": "beginner",   "words": [   {   "id": "sl_001",   "word": "amma",   "display_script": " ඇම්මා   ",   "phonemes": ["a","m","a"],   "reference_audio": "assets/audio/sl/sl_001.wav",   "slow_audio": "assets/audio/sl/sl_001_slow.wav",   "vmg_frames": "assets/vmg/phoneme_a.svg"   }   ] }  Appendix B: DTW Algorithm Overview  The Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) method is a dynamic programming method that attempts to evaluate the similarity of two time series by finding the best alignment of the two time series on the cost grid. If we are given feature sequences X = {x1, x2, ..., xN} and Y = {y1, y2, ..., yM}, then the DTW method fills an NxM matrix where each entry is defined as D(i,j) = dist(xi, yj) + min(D(i-1,j), D(i,j-1), D(i-1,j-1)). The ultimate result is the entry in the matrix D(N,M) that is normalized by the length of the alignment path. The normalization is crucial as it allows the score to be compared for words of different lengths as well as the difference in the speed of speech of the children. 4 | P a g e  ABSTRACT  This paper addresses a hard problem in contemporary educational institutions: grading  students’ assignments and providing structured, useful feedback is still largely a human -centric task. Most current tools are geared towards grading and rubric systems, b ut they don’t provide  actionable, conceptual advice that helps instructors target exactly what students are missing. To address this problem, this paper introduces an AI-based system for Automated Quality Assessment and Adaptive Mentorship. This system is conceptualized as an integral part of a broader project: The Intelligent Project Management System for Undergraduate Students (R26- IT-095). The problem statement is evident: there are no systems that go beyond grading to identify exactly where students are weak in their understanding. Rubric-based grading systems are labor-intensive, subjective, and unreliable. Computerized grading tools are mostly geared towards catching surface-level mistakes without providing instructors with actionable advice on how to   improve students’   understanding. Our system will employ a multi-step system: an NLP- based Semantic Grading Engine that will analyze how well a student’s report is  structured, how deep its technical content is, and how well it aligns with a given rubric system by using transformer models; An AI-driven Resource Recommendation Engine, which connects the identified gaps to relevant learning materials, e.g., academic papers and tutorials; An   Automated   Feedback   Generation   module,   which   produces   structured,   personalized improvement reports for each student. This shifts the focus of the grading process to intelligent mentorship, thus bridging the loop between grading and learning.  The key technologies used here include Python, BERT/Sentence Transformers for semantic analysis, spacey for NLP, a Neo4j-based knowledge graph for concept mapping, and a React.js- based dashboard. This system is intended to integrate well with the GitHub contribution and project planning features of the parent platform. It is expected that the system results will be a reduction in manual grading time by over 60 percent, concordance under 80 percent with the expert evaluator, and a demonstration of the improved report quality of students with repeat of the system. This element of the system is a direct contribution towards the attainment of the UN Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) through provision of fair, transparent and data balanced academic mentorship.  Keywords:   Automated Quality Assessment, NLP, Semantic Grading, Adaptive Mentorship, Resource Recommendation, Feedback Generation, Educational AI, BERT.  .

10 | P a g e  1. INTRODUCTION  Feedback and assessment is one of the key factors that a university can impact students at undergraduate level. Students working on research projects want timely, constructive and  relevant feedback to their work. It’s no good just getting a mark at the bottom of a page and  being told that is all the lecturers has to say. Currently, most universities including SLIIT are using manual methods for assessing and providing feedback to students. This is a very time- consuming task and the method of assessment and marking of the project is highly dependent on the lecturer.  This project is related to the subcomponent of R26-IT-095 Intelligent Project Management System; in this project, the subcomponent aims at developing an application to assess and evaluate the student research reports and to translate the assessment into valuable information that benefits the students. In other words, this part focuses on the written work in the  students’ reports and aims at delivering useful assessment comments that contribute to real  learning for the students as opposed to merely indicating mistakes. This project is hence related to UN SDG 4   –   Quality Education. In particular, it aims at ensuring that every student receives the adequate academic support in a timely manner that benefits the students, regardless of the workload facing the supervisor.  It is SDBI’s contribution to achieving the UN’s Sustainable Development Goal 4, to ensure  inclusive and effective quality education for all. It provides immediate, structured and meaningful feedback to students regarding their performance in a data-informed way. It indicates performance in relation to achievement for each learning outcome as well as highlighting gaps in relation to the expected level of achievement for the student in relation to the learning outcome. Ultimately it seeks to improve student performance to the highest standard of education possible, even when a Field Supervisor has heavy caseloads and cannot provide the required individual attention.  1.1 Background and Context  Marking research reports is genuinely time-consuming work. A supervisor looking after several groups has to go through each report, check the structure, the academic language, how well the student understands the topic, and whether it actually follows the rubric   all while juggling deadlines. Research consistently shows that the quality and speed of feedback is one of the strongest factors in whether students actually improve [1], yet in practice feedback tends to arrive late, stay quite general, and often have little connection to the specific problems in a student's work [2].  What is more significant is what occurs after the mark has been given. In the case that a student scores poorly on their literature review or their methodology section, what they actually require is not simply to know the score that they need to know what to read, what to revisit and how to correct it. Tools like Moodle and Blackboard can record grades and show rubric comments, but they cannot look at a student's work and figure out what the student still does not understand, or point them towards something that would actually help [3].  The integration of NLP and machine learning into academic assessment has started to change what is possible here. Models like BERT have shown they can compare student writing against reference content with real accuracy [4], and knowledge graphs offer a way to connect concepts so that when a weakness is detected, you can trace back what underlying understanding might be missing [5]. The idea behind this project is to bring those pieces together to build something that does not just score a report, but actually uses that score to help the student learn. This work

11 | P a g e  is also aligned with SDG 4 and the CoEAI research cluster at SLIIT, applying AI directly to improve the fairness and consistency of academic feedback.  This research proposes combining these technologies into a unified Automated Quality Assessment and Adaptive Mentorship system. The system will evaluate student reports using semantic   NLP,   map   identified   weaknesses   to   academic   concepts,   and   automatically recommend learning resources to guide improvement   effectively acting as a personal AI research mentor for every student in the program.  This element is also consistent with SDG 4 (Quality Education) and Co EAI research cluster (Centre of Excellence for AI) in SLIIT because it directly implements the progressive AI to enhance the equity, regularity, and achievement of education.  1.2 Literature Review  A fair amount of work has been done on using NLP and AI for educational assessment, though most of it stops short of what this project is trying to do. The following review goes through the key existing approaches and what each one is missing.  Rani and Sujatha [6] built an automated evaluation system for descriptive answers using keyword extraction and semantic similarity. It got reasonable accuracy but was designed for short answers only and did not give any structured feedback or try to identify what the student actually did not understand.  Ramachandran et al. [7] took things further with a BERT-based rubric grading system for essays, which lined up well with human graders on overall scores. The problem is it could not point to a specific weak section in the report or suggest anything for the student to do about it.  Cui et al. [8] showed that GNN-based models trained on knowledge graphs could predict student performance across connected concepts a useful insight for diagnosing learning gaps. But that work never connected to a practical feedback system, so there was no way for it to actually help a student act on those gaps.  Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, developed by Corbett and Anderson [9], has been widely used in tutoring systems to track student mastery over time, and more recent work has extended this with graph-based propagation [10]. These approaches work well for structured exercises but were never designed for evaluating long-form academic writing like research reports.  The ACORN system [11] tried something different by using multimodal analysis of classroom recordings to assess teacher performance. It is an interesting approach, but it looks at the teacher side only and has nothing to do with evaluating what students actually submit.  Liu et al. [12] built a recommendation system for academic resources using citation networks and reading history it worked well for personalized suggestions but was not connected to any assessment pipeline, so it could not react to what a specific student actually got wrong in their work.  Commercial tools, Turnitin and Grammarly, as to commercial tools, can identify the surface- level writing problems but not assess the technical depth, the rubric requirements, or the fact that the student comprehends the material he/she is writing about [2].They also do not generate any kind of improvement plan tied to learning resources.  Taken together, the gap is clear: there is no existing system that combines proper rubric-based semantic evaluation of research reports, knowledge graph-based weakness diagnosis, and

12 | P a g e  automated personalized resource recommendations in one place. That is exactly what this project is trying to build.  1.3 Research Gap  Looking at what is out there, the gap becomes fairly obvious. Existing tools either grade without explaining, or explain without diagnosing the actual problem. The table below sets out how the proposed system compares against what is currently available:  Aspect   Existing: Turnitin/LMS  Existing: Rubric Graders (BERT)  Proposed System  Grading Capability  Surface-level (plagiarism/grammar)  Holistic score, limited rubric  Section-by-section rubric compliance with semantic depth analysis  Weakness Identification  None   Score deduction only   Concept-level mapping to knowledge graph nodes  Feedback Generation  Generic comments   Rubric scores only   Structured, personalized improvement reports  Resource Recommendation  None   None   Targeted papers, tutorials, and examples based on identified gaps  Adaptive Learning Loop  None   None   Tracks improvement across submission iterations  Table 2: Research Gap Analysis   –   Existing Systems vs. Proposed System  What makes this project different is not just that it grades it is that it tries to understand why a student is struggling and does something about it. No existing tool currently combines semantic NLP-based   assessment   with   knowledge   graph   diagnosis   and   automated   resource recommendations for research report evaluation in an undergraduate setting. That is the gap this work is filling.

13 | P a g e  2. OBJECTIVES  2.1 Main Objective  The main goal of the project is to develop and create an AI-based tool that can automatically assess the quality of undergraduate research reports, identify the locations and reasons why a student is not performance, and give a student specific feedback and learning resources to correct the results.  2.2 Specific Objectives  Specific Objective 1: Implement NLP-based Semantic Grading Engine  •   Task 1: Implement an NLP pipeline that classifies, scores and provides feedback on each section of a research report (i.e. Introduction, Literature Review, Methodology, etc.) written by students based on a pre-defined academic rubric related to scientific quality, completeness and semantics. The intended base model is BERT or Sentence Transformers.  •   Measurable: - scoring accuracy of at least 80% (i.e. at least 80% agreement with  human grader scores) using Cohen’s Kappa coefficient on a validation dataset of 100  anonymized student feedback reports.  •   Achievable: This approach can easily utilize existing transformer-based models (such as those provided by Hugging Face) and NLP pre-processing provided by spaCy. The scoring rules for the model can be described in Python.  •   Realistic: It should ideally be possible to implement the suggested ideas on an existing dataset of anonymized historical project reports that are readily available in SLIIT after obtaining ethical clearance.  •   Time-bound: Expected completion within 2 months (Months 1 – 2 of implementation).  Specific Objective 2: Construct Academic Knowledge Graph for Concept Mapping  •   Focus: Design a structured Knowledge Graph to store IT research concepts, sub- topics, and prerequisite relationships. Identify gaps within the reports by linking them to the corresponding concept nodes within the graph.  •   Measurable target: Reach an accuracy rate of at least 85%, ensuring that the sections within the reports are correctly mapped to the corresponding concept nodes within the graph, based on expert opinions.  •   Feasible approach: Utilize the Neo4j graph database, NetworkX library, and existing IT research domain ontologies.  •   Real-world practicality: Developing an ontology for this purpose can be based on standard IT curriculum documents or taxonomies of IT research topics.  •   Schedule: To be completed within 1 month (Month 2).  Specific Objective 3: Developing an AI-Powered Resource Recommendation Engine  •   Focus :The objective of this task is to develop a recommendation system which takes concept level vulnerabilities as input and provides a list of learning resources (academic papers via the Semantic Scholar API, tutorials or coding examples) which are ranked in terms of their relevance to addressing the identified skills gaps.

14 | P a g e  •   Measurable target: A model that achieves an overall relevance score of at least 80% on a blinded validation set as measured by the academic supervisor.  •   Possible Solution: The suggested solution is based on applying collaborative filtering and content-based filtering in conjunction with the integration with open academic databases.  •   Real-World Practicality? Recommendation algorithms are widely used and practiced in many applications and various fields. It is easy to get access to academic databases such as Semantic Scholar and arXiv papers via Apis. Schedule: To be completed within 1.5 months (Months 3-4).  Specific Objective 4: Automate Structured Feedback Report Generation  •   Goal: Develop an automated module that integrates results from the grading process, identified weaknesses, and suggested resources to produce an understandable report for each submitted work.  •   Measurable: Target an 85% usability score (SUS) from both students and supervisors for the usability tests. The reports should cover all the dimensions identified by the rubric and include a minimum of three improvement suggestions.  •   Achievable: Utilize template-based Natural Language Generation for narrative sections, based on GPT-technologies; use a React.js dashboard for reporting.  •   Realistic: Aligns with the skill set of the project team for the front-end and standard educational feedback report formats.  •   Time-bound: To be completed within one month (Month 4).  Specific Objective 5: Assess System Performance and Confirm Learning Outcome  •   Specific: Perform end-to-end tests of the system with AI-generated grades and feedback compared with expert ratings, as well as the improvement in report quality with each iteration of student submission.  •   Measurable: At least a 15% increase in the average report quality score from the initial submission to the second submission with the help of AI feedback.  •   Achievable: A pilot group of 20-30 undergraduate IT4010 students will be used, with informed consent.  •   Realistic: The pilot testing is within the IT4010 research project timeframe of SLIIT.  •   Time-bound: The pilot testing should be completed within half a month (Month 5).

15 | P a g e  3. METHODOLOGY  This research adopts a Design Science Research (DSR) methodology, which is particularly well-suited for projects that aim to create and evaluate an innovative IT artifact that solves a clearly defined practical problem [13]. The methodology proceeds through five structured phases: Problem Definition, System Design, Prototype Development, Evaluation, and Iteration.  3.1 Research Approach  This project is being approached using a Design Science Research methodology. The overall goal of the research is to design and implement an innovative solution that can be validated against the problems identified. This approach as opposed to a theoretical approach is fitting to this problem because rather than being purely descriptive, the goal of the research is to be prescriptive and provide actionable solutions to students and educators while improving the assessment process. In this project, the problems of current assessment processes are clearly identified, with manual, inconsistent assessment not providing students with any tangible output. A working solution is then designed and implemented, validated through measurable metrics and then iteratively refined through the testing process.  3.2 Technical Methods and Algorithms  Semantic Grading Engine   Using Sentence-BERT (SBERT), the core grading module converts the rubric descriptors and the student report sections into the semantic space through the embedding of the semantic vectors using cosine similarity, providing a continuous score. For cases where the rubric compliance is categorical (e.g., Excellent/Good/Adequate/Poor), a classification head is added on top of the BERT encoder and the model is then fine-tuned on the training dataset of the annotated student reports along with the grades provided by the knowledgeable instructors.  Knowledge Graph Construction : The IT research domain The Knowledge Graph for the IT research domain is constructed by applying a semi-automated ontology extraction technique. The syllabi of Computer Science courses, general authoring guidelines for academic papers and a collection of   IT research papers are processed by applying spaCy’s NER (Named Entity  Recognition) and dependency parsing to derive concept entities and relationships. The derived entities and relationships are stored in a Neo4j graph database where node labels represent academic concepts (e.g., Machine Learning, Research Gap, Literature Review Structure) and the edges between the nodes represent the prerequisite/dependency relationship.  Weakness Propagation and Mapping   : They work on graded report sections corresponding to concepts located on Knowledge Graph for which the score is below the minimum threshold. From these report sections, they identify the essential concepts required to pass the skills that are analyzed through graph traversal algorithms and carry out the root-cause analysis of the weaknesses identified for each student who has been assessed.  Resource Recommendation :   The Resource Recommendation algorithm is a content-based recommendation algorithm. It takes the semantic representation of the identified concept gaps and matches them against a knowledge base built from academic resources we index from Semantic Scholar, arXiv and institutional repositories. The matched resources are then ranked based on the semantic similarity to the concept gaps, the publication date of the resource and the citation count.

16 | P a g e  Feedback Generation   : This block generates an improvement report based on templates and a large language model. Templates contain section feedback for each assignment and are populated based on the score given to each criterion, as well as the skills and knowledge gaps discovered, and recommended by the AI. For narrative summary sections, it utilizes GPT-4o via API to produce well-explained feedback for students .  3.3 Tools and Platforms  •   Programming languages: We use Python 3.10+ for the ML/NLP part, and JavaScript/TypeScript for the frontend.  •   NLP tools: We use HuggingFace Transformers for BERT and SBERT, and spaCy v3 for NLP  •   Knowledge Graph: Neo4j (graph database), NetworkX (graph algorithms), PyVis (visualization)  •   ML libraries: We use PyTorch and scikit-learn for machine learning.  •   Backend API tech stack: We use FastAPI in Python, along with Node.js/Express.js for integration with the parent system.  •   Frontend dashboard tech stack: We use React.js for the frontend, along with D3.js for graph visualization.  •   External API tech stack: We use the Semantic Scholar Academic Graph API and OpenAI GPT-4o API.  •   Databases: We use MongoDB for document-based data and PostgreSQL for relational databases.  •   Cloud hosting: We use AWS EC2 for model serving and AWS S3 for report storage.  •   Version control: We use GitHub, along with an integration with the parent system’s  contribution analytics.  3.4 Data Collection and Ethical Considerations  The following method has been proposed for data collection. Instead of collecting reports from SLIIT students, the dataset for this research will be obtained from the Kaggle platform, which provides publicly available datasets for research and machine learning development. Kaggle hosts a wide range of academic writing datasets, essays, and report-style documents that can be used for training and evaluating automated assessment systems.   The selected dataset will consist of report-like or essay-based academic documents that are already publicly available and permitted for research use. Since the data is publicly shared for research purposes, no personal identifiable information (PII) will be collected or stored in the proposed system. Any potential identifiers present in the dataset will be removed to ensure that all data used in the analysis remains fully anonymized. Even though the data is collected from a public dataset platform, the research will still follow ethical research practices and comply with relevant academic data protection standards. Ethical clearance will be requested before starting the research to ensure that the study follows proper research governance and ethical guidelines. To prepare a dataset of ground truth labels for training the automated grading system, a subset of 100 reports will be randomly selected from the collected dataset. These reports will then be evaluated   independently   by   three   experienced   academic   supervisors   with   significant  experience in assessing academic reports. After grading, the Cohen’s Kappa value will be  calculated to measure the level of agreement among the evaluators. Only the samples that show

17 | P a g e  a strong level of agreement (Kappa value greater than 0.70) will be selected for the final training dataset. This process ensures that the ground truth labels used for training the system are reliable and consistent. The final dataset will consist of the 100 samples with the highest agreement scores among the evaluators, ensuring the quality and accuracy of the training data used for the classification model.  3.5 Validation Strategy and Performance Metrics  •   Grading Accuracy: Cohen's Kappa ≥ 0.80 against expert grader consensus  •   Concept Mapping Accuracy: ≥ 85% precision in mapping to correct KG nodes (expert  validation)  •   Recommendation Relevance: ≥ 80% relevance score by academic supervisors  •   Feedback Report Usability: SUS Score ≥ 85 from student and supervisor evaluations  •   Learning Outcome Improvement: ≥ 15% improvement in mean report quality between  iterations

18 | P a g e  4. HIGH-LEVEL SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE  A new component has been developed as a pipeline of four individual modules. The main functionality of the component is grading received reports, identifying weaknesses and linking them to the relevant concepts, suggesting learning materials and summarizing all data in a student feedback report. The component integrates with IPMS system by receiving received reports, grading, identifying weaknesses, linking them to concepts, suggesting learning materials and sending back graded and marked report with recommended learning materials to student and academic advisor pages.  4.1 Component Overview  Input Layer:   The source document in PDF or DOCX format is inputted by the student through the IPMS portal. The source document is parsed for structured text, headings and metadata by the document parsing module. Pre-processing activities are carried out by utilising spaCy for sentence splitting, tokenization and entity recognition.  Semantic Grading Engine : The output of this block is fed into the Semantic Grading Engine, where each subsection is embedded using Sentence-BERT and compared against the rubric descriptions stored in the Semantic Grading Engine. This results in a score vector and a compliance flag for each subsection, and a list of sections that do not meet the threshold are marked as weaknesses.  Knowledge Graph Concept Mapper:   The marked sections and the concepts related to them are mapped to the nodes of the IT Research Knowledge Graph in Neo4j. The traversal in the graph gives the prerequisites which the students are not aware of, hence multi layered weakness detection.  Resource Recommendation Engine:   The identified weakness concepts are then inputted into the recommendation engine, which uses the Semantic Scholar API and an in-house curated resources database to generate a ranked list of relevant papers, tutorials, and examples for each concept.  Feedback Generation Module:   This module uses the grading results, weakness concepts and recommended resources to output a feedback report in an agreed structural format. The NLG (Natural Language Generation) component then generates detailed prose sentences to produce a concise and meaningful summary of the feedback given and the action required from the learner IPMS .  Dashboard Layer:   This deliverable will implement a complete feedback report for students on their IPMS student dashboard. This will be based on a dynamic Knowlege Graph that graphically represents for each student (as well as for the class by the supervisor, through an aggregate classroom view) the concepts and associated items they are strong and weak on

19 | P a g e  Figure 1: High-Level System Architecture of the Automated Quality Assessment and Adaptive Mentorship Component

20 | P a g e  4.2 Component Interactions and Data Flow  All our workflow does is move in one direction, from the starting point (submission) to the ending point (feedback). A report comes in, it is graded by the Grading Engine, and this grading results in the Knowledge Graph Mapper output which in turn gives us the list of weaknesses for the student. These weaknesses are then used by the Recommendation Engine and the outputs of the three components are then provided to the Feedback Generation module before reaching the dashboard. As the reporting is done asynchronously, the system is able to process many reports at the same time without slowing down the grading.  Parent IPMS connection is implemented through REST API. The parent application sends a submission event including the student ID, group ID and document URL, and the component returns a JSON response with grade vector, weaknesses, suggested resources and full feedback.  Figure 2: NLP Semantic Grading Pipeline  4.3 Scalability and Security Considerations  •   The model inference runs as a microservice on AWS EC2 with auto-scaling turned on so it can handle the spike in submissions around deadlines.  •   The Knowledge Graph sits on a dedicated Neo4j server with read-replicas to keep query times fast.  •   All communication between services goes over HTTPS/TLS.  •   Student reports are anonymized before processing and deleted from the pipeline once feedback has been generated nothing personally identifiable stays in the system.  •   Access is controlled by role students only see their own feedback, while supervisors see group and cohort-level data.

21 | P a g e  Figure 3: Adaptive Mentorship and Feedback Generation Workflow

22 | P a g e  5. USER REQUIREMENTS  5.1 Stakeholder Identification  •   Students are the main users   —   they submit their reports and receive the automated feedback and resource recommendations.  •   Supervisors review the AI-generated grades, check the feedback quality, and access class-level analytics to see patterns across their groups.  •   The IPMS system administrator manages rubric settings, keeps the knowledge graph updated, and monitors system health.  5.2 Functional Requirements  FR#   Requirement Name  Description  FR1   Report Submission   The system shall accept student research reports in PDF and DOCX formats through IPMS.  FR2   Automated Section Grading  The system should be able to use NLP analysis to evaluate every section in a report such as (Introduction, Lit. Review, Methodology, etc.) based on a given rubric.  FR3   Rubric Compliance Scoring  The system must assign a score and a compliance category (Excellent/Good/Adequate/Poor) per rubric criterion for each report section.  FR4   Weakness Identification  The system shall determine those sections of the report and  topics for which the student’s score is below a certain  benchmark.  FR5   Concept Mapping   The system must map detected vulnerabilities to nodes in the IT Research Knowledge Graph.  FR6   Resource Recommendation  The system must return a ranked list of at least three academic resources per weakness concept identified in the Analysis Step. 4 |   P a g e  ABSTRACT  Abstract Title:   Privacy-Preserving Audio-Based   Stranger Threat   Detection   for   Child Wearables using Context and On-Device Learning  Children are increasingly outfitted with wearable systems that provide location tracking and panic buttons; however solutions are reactionary and reliant heavily upon cloud-based audio processing that can compromise privacy. This pitch outlines a privacy-preserving audio-based stranger threat detection feature for the child wearable. Two light-weight models run fully off the watch. A Global Danger Sound Model detects acoustic distress events (e.g., screams, crying, threatening speech) by a compressed MobileNet-like convolutional network. A Personal “Circle of Trust” Model authenticates speakers for a determination of whether speech emanates from pre-registered trusted caregivers through on-device voice embeddings (Resemblyzer). Outputs from each model are fed into context (geofence status and distance from a connected parent device through Bluetooth Low Energy) and compute a risk score that triggers an alarm only when the score exceeds a threshold for a dwell time. All audio is stored locally; only a tiny number of metadata (event label, time and rough location) is uploaded to Guardians. An on-device adaptation component clusters repeating unknown speakers and adjusts thresholds to the usual play environment of the youngster. The work will: (i) collect and prepare a balanced dataset of the ensuing classes: a/distress, b/angry speech and c/benign; (ii) design and compress danger and trust models that meet latency (<<50 ms/frame) and power (<<10 % per-day battery) budget; (iii) define performance in laboratory and field trials aiming at >90 % recall and <5 % false alarm rate; and (iv) provide a prototype app for Wear OS. The feasibility of proactive, contextual threat detection at resource-limited wearables without sacrificing user privacy will be demonstrated in the results.  Key Terms:   audio-based threat detection, speaker verification, wearable neural networks, privacy safeguarding, wearable-aware contexts

8 |   P a g e  INTRODUCTION  1.1.   Background & Literature Survey  Stranger danger protection for children is a growing need as children are granted increasing mobility by their parents. Most commercial wearable for children has GPS location, geofencing, and simple SOS buttons but require the child to summon aid personally. Some research prototypes have explored automatic detection of distress from audio cues; many of those systems, though, transmit streamed audio to cloud servers for heavy computation that raises concerns about latency, cost, and privacy [1]. To offset, mobile and wearable design has shifted toward computation on device. An efficient encoder on the wearable device compacts raw input into latent codes at a much lower off-device transmission of data, a notable gain in latency, and preserving privacy [1]. Acoustic event detection has also been researched. YAMNet is a compact model for audio classification that is built off of the model of MobileNet V1, and it incorporates depth wise separable convolutions, allowing it to be very efficient for deployment in handhelds [2]. In speaker verification, there is a simple yet very effective way of obtaining high level voice embeddings through the Resemblyzer library; it makes it very easy for programmers to modify speech regions into vectors in a matter of a few statements [3]. They are typically 256 dimensions [3] and can be compared by cosine similarity. A few open datasets support exploration into the detection of distress and identification of emotion. Audio Signal for Danger Detection of Children and Women has a total of three classes (child danger, woman danger, and normal environment) and has 19,375 one-second audio segments [4], and is a seed set for positive examples for distress. Environmental sounds datasets such as UrbanSound8K (8,732 segments in 10 urban classes of sounds like children playing, siren, and car horn) [5], and ESC-50 (2,000 segments evenly dividing into 50 classes that encompass animal, natural, and household sounds) [6], provide negatives from the environment. To obtain raised-voice surrogates for threatening or anger speech, we borrow from the CREMA- D dataset that has a total of 7,442 segments from 91 performers that represent a variety of emotional states [7], and also from the RAVDESS corpus, a well-experimented multimodal corpus that has a total of 7,356 recordings for which 24 professional actors read sentences in a

9 |   P a g e  total of eight emotional states [8]. To attain complete multi-label diversity for sounds, FSD50K provides more than 51,000 audio segments that are labeled for a total of 200 classes [9]. Datasets such as SAVEE and TESS also provide some useful training data. Surrey Audio-Visual Expressed Emotion (SAVEE) contains 480 phonetically balanced British English speech utterances by four male speakers reproducing seven emotional states; we comment that based on the TensorFlow dataset description, only audio is utilized and the learning, validation, and testing splits are samples from speakers other than those in the learning and validation splits [10]. The Toronto Emotional Speech Set (TESS) contains 200 target words spoken by two actresses (26 and 64 years old) in seven emotional states (anger, disgust, fear, happiness, pleasant surprise, sadness, and neutral), yielding a total of 2,800 stimuli [11]. These datasets, complemented by some watch microphone datasets collected with permission for a balanced repertoire of distress, anger speech, and common sounds needed for learning models that are not sensitive to this kind of variability. Recent works of environmental sound classification and emotion recognition provide background for our approach. A systematic report about urban sound classification declares that CNNs and DenseNet-based deep learning architectures achieve very high accuracies (97.98%– 99.22%) in UrbanSound8K and ESC-50 datasets, while their models have yet not been validated in real-world deployments [12]. A work that applies the RAVDESS dataset applies log-Mel spectrograms and MFCCs and CNN and LSTM architectures; the networks receive the aggregated (positive, negative, and neutral) sentiments and the network consists of eight convolutional layers [13]. These works indicate the potential of deep learning for our chosen datasets and yet don't appraise privacy-preserving, on-device inference or context-aware fusing, thus highlighting the novelty of the component we propose.

10 |   P a g e  1.2.   Research Gap  Existing child safety wearables focus on location tracking and manual SOS activation. They lack proactive detection of acoustic distress and do not personalize alerts to the child’s trusted caregivers. Many cloud-based audio monitoring solutions upload raw audio, posing privacy risks and introducing latency and connectivity dependencies [1]. Furthermore, children’s play naturally involves shouting and laughter; therefore, a naive screaming detector would generate frequent false alarms. No commercial product currently combines distress detection, speaker verification, contextual information, and on-device learning into a single wearable component. The research gap lies in designing a tiny dual-model pipeline that runs entirely on the watch, adapts to the child’s normal environment, utilizes context cues to reduce false positives, and preserves privacy by keeping raw audio on the device.
